Chapters trace migrations: southern limits of winter range, spring movement in the Churchill and Nueltin Lake regions, a summer interlude, fall migration and retrograde autumn movement. Ecology sections cover habitats, trails, weather, food, insects, relations to people, bears, foxes, wolves, birds of prey, flies, parasites, and reindeer. Harper's study remains a classic of northern wildlife research.
33833-glories-of-spain:
Charles W. Wood wrote this travel book on Spain, published in London and New York in 1901 with eighty-five pictures. The journey starts at Calais, crosses France by way of Paris and the Garonne, and then turns to Spanish towns, cathedrals, and inns. Wood lingers over Zaragoza Cathedral, whose interior fronts the book.

Chapters mix road scenes, hotel talk, and notes on art, faith, and local custom. Wood writes as a leisurely English traveler, keen to praise beauty and to note odd characters met on the way. The book gives a rich, old-world picture of Spain before modern travel changed it.
33964-the-man-who-rose-again:
Joseph Hocking wrote this novel, printed at Cincinnati in 1907 with four color pictures. Hocking says its central idea came from a real incident told him by C. Hagberg Wright of the London Library. A cynic's challenge is accepted, a man and a woman meet, and a double personality tightens its chain through Leicester's wooing.

Later chapters follow Olive's life in Devonshire, a man with a fez, Signor Ricordo, and the coming of Winfield, toward revelations and a chapter called God and the Man. Hocking writes of fall and rising again. The novel offers a moral romance of a man remade.
34108-the-sacred-egoism-of-sinn-fe-in:
Gnathaí Gan Iarraidh wrote this Irish political tract, published in Dublin and London in 1918 by Maunsel and Company, as passed by the censor. The opening chapter, The Cult of Altruism, argues that in an age of sacred egoisms and oppressed nationalities, small nations became distressed heroines whose rescue inspired professions of altruism.

The author notes that presses of the Latin and Anglo-Saxon worlds poured out sentiment on subject races, though before August 1914 small nations were glad to escape notice. The tract defends a nation's right to its own interest. It remains a sharp document of Irish nationalist thought in wartime.
34193-the-true-benjamin-franklin:
The True Benjamin Franklin, by Sydney George Fisher, reached a fifth edition with an appendix at Philadelphia in 1903, from an 1898 copyright. Fisher wrote on colonial manners and the making of Pennsylvania. A Duplessis portrait of Franklin, painted from life in Paris in 1778, fronts the book and is called the best likeness of him.

Chapters treat Franklin's build and face, schooling, religion and morals, business and writing, and science. Later parts cover his Pennsylvania politics, failure in England, and embassy to France with its pleasures and scandals. A motto from Charles Francis Adams demands rigid moral study in history. Fisher aims at the real man behind the myth, kite, and almanac wit.
34208-the-law-of-hemlock-mountain:
Hugh Lundsford's 1920 novel The Law of Hemlock Mountain opens among army officers at cards, then moves to a mountain land where written law runs weak. Lieutenant Spurrier, the young officer at its centre, must live among folk who settle wrongs by their own code.

Spurrier shares a roof with Sam Mosebury, a man the law could not hang, and guards his conduct toward a mountain girl with no road out of her world. The tale weighs formal justice against mountain custom, and asks what law means where the court sits far away. The frontispiece shows Spurrier owning that he took pets for wild birds.
34300-leonardo-da-vinci-a-psychosexual-s:
Leonardo da Vinci: A Psychosexual Study of an Infantile Reminiscence, by Sigmund Freud of the University of Vienna, appeared in English in 1916 in Brill's translation. Freud applies psychoanalysis to the most universal genius of the Renaissance, asking how the artist and the naturalist in Leonardo warred within one mind. Illustrations reproduce the Mona Lisa, Saint Anne, and John the Baptist.

The study turns on a childhood memory Leonardo recorded, involving a bird, and reads his art and his unfinished projects through it. Freud notes that Leonardo reproached himself on his deathbed, in Vasari's account, for failing his art, and he traces that guilt to early life. Famous and contested, the essay founded the genre of psychoanalytic biography.
3463-the-boys-life-of-mark-twain:
Albert Bigelow Paine writes a life of Mark Twain meant for young readers, drawn from his larger biography of the author. The chapters follow Samuel Clemens from his Missouri family and his uncle's farm through school, his apprenticeship in print, and his years learning the Mississippi River as a pilot. Later chapters cover the wreck of the Pennsylvania, the end of piloting, and his turn to soldiering and the frontier.

Paine keeps the story brisk and full of incident, from Tom Sawyer's band of boys to Twain at seventy, honored by Missouri. The book gives boys and girls a true account of how a river boy became America's most famous humorist. Older readers will also enjoy it as a clear, short life of Twain.
34730-charles-darwin:
Grant Allen wrote a life of Charles Darwin for the English Worthies series, edited by Andrew Lang and printed at London in 1885. My obligations to Professor Huxley, to Herbert Spencer, to Professor Sachs, to Hermann Muller, and to Darwin himself will be obvious to all instructed readers, Allen begins. It would be absurd to overload so small and popularly written a book with references, he owns.

Three persons get special thanks. From Woodall's admirable paper on Darwin he took much on the hero's ancestry and early days. From Samuel Butler, author of Evolution Old and New, he derived many pregnant suggestions on Buffon, Erasmus Darwin, and the early evolutionists. Such a life, never before written down in full, must probably hold many errors of detail, he warns. Allen tells Darwin's story plainly for common readers, three years after his death.
34745-comrade-kropotkin:
Comrade Kropotkin is a biography of the anarchist prince by Victor Robinson. The Altrurians published it in New York in 1908. It belongs to a series called Lives of Great Altrurians. The book is pointedly not copyrighted. A portrait of Kropotkin forms the frontispiece.

The contents trace a dramatic life. Chapters cover serfdom and explorations. The nihilists and the terrorists follow. One chapter treats Sophia Perovskaya, the regicide. Another treats the fortress of Peter and Paul. Robinson dedicated the book to George Kennan, the traveller on Siberia. He calls his own pages bitter and bloody. The opening scene quotes a newspaper notice selling serfs and pianos together.
34795-the-golden-triangle-the-return-of-:
Maurice Le Blanc brings back his gentleman thief in The Golden Triangle, the return of Arsene Lupin, printed in New York with copyright in 1917. The Macaulay Company made the book. Le Blanc had writ The Woman of Mystery and the Confessions of Arsene Lupin. A plate quotes a threat from a scroll: send Coralie up by herself and her life shall be saved.

Nineteen chapters run from Coralie to a blaze of light. Right hand and left leg, the rusty key, and before the flames open the case. Husband and wife and Essares Bey's work drive the mid run. The red cord, on the brink, and in the abyss raise the peril. Chapter one opens at dusk in Paris. Two soldiers reached a little space of trees opposite a museum: one had lost his right leg, the other his left arm.
34864-the-boys-of-old-monmouth-a-story-o:
The Boys of Old Monmouth is a story of Washington's campaign in New Jersey in 1778 by Everett Tomlinson, printed at Boston and New York with copyright in 1898. Tomlinson also wrote Washington's Young Aids and Guarding the Border. Thirty-two chapters carry the tale to the battle itself.

Old Monmouth, the first chapter says, is an expression dear to every native-born Jerseyman. The visitor sees pines, shore, and fertile farmland, but never speaks the name with the same love. Chapters follow Tom through meetings on the river, a visit to Refugee Town, and time with the redcoats. A soldier woman and Indian John cross the path. The great fight of Monmouth closes the boys' service in the campaign.
34875-spain:
Spain is a land book by Wentworth Webster, a church man of Oxford. A Sampson Low house of London brought it out in eighteen eighty two. One part is by a mate of the School of Mines in its scheme. A front word owns the hard task of writ on this land in plain terms. State counts in Spain can not be took as trust, that word warns at once.

Ease, sloth, and bent fraud mar its tax and trade counts in that word. Cheat trade on a vast scale warps each count more in its claim. Shire gaps foil broad claims: one shire truth is next shire false there. Five Irelands is the tag that word gives those split realm parts. Castile and south types hog most past books and slight the rest.
34928-the-ranch-girls-at-home-again:
The Ranch Girls at Home Again is a girls' series novel by Margaret Vandercook, part of the Ranch Girls books. The front matter lists the run of the set: the girls at Rainbow Lodge, their pot of gold, boarding school, a trip to Europe, and later adventures. Vandercook also wrote the Camp Fire Girls series.

The chapter heads promise the tone. One declares that courage makes the man, another holds a midnight conference, and a third poses a dilemma and a visitor. Two conversations fill a long chapter of their own. The action returns the ranch girls to Rainbow Lodge and its circle. As with the sister series on the Camp Fire Girls, the book trades in friendship, pluck, and outdoor life for its young readers. The 1915 printing places it in the full flow of American series fiction.
35022-the-diamond-pin:
Carolyn Wells wrote The Diamond Pin, a Fleming Stone detective tale printed in nineteen nineteen, with a colour front plate by Gayle Hoskins. Stone is billed in the front pages as the great American detective, famed for unravelling hard cases. The tale opens with a sharp talk in the Clyde house. Ursula Pell scolds her niece Iris for a wish to act on the stage.

Iris smiles, says the scheme was her own, and takes a one cent coin for the church plate from her aunt. Chapter heads promise a locked room, the proof of a checkbook, and a case built against Bannard. Stone comes late to the case, with his aide Fibsy, and a cipher and a fresh kidnapping fill the last parts. The close is billed as a solution at last.
35272-a-catalogue-of-books-in-english-la:
A Catalogue of Books in English Later than 1700, Volume One, lists part of the library of Robert Hoe of New York, printed in private in 1905 in one hundred copies. Carolyn Shipman compiled the list. Three copies were printed on Imperial Japanese vellum. The University Press at Cambridge did the printing.

Entries keep the spelling and marks of each title page as first printed. Large spaces stand for marks in some entries, a note warns. The first entry is Jaques Abbadie on chemical change in the Eucharist. That book came in four letters on faith and sense, from the French. Each entry gives place, seller, date, size, and binding in brief code. The list serves book men who study rare English books and their forms.
35273-a-catalogue-of-books-in-english-la:
A Catalogue of Books in English Later Than 1700 is the catalogue of part of the library of Robert Hoe of New York. This text is volume two, printed in 1905. Only one hundred copies were made, three of them on imperial Japanese vellum. The University Press at Cambridge printed the edition.

Hoe was a great American book collector, and his library held fine copies of English literature after 1700. Each entry copies the spelling and punctuation of its title page. The transcriber's note stresses that no corrections have been made to the entries. The catalogue remains a record of a famous private library before its dispersal at auction.
35274-a-catalogue-of-books-in-english-la:
A Catalogue of Books in English Later Than 1700 is the catalogue of part of the library of Robert Hoe of New York. This text is volume three, printed in 1905. Only one hundred copies were made, three of them on imperial Japanese vellum. The University Press at Cambridge printed the edition. Hoe's bookplate fronts the volume.

Each entry copies the spelling and punctuation of its title page, with no corrections made. The entries record the fine copies of English literature that Hoe gathered, the greatest private library in America of its day. After his death the sale of the library set records. The catalogue remains its permanent record.
35308-the-cape-and-the-kaffirs-a-diary-o:
Harriet Ward spent five years in South Africa and set down her life there in a diary style book, reshaped for this 1851 London form. Much of it first ran as Five Years in Kaffirland and went through two print runs. Ward made this shorter, cheaper form for Britons who thought of moving to the Cape or Natal.

Early parts map the Cape Colony, British Kaffraria, and Natal, and tell who held each tract of land. Ward writes from her own time on the ground, praising the work of Sir Harry Smith yet noting fresh war clouds. Notes on Natal rest on state reports, since she had not seen that district herself.
35310-the-childrens-story-of-the-war-vol:
The Children Story of the War, volume one of ten, was edited by Sir Edward Parrott. Verse by Kipling stands at the front of the volume by kind permission. Once more we hear the word that sickened earth of old, that poem begins. No law except the sword unsheathed and uncontrolled, it goes on in stern lines.

A plate shows how the Boy Scouts helped at the start of the war. The war found the scouts true to their motto, be prepared, the caption says. In London alone 25000 scouts were organized for service, that caption reports in pride. The story runs from the beginning of the Great War for young readers at home. Battles, heroes, and home front duty fill the ten volumes of the set.
35508-benjamin-franklin:
Frank Luther Mott and Chester Jorgenson gathered a volume of Benjamin Franklin's writings for a series of American authors. Harry Hayden Clark of Wisconsin directed the set. Each volume gives chosen pieces with a scholar's account of the man. The list of the series runs wide, from Bryant and Cooper to Emerson and Hawthorne.

Franklin's papers are the heart of the book. A long opening treats his life and work in seven parts. The pieces themselves follow, with notes set under each. A picture text of Poor Richard's Almanack is given whole, from the old sheets. Spelling quirks of the first printings are kept as they stand. The aim is a sound school and college text: enough of Franklin to know him, in his own words, with the learning kept at hand and out of the way.
35661-mysterious-mr-sabin:
Mysterious Mr Sabin is a spy novel by E. Phillips Oppenheim, copyright 1905, set among London supper parties and foreign embassies. A charming stranger named Sabin moves through high society with a plan no one can quite see, while young Wolfenden falls in love and Felix warns and schemes at the edges.

Fifty two chapters run from a supper at the Milan to a harbour tragedy, with a war storm gathering over Europe. Cards, coded meetings, and a great stake drive the plot. Oppenheim helped invent the modern thriller, and this early book shows his gift for glamour, pace, and plots within plots.
35712-wake-robin:
Wake Robin is a nature book by John Burroughs, shown here in a second edition issued at New York in 1877. The edition is corrected, enlarged, and illustrated, the title page says. Copyright entries reach back to 1871 and forward to 1876. A publishers' note explains what the second edition adds to the first. A chapter on the bluebird is new.

The text was also enlarged and corrected here and there throughout, the note adds. Its illustrations come from a history of North American birds by three named naturalists, lent by a professor. The wake robin of the title is a spring flower, and the book takes its name from the season of first birds and blooms. Burroughs built his name on such close, plain watching of the woods and fields near home.
36147-george-gemu-nder-s-progress-in-vio:
George Gemunder's Progress in Violin Making is a trade memoir printed at Astoria in 1881. Gemunder published it himself. Its subtitle promises facts about the art and its critics. A biography of the maker opens the book. He was born at Ingelfingen in Germany in 1816. His father made bow instruments before him. The boy's fine handwriting once marked him for teaching. He followed that plan for only three weeks.

His gift for the bench won out over the schoolroom. After his father's death he worked abroad. Pesth, Pressburg, Vienna, and Munich employed him in turn. Offers of commonplace business could not hold him. He crossed to America and built fine violins there. Makers of his rank signed their work like artists. The book is partly a record, partly a defence. Critics of his art are answered in its pages.
36261-the-chain-of-life-in-geological-ti:
The Chain of Life in Geological Time, a Sketch of the Origin and Succession of Animals and Plants, is Sir J William Dawson's survey of the fossil record. The Religious Tract Society of London published this third and revised edition in 1888, with numerous illustrations. A frontispiece shows life in the Silurian age. Dawson had written Acadian Geology and The Story of the Earth before it.

Dawson's preface states his position at once. The facts of geology give sure means of reaching certain conclusions about the history of life on earth. Yet those same facts, he warns, have furnished material for hypotheses confidently called indisputable that have no real foundation in nature. Some of those hypotheses, he holds, strike indirectly at the most sacred beliefs of mankind. The book reads the rocks with a scientist's rigor and a churchman's care.
36399-missing-friends-being-the-adventur:
Missing Friends tells the adventures of a Danish emigrant, issued in the Adventure Series at five shillings. A swagsman stands as frontispiece. Adventures are to the adventurous, Beaconsfield's motto heads the book. I was born in Copenhagen in the year 1850, the narrator begins. My father was a builder there in fairly good circumstances.

I was the second son of a large family, he says. It was my parents' great ambition that we all should rise. The tale follows the young Dane out to the Australian bush, where a swagman's life meant walking vast tracks with his pack, seeking work and missing friends. Emigrant memoirs of this kind taught stay at home readers what the colonies cost and gave. Hunger, mateship, and strange country fill the road.
36412-ten-years-near-the-german-frontier:
Maurice Francis Egan wrote Ten Years Near the German Frontier, a retrospect and a warning, in 1918. Egan had been the United States minister to Denmark, and Hodder and Stoughton sold the book. One chapter starts with the torn scrap of paper that began the war. Others name the threat from the neighbour to the south and weigh the Kaiser and the King of England side by side.

Later parts trace German plans in Sweden and Norway and German church work as a tool of state. Egan also tells how talks began for the sale of the Danish Antilles to the United States. The last part runs from the start of 1917 to the end of his post. The book warns free lands what life near a hard empire can teach.
36426-the-motor-girls-at-camp-surprise-o:
Margaret Penrose wrote a girls adventure tale about young women who drive their own motor cars. Cora Kimball drives at the start, with Bess Robinson at her side. The girls head out for a camp called Camp Surprise. A lost trail and two strange men give the trip an early edge of risk.

At camp the girls face a storm, a night ride, and odd noises in the dark. A cave in the mountain holds a secret passage and more than one surprise. The girls are tied up, lost, and held as prisoners at points in the tale. Friends ride to the rescue, and the last chapter sets all things right at last.
365-the-land-of-little-rain:
Mary Austin sketches the dry country of eastern California in this set of linked essays. She names the land by its scant rain, then walks its water trails, mesas, and small towns. The Ceriso desert, Shoshone land, Jimville, and the grape-vine town all take their turn in her pages.

Austin watches pocket hunters, basket makers, scavengers, and neighbors with a poet's eye and a neighbor's ear. She gives places Indian names where they fit better than map names. The book endures as a loving, close portrait of desert life, where water rules all and small things matter most.
36614-the-child-who-died-and-lived-again:
The Child Who Died and Lived Again is a tract tale for the young. Its author also wrote a famed first book of faith for small children. The tract is number twenty three in its set list for home use. The book came out in London in the year eighteen forty eight.

Plain talk first tells what death is: breath gone, cheek pale, frame cold. The soul, it says, does not die, though the frame turns to dust. One man in the tale of Christ raised the dead in past days. That frame tale then leads to a child brought back to life by grace. The small book aims to calm fear of death in young hearts.
36627-how-the-bible-was-invented-a-lectu:
How the Bible Was Invented is a lecture by M M Mangasarian, given before the Independent Religious Society at Orchestra Hall, Chicago, on Sunday at eleven in the morning. The print stands in a tenth edition. Its motto is that not to undeceive is to deceive.

Mangasarian opens by saying many good people believe the Bible was given by inspiration of God. The wording of his subject suggests it is the work of men, and not always of honest men either. On the contrary, he is exposing himself to criticism by telling these good people the truth about the Bible. He grants his love and reverence for whatever is sweet and sane in the Gospels. Yet he protests against one text as a suggestion to violence. Freethought fans get a Rationalist lecture in full.
36698-history-of-the-discovery-of-the-no:
Butterfield wrote a history dated 1881 of the find of the Northwest by John Nicolet in 1634, with a sketch of his life. Nicolet was the first white man to set foot in the lands now held by five states of the west. He found a fresh water sea, Lake Michigan, past Lake Huron, and met tribes no white ear had heard of.

Bold past care, Nicolet sought a near sea road to China and Japan past the great lakes. Chief proof comes from the Jesuit Relations, writ close to the time and held sound on fact. Butterfield weighs late tales and fresh search next to those first French church reports.
36842-the-issue-the-case-for-sinn-fein:
Lector wrote a pamphlet making the case for Sinn Fein, priced at twopence. The New Ireland Publishing Company issued it at Dublin in 1918. The piece is marked as passed by the censor on its title page. It stands as Number Three in the New Ireland Pamphlets set.

The writer holds that one question rules all: does Ireland wish to be free? Small grants and fine talk at Westminster count for nothing, the piece argues. John Dillon is scolded for turning from a free Ireland he once praised. Parnell's words at Cincinnati in 1880 are called as proof of the old creed.
36999-the-land-of-lure-a-story-of-the-co:
The Land of Lure, a story of the Columbia river basin by Elliott Smith, appeared in 1920. A Tacoma press printed it in Washington state in that year. Smith also wrote The Bells of the Bosque and Hull 97, the title page lists. He dedicates the book to Marie Smith, his wife, in warm lines.

He was one of those who tried, failed, and went away to forget, he writes there. Her unfaltering faithfulness made it possible for him to see and feel these things. Misshapen and dwarfed by desert sun, a plate caption describes the dry country. Chapters run past eleven in the index of the homestead tale. Dry land farming hope and hardship in the inland Northwest fill the story.
37214-the-adventures-of-seumas-beg-the-r:
James Stephens published these two books of verse with Macmillan in 1915, by the author of The Crock of Gold. The first, The Adventures of Seumas Beg, is written from a child's eye; the second, The Rocky Road to Dublin, walks the city street by street.

Seumas Beg opens with a summons to rise and play beneath the cherry bush, then breakfast time, where the child wonders who wakes the sun and decides it must be mother. A giant peers over the orchard wall, twice as fat as the apple tree. The Dublin poems name Grafton Street, Portobello Bridge, College Green, O'Connell Bridge, and Stephen's Green, with the Dodder bank and Donnybrook at the end. Poetry readers get Stephens's two small masterpieces in one volume.
37223-the-moors-in-spain:
The Moors in Spain is a history by Stanley Lane-Poole in the Story of the Nations set. Arthur Gilman, a writer on Rome and the Saracens, helped with the work. Putnam's Sons in New York and Fisher Unwin in London shared the book. The rights date from 1886, and this copy came out in 1903. Its preface sets Moorish Spain against a sadder later Spain.

Tarik the Moor took the land of the Visigoths some twelve hundred years back. For near eight hundred years Spain led Europe in learning under Muslim rule. Rich farms, watered by skilled hands, bore fruit a hundredfold, he writes. Cities rose in the valleys of the Guadalquivir and the Guadiana. Students came from France, Germany, and England to drink at that spring. Doctors, weavers, and builders of Andalusia stood first in their crafts.
3744-the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-dais:
Charlotte Yonge continues her Daisy Chain family chronicle in this long sequel, subtitled The Trial. The May family gathers at Cocksmoor and at home, where Richard, the young incumbent, tends a parish shadowed by scarlatina and bad drains. Letters from Edinburgh, family jokes about an infants' honeymoon, and the knell for a dead child mix the comic and the sorrowful in Yonge's usual way.

Later chapters follow orphaned girls Minna and Ella as a year of growth parts them, one learning to comfort and the other still fleeing pain. Yonge writes for readers who know the Mays already, though newcomers can still follow the parish round. The book rewards patience, with church life, family duty, and quiet heroism taking the place of grand adventure.
37599-the-legend-of-the-glorious-adventu:
The Legend of the Glorious Adventures of Tyl Ulenspiegel retells Charles De Coster's Flemish epic. Geoffrey Whitworth translated it from the French. The illustrations list scenes from Damme to the death of Betkin. Lamme and Ulenspiegel at the Minne-Water fronts the book. The first book of the legend opens at Damme in Flanders, when the May hawthorn flowered.

Ulenspiegel is born there, the son of Claes. Katheline the midwife examines the infant's head. A caul hangs from it: born under a lucky star, she cries. Then she finds a small black mole on his shoulder. It is, she wails, the black finger-print of the devil. Claes jokes that Satan rose early to mark his son. At dawn Claes holds the baby to the rising sun. Be sincere as that brightness, Claes tells him, and virtuous as that warmth.
38378-the-christian-sabbath-is-it-of-div:
The Christian Sabbath is a freethought pamphlet by Remsburg asking whether the Sunday Sabbath is of divine origin. His answer is given at once, in the negative. The author proposes to show that Sunday has no divine warrant. No more holiness, he argues, belongs to it than to any other day.

His case runs on several heads, each announced in turn. The claim that Sunday replaced the Jewish Sabbath by God's command is false, he says. The day began, on his showing, as a heathen holiday of the sun. He calls the institution a fraud imposed by a tyrannical priesthood. His witnesses, he stresses, are friends of Christianity, not its enemies. Paul, the church fathers, and the reformers head that list.
38495-the-memoirs-of-charles-lewis-baron:
The Memoirs of Charles Lewis, Baron de Pollnitz, volume one, in a second edition with additions, was printed for Daniel Browne in London in 1739. The title page describes the contents: observations made in his late travels from Prussia through Germany, Italy, France, Flanders, Holland, and England, in letters to his friend.

The letters promise two kinds of matter. They discover the present state of the chief cities and towns, and they give the characters of the principal persons at the several courts. A dedication offers the translation to Lord Hardwicke, lord high chancellor of Great Britain. The translator was encouraged by the good reception the memoirs met abroad, and by the favour the author obtained at a chief Protestant court. Twenty seven letters fill this volume, followed by an index. Prefaces by translator, author, and editor stand at the front, with addenda to both volumes.
38530-legends-romances-of-spain:
Legends and Romances of Spain is a survey by Lewis Spence, issued at London in June 1920. Spence had written kindred books on Brittany and the Rhine, and a dictionary of medieval romance. The contents open with the sources of Spanish romance. The songs of deeds and the poem of the Cid fill the second chapter at length.

Amadis of Gaul, the great romance of chivalry, takes the third chapter, and its sequels the fourth. The Palmerin romances and the romances of Catalonia follow. Roderic, last of the Goths, and Moorish ballad heroes fill the middle heads. Two chapters treat the ballad collections themselves. Moorish romances, tales of Spanish magic, and humorous romances close the list, with a bibliography at the end. Spence maps the whole story hoard of old Spain for English readers.
38795-with-drake-on-the-spanish-main:
With Drake on the Spanish Main, by Herbert Strang, is a sea adventure tale. Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton issued it at London in 1908. Colour plates by Archibald Webb and maps of Drake routes fill the book. A storm beach at daybreak opens chapter one, Jetsam, in Darien.

Waves hurl seaweed, logs, and a lone human form onto the sand. Chapters promise a wreck, salvage, the Spanish whip, and maroon allies in turn. Fort Aguila falls, mule trains are chased, and Drake camp is reached. Half pikes and machetes, a long chase, and a cliff fight fill the middle. Skeleton Cave leaguer and Maiden Isle close the twenty five chapters.
39112-the-blessed-hope-a-sermon-on-the-d:
The Blessed Hope is a funeral sermon by the Reverend E Hoare, incumbent of Trinity Church, Tunbridge Wells, printed by John Colbran of that town in 1855. Hoare preached the substance of it at St Peter's, Lowestoft, on Sunday the nineteenth of August 1855. The occasion was the death of Mrs Francis Cunningham, the beloved wife of the parish's beloved vicar.

Mrs Cunningham had labored forty years in the parishes of Pakefield, Kirkly, and Lowestoft. Hoare praises her unwearied watchfulness over the young, her care for their parents, her missionary zeal, and her tender sympathy for the afflicted. She fell asleep on the twelfth of August after a gradual decay of voice and strength. Such printed sermons were the age's monuments to local saints, sold to a whole congregation.
39246-heroic-spain:
Boyle O'Reilly wrote Heroic Spain, for Duffield at New York in 1910. A Spanish hidalgo by El Greco fronts the travel book. Contents open with practical hints for the road in Spain. Verses called Espana la Heroica follow the introduction. The Basque country and Loyola, the shrine town, come first on the route.

Burgos and the Cid, Valladolid, and Oviedo in the Asturias follow. The sleeping cities of Leon, Galicia, and Salamanca take their chapters. Segovia, Saint Teresa and Avila, and Madrid with the Escorial come next. Toledo, Cordova and Granada, and vignettes of Seville fill the south. Holy Week in Seville and Cadiz close the Andalusian leg. A chapter on a few modern novels stands near the end. O'Reilly gives Spain as a land of heroes, saints, and old proud towns.
39321-old-flies-in-new-dresses-how-to-dr:
Old Flies in New Dresses, by Charles Edward Walker, teaches how to dress dry flies with the wings in the natural pose. Lawrence and Bullen printed the book in London in 1898. Walker drew many of the plates himself, with help from Edward Wilson.

The first plate shows fifteen natural flies and kindred creatures, each named in Latin and English. The alder-fly, the caperer, and the red sedge lead the set. Part one treats dry flies, starting with colour perception in fish. Chapters then work through the alder, the caddis flies, the stoneflies, and the two-winged flies. Winged ants and caterpillars close the dry half. Part two turns to wet flies, with a theory, the water boatmen, and the fresh-water shrimp. The aim is likeness to the living insect on the water.
39602-the-industrial-arts-in-spain:
Industrial Arts in Spain is a museum art handbook by Juan Riano, of the South Kensington series. The volume was prepared under the Committee of Council on Education authority in London. Riano, a Spanish scholar, surveys the applied arts of his own country for English readers. Metalwork, pottery, textiles, and glass of Spain form the ground of the handbook.

South Kensington art handbooks taught artisans and buyers from the museum great stores. Photographs and pictured marks illustrate Spanish craft pieces through the survey of the arts. A cover image in the file shows the book as Spanish Arts in short title. Students of design gained Spain workshops in one compact museum volume.
39760-saddle-and-mocassin:
Saddle and Mocassin is a book of American sporting sketches by Francis Francis Jun. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1887. Francis dedicates it to the memory of his father. The elder Francis Francis wrote A Book on Angling and was an old-fashioned sportsman, sans peur et sans reproche. The sketches were made during various cruises in the States.

Two chapters tour the Yellowstone Park and its geysers. Quail shooting in the Sierras and a glimpse of Sonora follow. The Winchester water meads and Pend d'Oreille Lake supply northern chapters. Six chapters settle in the Animas Valley. A cruise in northern Mexico fills the last six. Francis admits in his preface that the later sketches are composite. His movements were too desultory for bare records. He aimed instead at characteristic studies of local colour, with characters placed where they best belonged.
4014-arse-ne-lupin:
Edgar Jepson and Maurice Leblanc team up for a tale of Arsene Lupin, the gentleman thief, now cast as a duke's rival in love and crime. A letter from Lupin sets the game in motion, while the duke smokes on a terrace and studies the morocco case that holds a pendant.

Sonia, the duke, and Lupin move through drawing rooms and country houses, trading charm, theft, and pursuit. The novel mixes romance with detection, as Lupin steals hearts and jewels with equal ease. Readers who enjoy suave, fast-moving adventure will find a polished entry in the Lupin series.
4017-the-hollow-needle-further-adventure:
Maurice Leblanc's mystery follows the schoolboy detective Isidore Beautrelet as he tracks Arsene Lupin, the gentleman thief, through a puzzle of carts, inns, and a river crossing. No motor car crossed on Thursday the twenty-third of April, and a waiter who came back from training saw a cart that did not cross.

Beautrelet pieces small clues into a bold theory about a secret hiding place, the Hollow Needle, said to hold the treasure of French kings. Lupin stays one step ahead, witty and cool, while the boy reasons his way after him. Readers who like clever, fast-moving detective tales will enjoy this duel of brains.
40210-thomas-paine-the-apostle-of-libert:
Thomas Paine, the Apostle of Liberty is an address by John Remsburg, president of the American Secular Union. He delivered it at Chicago on January 29, 1916, and it was printed in 1917. The title page adds the testimony of five hundred witnesses, gathered in Paine's defence.

Remsburg sets Paine beside Washington and Lincoln as creator, defender, and saviour of the republic. His charge is that Paine, of the three, has met with deep injustice. Church power, he argues, has taught the public to hate the man who did most to free it. The address is a freethinker's plea that Paine be judged by his work, not by slander.
40347-the-coward-behind-the-curtain:
Richard Marsh published this novel with Methuen in London in 1908. Marsh was also the author of 'The Beetle' and many other tales of mystery. The opening chapters send Dorothy off with her guardian, then bring in a curtain, a coward and a man in a chair.

Dorothy is left alone with her guardian for a night, and soon makes her exit by a bold route. A caravan, a shopping trip and the girl's own account to a man follow in the contents. Danger ahead and newspaper headlines promise the tense, theatrical turns Marsh's readers knew well.
40356-cathedral-cities-of-spain:
Collins wrote and drew this 1909 travel book on the cathedral cities of Spain. The route runs from Cadiz, Seville, Cordova and Granada in the south to Barcelona, Toledo, Salamanca and Burgos, with stops at places such as Valencia, Avila, Segovia and Leon. Each city gets a short chapter paired with his water-colour views.

Readers get both the great churches and the streets around them. The plates show markets, bridges, towers, cloisters and views over each town, from the Giralda at Seville to the Alhambra at Granada. The book works as a guided tour for travellers, and as a record of how these cities looked at the time.
40357-four-months-afoot-in-spain:
Four Months Afoot in Spain, by Harry Franck, was first published in 1911. Franck taught languages in New York and had four months free. He walked a thousand miles of Spain and rode twice that by third class rail. The trip cost him 172 dollars, a fact he says readers kept asking about. His foreword offers no wild adventure, only facts and impressions picked up among common folk.

Chapters tramp from Andalusia to the banks of the Guadalquivir. A bullfighter at home gets one chapter. La Mancha, crumbling cities, and the Basque land follow. Roads, roadsters, priests, and the Philips cast long shadows. The book suits walkers who want Spain at ground level, on foot and on the cheap.
40483-these-twain:
These Twain is a novel by Arnold Bennett, copyright nineteen fifteen and issued at New York. Bennett is billed as author of The Old Wives' Tale and Clayhanger. Its contents split into three books, called The Woman in the House, The Past, and Equilibrium. Chapter heads name Hilda on the stairs, an attack and repulse, and a family at home.

The opening chapter surveys the suburb of Bleakridge in eighteen ninety two. Old houses of dull red or yellow stand against new ones of bright red with terra cotta trim. The two sorts ran into each other and mingled but never mixed, the narrator says. Chief among the old stands the house of the local member of parliament, a widower on a mound above the town.
40616-fiends-ghosts-and-sprites-includin:
Fiends, Ghosts, and Sprites is a study of belief in the supernatural by John Netten Radcliffe. Richard Bentley published it in London in 1854. Its full title promises an account of the origin and nature of that belief. Radcliffe opens with a plain claim: the belief has existed in all ages and among all nations. He sets out to trace where it came from and how it changed.

The passions and affections of human nature drive those changes, he argues. He disputes the idea that belief in a supreme power is inborn in man. Knowledge, he holds, comes through the senses and reason, not from innate ideas. Others had argued that self reflection alone leads man to knowledge of a deity. Radcliffe weighs those claims against the facts of how minds learn. Fiends and ghosts are thus treated as products of the human mind.
40708-beast-and-man-in-india-a-popular-s:
Beast and Man in India is a plain sketch of the beasts of that land in their ties with its folk, by Kipling. He was the dad of a more famed pen of that name. Prints fill its form, put out at London and New York in the first years of the last age.

A verse from a bard of America heads the book. I think I could turn and live with beasts, it runs. They are so calm and self held. I stand and look at them long and long. They do not sweat and moan on their state, it goes on. They do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins.
40751-the-old-man-of-the-mountain:
Herbert Strang wrote The Old Man of the Mountain, first printed in 1916. Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton published it at London. Cyrus Cuneo painted the colour frontispiece, and Rene Bull drew the black-and-white plates. The frontispiece shows a man crying stop with his hands raised. The chapters open out of the night, with a council of war. Refugees and more mystery follow.

The Eye gives the middle chapters their law: the iron shutter, the law of the Eye, and the monster on the wall. The underworld, alchemy, and a dry bone come next. The moles, a hole in the wall, and a carnivore raise the pace. A fight in the pagoda and the bursting of bonds lead to doom. The Nagas point at the old man in the plates, crying the Eye.
40776-poor-folk-in-spain:
Poor Folk in Spain is a book of trips by Jan and Cora Gordon. Their own hands made its plates. It was first put out in nineteen twenty two at London. The same hand's past book on the art men of France is named at the front. A book of dame and child, with draw work by a named hand, stands there as well. The front plate shows a yard of Spain.

The list of parts is a walk through that land. London heads the book, as the start of the trip. A man of the land, the edge of the realm, and two old towns come next. The chief town, a hot night, and a south town in three parts fill the first run.
41040-some-account-of-gothic-architectur:
George Edmund Street, an architect, wrote a full account of Gothic building in Spain, in a second edition from John Murray in 1869. He gave the book to Gladstone. The frontispiece shows the Portico de la Gloria of Santiago Cathedral. In his preface Street owns that a working artist has scant spare time for such a task.

His plea is that study of old work in all lands is a duty owed to the art itself. Only by tracing Gothic work across Europe, he says, can men judge the force that raised such wonders in four centuries. Street loved the old buildings of England all the more for his trips abroad. He wrote in an age of revival, when new churches rose in the old style. His aim was to teach builders to learn from the great men of the past by patient, loving study.
41055-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, is represented here by a transcribed slice of one volume. The slice covers articles in the J range of the alphabet, as its title states. Transcriber notes at the head explain the marks used for subscripts, superscripts, and Greek letters in the text. Side notes have been moved to stand as titles of their paragraphs.

Corrections listed in the notes show the care taken with the text. A note on the article Jewelry fixes a spelling and gives sources for the jewels of Queen Aah hotep in Egypt. The sample text in the catalogue speaks of the Jews of Austria and their place at the fairs of the provinces. Readers get both the text of the famed edition and a clear account of how its print signs were rendered for the screen.
41167-military-roads-of-the-mississippi-:
Military Roads of the Mississippi Basin, subtitled The Conquest of the Old Northwest, is volume eight of Archer Butler Hulbert's Historic Highways of America series. The Arthur H. Clark Company of Cleveland published it in 1904, with maps and illustrations. Its frontispiece shows the old Vincennes Trace near Xenia, Illinois.

Four chapters trace the campaigns that won the Northwest for the United States. The first follows the Clark routes through Illinois in the Revolution. The second covers the Miami Valley campaigns, and the third St. Clair's disastrous expedition. The fourth ends with Wayne and the victory at Fallen Timber. The illustrations include Hutchins's sketch of the Wabash from 1768 and Belknap's map of Wayne's route. Hulbert's series treated America's roads and trails as documents of its expansion.
41419-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-132:
Notes and Queries for May eighth, eighteen fifty-two, is number one hundred and thirty-two of volume five. The weekly paper called itself a means of shared talk for literary men, artists, and family historians. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

The lead piece weighs Sir Robert Peel's claims to be recalled by men of letters. Notes treat a passage in Measure for Measure, folk lore, and an old song. Queries ask about the Azores, crown jewels once kept at Holt Castle, and the height of Queen Elizabeth. Short answers close the number, at fourpence a copy.
41464-lords-of-the-world-a-story-of-the-:
Alfred Church wrote this tale of the fall of Carthage and Corinth. Blackie and Son sold his Roman tales in crown octavo cloth. A past Church book, Two Thousand Years Ago, gets strong press praise. The Times called it entertaining and useful with fresh Roman scenes.

The Spectator praised that past tale as entertaining from start to end. The Guardian said no book makes Romans live again so well. Lords of the World tells how Rome broke two great rival cities. Church wrote for young readers who love history in story form.
41528-memoirs-of-a-veteran-who-served-as:
Memoirs of a Veteran was written by Captain Hermann. Byrd printed the book at Atlanta in 1911. Hermann served as a private in the sixties, his title says. The war between the states is his ground. He served, he adds, in three branches of the Confederate army. An introduction explains why an old soldier writes. The young stand at the gates of manhood with shining illusions, he warns. Such hopes are seldom won, and then by chance. If his pages make a reader think before acting, he is content. Chapter one is called A Picture. A glowing recruiting poster hangs in a post office lobby. Soldiers in spotless uniforms promise a life of ease.

His own uniform was the reverse of that picture, Hermann writes. He enlisted in 1861, when homes were invaded, he says.
41593-unexplored-spain:
Unexplored Spain is a book of sport and wild lore by Abel Chapman and Walter Buck. Buck was a vice chief of his land at a town of that realm. Two mint and nine plates by three hands and from light prints stand in it. It was put out at New York and London in nineteen ten. The past books of Chapman are list at the front.

The book is writ past the leave of the king and queen of that land. The king is named there as a fine man of sport in his own right. The front plate shows that king at the spear of a boar. The first parts of the book bear its name with a plain mark: lead in, and lead in once more.
41663-the-fort-dearborn-massacre-written:
Lieutenant Linai T Helm wrote an account of the Fort Dearborn Massacre in eighteen fourteen, here edited by Nelly Kinzie Gordon and issued by Rand McNally and Company in nineteen twelve. Helm was one of the survivors. Gordon gave the book to her native city Chicago, whose growth she had watched since eighteen thirty five. A monument plate is the frontispiece. Letters and narratives of contemporary interest fill the volume.

Judge Woodward letter to Colonel Proctor, dated Territory of Michigan, October eighth, eighteen twelve, stands first. It is already known to you that on Saturday the fifteenth day of August last an order was given, he begins. Helm letter and narrative follow, then The Massacre at Chicago at length. John Kinzie and the capture of little Eleanor Lytle close the book. Chicago historians get a survivor own record of eighteen twelve.
41708-jack-the-hunchback-a-story-of-adve:
James Otis wrote this adventure of Jack the Hunchback on Maine coast. Burt printed it in New York, copyright 1892, for boys. Contents open adrift, then at Aunt Nancy house on shore. Learning to milk, pursued, and an encounter fill early chapters.

A mental struggle, Farmer Pratt, and a second warning follow next. The alarm, sickness, gardening, and Louis adventure fill the middle. Chapter one sets Tom Pratt carting seaweed on a June morning. Tom thought himself the most unfortunate boy in Maine that day. A ship lifeboat of eighteen feet came out of the east that bright June morning.
41885-kwan-yin:
Stella Benson wrote Kwan-yin, a stage piece set in the temple of Kwan-yin, goddess of mercy. The hosted text opens with full stage directions, not dialogue. A wide altar fills the back of the stage.

The seated goddess is dimly seen, only her golden face clear, calm and aloof. Before her stand a table with her carved name tablet, a brass bowl of joss-sticks, and plates of waxen fruit and cakes. Horn lanterns give the only light. Four priests and two boy acolytes move like shadows. One boy beats a small hoarse bell in a fixed rhythm through the scene. A drum sounds at set points.
41886-chardin:
Chardin is a volume of the Masterpieces in Colour series, edited by T Leman Hare, with text by Paul G Konody. The series gave short lives of the great painters with colour plates of their works. Its list runs from Velazquez and Rembrandt to Whistler and Burne-Jones. The frontispiece here is a still-life by Chardin in the Louvre.

That picture, the caption says, shows the master's supreme skill in rendering the surface qualities and textures of varied objects: porcelain, metals, linen, and foodstuffs. Jean-Baptiste Simeon Chardin occupies a curious position among the artists of his time and country. His art was neglected and despised for many decades after his death. It is now admitted, by those best able to judge, to be supreme as regards technical excellence. Within the narrow limits of its subject matter it holds merits of far greater scope.
41951-a-tale-of-red-pekin:
Constancia Serjeant's A Tale of Red Pekin was published in London in 1902 by Marshall Brothers. Serjeant had written A Threefold Mystery and The Young Acrobats before it. A cover line gives the book's temper in one sentence: I have counted the cost.

Cecilia tells the story. She is twelve, the eldest of six children of a family that came to China four years before: Rachel, Jack, Jill, Tim, and baby Anna, whose solemn look troubles her mother. The contents run from a letter from Pekin to a rising in the village, a terrible walk, and the children taken prisoner. Mr Li's wonderful house, and wandering in dens and caves of the earth, close the list.
41976-mpuke-our-little-african-cousin:
Mpuke, Our Little African Cousin, belongs to the Little Cousin series for children of 1902. Each volume carried six or more full page plates in tint at sixty cents. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote most of the titles in the series list. Our Little African Cousin leads that long roll of child guides to far lands.

Alaskan, Arabian, Armenian, and Australian cousins follow in the series advertisement. Brazilian, Canadian, Chinese, and Cuban cousins fill out the world tour in print. Dutch, Egyptian, English, and Eskimo volumes stand further down the list. Through Mpuke a young reader met Africa, its villages, and its daily life. The series sold geography as friendship with children of every land in its day.
41977-our-little-hindu-cousin:
Our Little Hindu Cousin, by Blanche McManus, was printed at Boston in 1907. Page issued it in the Little Cousin Series. McManus drew the pictures herself. The series promised six or more full-page tinted plates in each volume. Its list ran from African to Turkish cousins, each a child of another land. This volume's hero is Chola. A plate shows him in his father's shop. Five chapters make the book. Chola at Home opens it. A Day in the Bazaar follows.

The Children's Holiday and a trip in the big ox-wagon come next. The children see Benares and go home for a wedding in the last chapter. A second impression was called for by August 1908. The series taught American children the homes and customs of far countries through one child's daily life.
41978-our-little-irish-cousin:
Our Little Irish Cousin is a children's geography reader by Mary Hazelton Wade, published in 1904. It belongs to the Little Cousin series, sold at a dollar a volume. Each book carried six or more full page plates in tint. The series ran to dozens of peoples, from African to Welsh cousins. Wade's Irish volume follows the same plan as its sisters. A child of the country guides young American readers through it.

Series lists like this one show the scale of the venture. Quebec, Roumanian, and Czecho-Slovac cousins all have volumes. So do cousins in Siam, Servia, and the West Indies. The books taught children the homes and customs of other lands. Stories of one child's daily life carried the facts. Wade wrote many of the volumes herself. Ireland's cousin stands mid list in the alphabet of nations.
42003-notes-and-queries-number-224-febru:
Notes and Queries, number 224, is a weekly antiquarian paper dated February eleventh 1854. Its motto, when found make a note of, comes from Captain Cuttle in Dickens. The stamped edition cost five pence for literary men, artists, and genealogists. Contents open with notes on the word eliminate and on Cranmer Bible.

Sovereigns dining in public and parallel ideas from poets fill the notes columns. The great alphabetic psalm and the songs of degrees get a learned note here. Minor notes touch gravestones, Newton and Milton, and Churchill grave in passing. Queries ask after the coronation stone and old Mereworth Castle in Kent.
42004-notes-and-queries-number-225-febru:
Notes and Queries, number 225, is the issue of Saturday, February 18, 1854. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs when found, make a note of. Price was fourpence, or fivepence for the stamped edition of the weekly. Remarkable imprints opens the notes at page 143 of the number.

Legends of the county Clare and canting arms follow in the contents list. Minor notes treat selleridge, tombs of bishops, and lines on a Bath palace visit. An acrostic in Ash church and a hint to publishers fill that minor roll. Queries ask after the Shippen family and John White in the next section. Books issued in parts and not completed gets a query of its own here. Literary men and genealogists traded small facts in this famed Victorian weekly.
42005-notes-and-queries-number-226-febru:
Notes and Queries, Number 226, came out on February 25, 1854. The weekly called itself a medium for literary men. Artists, antiquaries, and genealogists shared its pages. When found, make a note of, its motto runs. Captain Cuttle's words supply that line. The price was fourpence a number.

Legends and lore respecting bees lead the notes. An Oxford jeu d'esprit follows in the list. Ansareys in Mount Lebanon gets a note too. Thomas Lathbury writes on Elizabethan primers there. Minor notes treat Lucy Walters and General Haynau's corpse. Queries ask after pictures from Lord Vane's collection. Thurstan of York's burial place gets a query too. Minor queries crowd two full pages here. Replies treat Hardman's Waterloo account at length. A whole republic of letters in fourpenny form, the paper let scholars swap facts across Britain each week.
4203-wake-robin:
John Burroughs's Wake Robin, his first book of nature essays, takes its name from the spring flower and the birds that return with it. A scarlet bird in holiday suit, black wings and tail set against deep red, turns dull yellow-green in fall, like the female all season.

The purple finch, or linnet, sings apart on a dead hemlock, one of the finest songsters in the choir of the old barkpeeling. Burroughs writes of walks, songs, and seasons with a naturalist's ear. Readers who love birds and spring will find a gentle classic of American nature writing.
42079-mari-our-little-norwegian-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote Mari, a book for the young on a girl of Norway, put out at Boston in 1903. L J Bridgman drew the plates for the book. It sits in a set of books on the young of all lands, at sixty cents a book. The set runs from Africa to Turkey in its long roll of lands.

A first word tells of the Vikings, the bold sea men of the north of old. Long past the find of this land by Columbus, those men dared the unknown seas. Their home was the long land that now splits into Norway and Sweden. On shores of deep bays, with rough hills at their back, they learnt to rule their high prow ships. Fear of wind and storm left them on those hard coasts.
4213-the-founder-of-new-france-a-chronic:
Charles W. Colby's chronicle of Champlain follows the founder of New France to Port Royal. Lawsuits had kept one party from returning to Acadia, so the roadstead stood empty when De Monts, Champlain, and Pontgrave brought the people of St. Croix thither in August 1605.

Not only the people went: even the framework of houses was shipped across the bay and set up in a haven of better hope, on the bay's north side. Colby tells the founding in the clear style of the Chronicles of Canada. Readers who like exploration history will enjoy a brisk life of Champlain.
42204-our-little-turkish-cousin: Our Little Turkish Cousin, published in 1904, belongs to the Little Cousin Series, books that introduced American children to child life in lands around the world. Mary Hazelton Wade, named on the series page, wrote many of the volumes. The list here runs from African and Alaskan cousins to cousins in Turkey itself. Each volume had six or more full-page plates in tint and sold for sixty cents. The opening pages given here are the series list alone, so the Turkish story itself lies beyond this head.
42225-the-ordeal-of-mark-twain:
The Ordeal of Mark Twain, by Van Wyck Brooks, is a critical study of the great humorist's inner life. Heinemann published it at London in 1922. The contents open with Mark Twain's despair, then the candidate for life.

Later chapters treat the Gilded Age, the crucible, and the candidate for gentility. Everybody's neighbour, the playboy in letters, and those extraordinary twins lead to a chapter on Mark Twain's humour itself. Brooks begins with a marginal note of Twain's: what a man sees in the human race is merely himself in the honest privacy of his heart. Twain's belief that man is the meanest of animals, Brooks argues, was no pose, as his friends claimed. His book set off a famous quarrel over Twain's legacy, and still shapes how readers see him.
42320-the-shadow-of-a-sin:
The Shadow of a Sin, a novel by Bertha Clay, was issued in Philadelphia by the Royal Publishing Company. Clay also wrote Thrown on the World, Lady Damer's Secret, A Passionate Love, and Her Faithful Heart. Thirty-seven chapters, listed by number only, carry the long tale. A bound-in ad for a marriage guide by a doctor follows the title pages in this copy.

Clay was a famed writer of sensation tales for a wide popular market. Her plots turn on secrets, wrong choices, and the long reach of one fault over love and family honor. The shadow of a sin, in her world, falls on the guiltless as well as the guilty, and only truth and sacrifice can lift it. Readers of cheap romance prized her strong feeling and fast turns.
42343-life-and-times-of-david-miscellane:
Life and Times of David gathers miscellaneous writings of Mackintosh, the famed Brethren teacher, in volume six of his works. Loizeaux Brothers published it at New York, first in 1898 and in a tenth printing in 1960. The house was a nonprofit body devoted to spreading the truth, its title page says. Short pieces fill the front of the book, with the long David study behind.

Bethany, Restoration, Jericho and Achor, and The Three Appearings stand among the pieces, with poems between them. Christ in the Vessel opens the set, on the storm in Mark's gospel. Man's extremity is God's opportunity, Mackintosh begins, yet believers still grow perplexed and agitated when their own extremity comes. The Life and Times of David itself runs to two hundred pages. Mackintosh's plain, searching Bible teaching shaped the Plymouth Brethren and many readers beyond them.
42461-the-motor-boys-or-chums-through-th:
Clarence Young wrote The Motor Boys, or Chums Through Thick and Thin, in 1906. Cupples and Leon at New York hold the rights from that year. The volume opens the Motor Boys series, sold at sixty cents each. A front plate cries disaster: he is killed, they are killed, scores shout. The series list runs to Mexico, the plains, and the Pacific.

Contents in the wider line promise a wild night ride and adventures on the road. A fire and a discovery, and Ned under suspicion, stand in the heads. The boys are chums through thick and thin, as the subtitle vows. Motor Boys Overland and Motor Boys Afloat stand among the sequels. The Jack Ranger books by Young fill the facing list. Young gives boy motorists speed, scrapes, and loyalty in brisk chapters.
42723-the-unmasking-of-robert-houdin:
Harry Houdini wrote The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin, printed at New York in 1908 and given to the memory of his father. Chapters work through the famous tricks one by one. They cover the orange-tree trick, a writing and drawing figure, and a pastry cook of the Palais Royal. Obedient cards, an endless bottle, second sight, and a suspension trick follow in the list.

Houdini says his research brought only bitter disappointment with his hero. He holds that the famous Memoirs were written by a Paris journalist hired for the work. In his account, Robert-Houdin claimed tricks and machines devised by earlier masters as his own. Each claim, Houdini argues, fails when tested against the record in order.
42787-notes-and-queries-number-172-febru:
Notes and Queries, number 172, for Saturday, February 12, 1853, is one issue of the paper. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's rule heads it: when found, make a note of.

The issue costs fourpence, and its pages sort into notes, queries, and replies. Notes treat Italian English, Saint Nicholas Church at Brighton, and a key to Dibdin's Bibliomania. Temple gives parallel passages, and Westby Gibson seven score superstitious sayings. Minor notes give Mormon etymologies, an electric clock, and the earldom of Oxford. Queries ask after Collier's emendations and Hone's history of parody. A countess's letter to Sir Joseph Williamson is sought. Replies settle the rod poem, the Dutch East India Company, the word its, and when the year should begin.
42788-notes-and-queries-number-173-febru:
Notes and Queries was a weekly medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Number 173 appeared on Saturday, February 19, 1853, at fourpence the copy. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note of things when found.

Sternberg writes on predictions of the Fire and Plague of London in this number. Pinkerton gives examples of the French sizain, and George Daniel's poem 'Goe, soule, the bodies guest' appears among the notes. Folk lore covers Lancashire fairy tales, superstitions about teeth and new moon divination, while queries and minor notes fill the rest.
42789-notes-and-queries-number-174-febru:
Notes and Queries, number one hundred seventy four, is the issue of February twenty sixth, eighteen fifty three. The weekly served as a swap shop for literary men, antiquaries, and family historians. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids readers make a note of what they find. The number sold for fourpence, or fivepence in its stamped form.

Notes open with Mary Stuart's chair at Conington Church and a Hastings letter. Folk lore brings buried bells, weather sayings, and a harvest home song. Minor notes touch Ossian, epitaphs, and Johnson in short, sharp paragraphs. Queries ask after heraldry, a passage in Acts, and the Rigby letters. Replies settle old satchels, a statue of Saint Peter, and the finding of planets. A new section takes up the young art of photography and its methods.
42838-fromentin:
Roujon edited this study of Fromentin for the Masterpieces in Colour series, covering the painter's life from 1820 to 1876. A long list of companion volumes fills the front, from Reynolds and Velasquez to Whistler and Sargent. Plate one, 'A Halt,' comes from the Sarlin collection as its caption notes.

The caption praises how Fromentin arranges his masses of colour on that canvas. Light falls in a balanced, harmonious way across the scene, it says. Fromentin, a French painter of North African subjects and a noted writer too, gets a short, plate-led life in this popular art series.
43109-the-third-miss-st-quentin:
Molesworth tells a child's tale in The Third Miss St Quentin, in an edition dated 1888 from Hatchards of London. The heroine starts the book at six years old, as the first head states. Her name in the text is Ella, and she is ill at home.

Ella sits on the rug by a bright fire with her picture books strewn round. Her face is flushed, her eyes are heavy, and a bad cold plagues her. She begs her nurse Harvey to read to her. Harvey is busy with the breakfast things and bids her wait. Mamma is ill too, Harvey says, and there is plenty to do in the house. Ella flares scarlet at the word nonsense.
43207-scenes-and-characters-from-the-wor:
Scenes and Characters from the Works of Charles Dickens gathers 866 pictures printed from the original wood blocks engraved for the Household Edition of Dickens. The Musson Book Company issued it in London and Toronto. The blocks themselves, cut for the great Victorian reissue of the novels, are the book's whole reason to exist.

The artists' list reads like the roll of Dickens illustration. Fred Barnard drew the most: Nicholas Nickleby, Dombey and Son, David Copperfield, and Bleak House among them. Phiz, Hablot Browne himself, supplies the 57 Pickwick plates. Mahoney takes Oliver Twist and Little Dorrit. Charles Green draws The Old Curiosity Shop. Each novel gets its gallery, with the counts printed: 62 plates for Dombey, 61 for Copperfield. Dickens lovers get the Household Edition's picture world between two covers.
43212-fairy-tales-from-spain:
J Munoz Escomez told fairy tales from Spain for young readers in a set for many lands. J M Dent and Sons issued the book in London, first in this form in 1913. F C Tilney shaped the wider set, and W Matthews drew the pictures. Nineteen tales fill the contents, from Khing-Chu-Fu to Don Suero the Proud.

The first tale tells of an empress of China who finds a white hair. Seers warn that the silver thread means a tooth will ache, to her court's dread. Dragons, quack doctors, dwarfs, and proud men crowd the rest. Children gain brisk, odd tales with a Spanish tang and bright art.
43249-our-little-canadian-cousin:
Elizabeth Roberts MacDonald wrote Our Little Canadian Cousin, printed at Boston under a 1904 copyright with pictures by Bridgman. The hosted copy opens with the publisher's list of the Little Cousin series, to which this volume belongs. Each volume of the series, the list says, is illustrated with six or more full-page plates in tint, bound in cloth with a decorative cover. Most of the titles are by Mary Hazelton Wade, unless otherwise named.

The list runs the world: African, Alaskan, Arabian, Armenian, Australian, and Brazilian cousins stand there. Chinese, Cuban, Dutch, Egyptian, English, and French cousins follow. Japanese, Korean, Mexican, Philippine, Russian, Scotch, Spanish, and Turkish cousins fill out the roll. The Canadian volume is MacDonald's own work in the series. A picture caption in the front matter shows two children sitting on the grass under the lilacs.
43251-yellow-thunder-our-little-indian-c:
Yellow Thunder is a book for the young by Mary Hazelton Wade. It stands in the set of the small kin books. Each book of that set is bound in cloth with a fine case. Each holds six or more full page plates in soft hue. The price of each is set at the head of the list. The list of the set is long.

That list runs from the dark main to the cold north. Wade wrote most of the set her self. More hands wrote a few of the books, as the list owns. Each book tells the life of a child of one folk, for the child of this land to know. This book tells of a child of the first folk of this land. Its front plate shows the hero in his wild home.
43252-tessa-our-little-italian-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote Tessa, Our Little Italian Cousin, for the Little Cousin Series, with six or more tinted plates. Ads at the front list the whole set, with cousins from Africa to Turkey, most by Wade or her fellow hands. Each small cloth book sold for sixty cents.

The set was made to teach American children how children live in other lands, through the eyes of one child in each. Tessa stands for Italy in that world tour. Her days would show home, school, feasts, and play in an Italian town, in the warm, plain style of the set. The books were a staple of home and school shelves for years, and this one holds Italy's place in the row.
43254-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
A slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Luray Cavern toward the early letter M. Side notes were moved to stand as titles of their paragraphs in this copy, the transcriber says. Macrons and breves above letters and dots below were not inserted. Greek letters are given as alpha, beta, and so on in brackets.

Fixed errors are listed at the front: in the article on Luther, a German and was restored where and had crept in. In the Lyly article, between was amended from a misprint. The article on the lyre finds that two early instruments show traits which have persisted through the middle ages to the present day in instruments evolved from them. The letter M, Mabuse, and their neighbors fill the slice. Scholars get the great 1911 Britannica in its dense, learned dress.
4336-an-inquiry-into-the-nature-and-prog:
The Reverend T. R. Malthus, professor of history and political economy at the East India College, published this inquiry on rent in London in 1815. It grew from notes he had collected for his teaching, and the pressure of current debate hastened its appearance. Rent, he argues, follows principles that can be stated and tested.

Malthus examines how rent arises from differences in soil and situation, and how it moves with prices and cultivation. The tract is short and technical, aimed at fellow economists rather than general readers. It stands beside his corn law pamphlet as a key text of classical political economy.
43371-our-little-hungarian-cousin:
Our Little Hungarian Cousin belongs to the Little Cousin Series of books for children. Each volume in the set has six or more full-page plates in tint and sold for sixty cents. The series list at the front runs to dozens of lands, from Alaska to Persia.

Most of the books are by Mary Hazelton Wade, but the Hungarian volume is credited to Nixon-Roulet. Other hands wrote the Cuban, Korean, and Panama volumes in the same dress. The plan of the set is plain: a child in each land stands as cousin to young readers at home. Through that young guide the book shows the land's dress, food, games, and daily life. Music for the Hungarian volume was transcribed by Linda Cantoni, whose name the credits carry.
43424-francisco-our-little-argentine-cou:
Francisco, Our Little Argentine Cousin is a book for young readers by Eva Cannon Brooks. It came out in Boston in 1910, with pictures by John Goss. The book belongs to the Little Cousin series, which took children round the world.

The preface traces the long sea trip from New York to Buenos Aires. The steamer calls at Barbados, then at ports in Brazil, then at Montevideo. Through the boy Francisco, readers meet the land, the towns and the daily life of Argentina. The book gives young readers abroad a first, friendly look at a far off home. Six or more tinted plates in each volume of the series add colour for young eyes.
43425-jean-our-little-australian-cousin:
Our Little Australian Cousin is a children's geography story by Mary Nixon-Roulet, dated 1908. It belongs to the Little Cousin Series. Each volume in the series carries six or more full page plates in tint. The cloth books sold at sixty cents apiece. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote most of the long list. Nixon-Roulet supplied the Alaskan, Brazilian, Greek, Hungarian, and Spanish cousins besides this one.

Other hands took the Arabian, Canadian, Chinese, and Mexican children. The series tours the world one child at a time. An American child reader meets a cousin abroad in each volume. Home life, dress, school, and custom come through the cousin's days. Australia gets its turn through Jean, the cousin of this title. Such series taught geography as friendship rather than as lists. The publisher's catalogue of cousins fills the front matter here.
43426-our-little-finnish-cousin:
Our Little Finnish Cousin stands in the Little Cousin series of books. The series is cloth bound and illustrated, at a set price per volume. Richards, Winlow, and others wrote the volumes of the set. Cousins from Africa to Jugoslavia fill the long list of titles. Each volume gives a child of one country to young readers.

The Finnish cousin shows his home, his school, and his land. Snow, lakes, and forests make the ground of his daily life. The series pattern makes the far country a friend's house. Young readers learn customs, dress, food, and seasons by visiting. The list runs through more than fifty lands in the same dress. Arctics and tropics stand neighbour to neighbour in the catalogue. The Finnish volume gives the north in a child's own measure.
4346-the-effects-of-cross-self-fertilisa:
Charles Darwin wrote this large experimental work on the effects of cross-fertilization and self-fertilization in plants. His first chapter sets out the means that favor crossing, the benefits it brings, and the history of the subject. He then explains his experiments, carried on over successive generations under uniform conditions.

Darwin measured crossed and self-fertilized plants with care, weighing sources of error and the amount of pollen used. The work supports his broader argument that crossing generally strengthens offspring, while close self-fertilization weakens them. It is a patient record of experiment, and a key text for the history of plant breeding.
43462-our-little-hawaiian-cousin:
Our Little Hawaiian Cousin is a children's book by Mary Hazelton Wade, published in 1902 in the Little Cousin series. Each volume of the series was bound in cloth with six or more tinted pictures and sold for sixty cents. The series list names cousins from Africa, Arabia, Armenia, and many other lands, most of them also by Wade.

The books were made to teach American children how children live in other countries. Each follows a child of the land through home life, school, food, dress, and play. The Hawaiian volume presents the islands soon after they came under the United States. It gives young readers a first picture of Hawaiian life in simple story form.
43513-our-little-polish-cousin:
Our Little Polish Cousin is a children's book by Florence Mendel, in the Little Cousin series of the day. The hosted text opens with the series list. Each cloth volume held six or more full-page plates and sold for sixty cents.

The series took young readers round the world by means of a child guide in each land. The list runs from an African cousin to a Turkish one, by way of Alaska, Arabia, China, Cuba, and Japan. Most volumes were written by Mary Hazelton Wade. Other hands wrote the Polish, Armenian, and Korean volumes. Mendel's book gives Poland the same treatment. A Polish child stands at the centre, and the daily life, dress, and ways of the country are shown through that child.
43546-our-little-scotch-cousin:
Our Little Scotch Cousin is a children's book by Blanche McManus, published at Boston by Page in 1906. It is one of the Little Cousin series, a run of small lands told for small readers. McManus drew the illustrations herself. A portrait of Donald Gordon stands at the front. The preface speaks to the thousands of little American cousins. It brings them their Scotch cousins to know and love. Each book in the series treats one land through one child's life.

The child here is a Scotch boy, and Scotland is shown through his days. Home, school, dress, games, and tales fill the short chapters. Six or more plates in tint go with each volume of the series. The books sold for sixty cents each in cloth. McManus made the French and English cousins as well. The series was a first geography for the nursery.
43585-our-little-jewish-cousin:
Our Little Jewish Cousin is a child's guide in the Little Cousin Series. Each series volume holds six or more full page plates in tint. Cloth volumes with decorative covers sold at one dollar each here. A list of titles spans cousins from Africa to the Eskimo. Postnikov, Headland, Butler, and others wrote volumes in that long list.

Canadian, Chinese, Cossack, Cuban, and Czecho Slovak cousins stand there too. Danish, Dutch, Egyptian, English, and Finnish volumes fill the middle. Through one child's daily life, American children met a far people. Home, school, food, dress, and feast days make the portrait concrete. The Jewish volume shows customs, holidays, and home life to young readers.
43636-our-little-cuban-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote a children's geography of Cuba for the Little Cousin series, with six tinted plates by L J Bridgman, sold at fifty cents. Earlier cousins visited Japan, India, and Russia. New volumes add Cuba, Hawaii, the Eskimo, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Africa. A portrait of Maria fronts this volume. Wade tells Cuba through a child of the island.

The series taught American children the peoples of the new empire after 1898. Cuba, newly independent under American tutelage, got its cousin early. Page published the set at Boston. Each volume mixes story, custom, and scenery for young readers. Maria guides the tour of her island home.
43637-our-little-roumanian-cousin: Clara Vostrovsky Winlow wrote this book on the land of Roumania for the young, printed in 1917. It is one of the Little Cousin set. Each book of the set holds six or more full plates in tint, and cost sixty cents. The set runs to lands of all parts of the world: Africa, Alaska, Arabia, and more, each told through a child of the land. This book gives the young of America a small guide to the life of a child in Roumania.
43639-our-little-swiss-cousin:
Our Little Swiss Cousin stands in the Little Cousin Series of land books for children, printed with six or more full page plates in tint at sixty cents a volume. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote most of the set. Twin titles treat African, Armenian, Chinese, Cuban, Dutch, and Eskimo cousins, among many more.

The Swiss volume follows a boy named Carl through his school year and his home life among the mountains. Carl pictures in his mind the grand march of the next day, which will mark the close of school before the summer vacation. Thousands of children would march in the line. The set aimed to teach American children how their young kin in other lands live, work, and play. Young readers get Swiss school and festival days in story form.
4369-the-verse-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein wrote this self-critique of his own verse, because he believed many readers misunderstood it. He divides his work plainly: his first eighty pieces are love lyrics of the usual kind, much like garden verse. Their content is the distress of love, death, and universal longing.
