Lichtenstein adds that the impulse to write in a cynical vein, like cabaret songs, may have come from a wish to seem above it all. Most of the eighty poems, he says, are insignificant and were not shown to the public. The text gives a rare thing: a poet judging his early work aloud, with one quoted poem on burying himself in the night.
43750-ancient-man-in-britain:
Ancient Man in Britain is an archaeology book by Donald Mackenzie, author of Egyptian Myth and Legend and Myths of Crete and Pre-Hellenic Europe. Scribner's Sons copyrighted the work in 1915. A frontispiece shows the head of a Cro-Magnon man, after a restoration modelled by McGregor and borrowed from Osborn's Men of the Old Stone Age.

Mackenzie surveys the earliest inhabitants of Britain, their tools, dwellings and beliefs. The argument, as he frames it, warns against trusting one class of evidence alone. The physical characters of a series of skulls, he writes, can give no reliable information unless their exact provenance and relative age are known. Text and index bristle with the diacritical marks of the Celtic and prehistoric names he handles. The book is a period piece of early prehistory, written when the Old Stone Age in Britain was still being pieced together.
43831-our-little-french-cousin: Our Little French Cousin belongs to the Little Cousin Series, books that introduced American children to child life in lands around the world. The series list printed here runs from an African cousin to cousins in Arabia, Argentina, Armenia, and dozens more countries. Each volume had six or more full-page plates in tint and sold for one dollar. This volume's subject is France. The opening pages given here are the series list alone, so the story itself lies beyond this head.
43832-our-little-german-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade's series of Little Cousin books takes young readers to Germany in this volume. The series sold at sixty cents a book. Each copy holds six or more full-page plates in tint.

The list of titles maps the whole childhood world. African, Alaskan, Arabian, and Armenian cousins stand in the row. Dutch, Eskimo, French, and Japanese cousins follow. The German volume follows the series plan. A child of the country shows her home, school, and feasts to American readers. One scene in the text turns on Christmas baking. The mother promises cakes, and the girls must shell and chop the nuts early next morning. Wade wrote most of the series herself. These books taught geography through a child's day.
43833-our-little-japanese-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote this children's book about Japan for the Little Cousin series, published by Page and Company at Boston in 1901 with illustrations by Bridgman. Its small heroine is Lotus Blossom, presented as the dearest little girl in the Eastern world, living far across the Pacific.

Wade describes Lotus Blossom's round face, pearl teeth, and black hair braided behind. Her life is happy and unhurried: she never remembers crying, sleeps and rises with her parents, and is never sent to bed alone in the dark. Japanese children, readers learn, are taught to be polite above everything else. Pictures show Toyo feeding the pigeons, the candy man, Aunt Ocho's garden, and a lesson in arranging flowers. Lotus Blossom wears cloth stockings with a separate place for the big toe, and sandals outdoors.
4386-life-of-chopin:
Franz Liszt wrote this life of Frederic Chopin, translated from the French by Martha Walker Cook. The present text follows the fourth revised edition of 1880, reproducing the 1863 original essentially unabridged, with original spellings kept and italics shown as capitals. Liszt knew Chopin well, and he writes as a fellow artist.

The eight chapters trace Chopin's youth in Poland, his Paris years, his music, and his early death. Liszt treats the piano works as the key to the man, with passages on national feeling and on the poetry of the nocturnes and mazurkas. The book is both biography and criticism, by one great pianist about another.
43885-alila-our-little-philippine-cousin:
Alila, Our Little Philippine Cousin, by Mary Hazelton Wade, belongs to the Little Cousin series of books for young readers, and it is dated 1902. Each volume of the series held six or more full page plates in tint. The cloth books sold at sixty cents apiece. Wade wrote most of the titles in the long list.

The series took child readers to meet a child of another land in each book. Cousins from Africa, Arabia, Armenia, and Australia fill the list of titles. The Philippine volume came when those islands were new to American rule. Its purpose was to show American children how a Filipino child lived. Dress, food, home, and play would fill such a portrait. The book is a sample of the geography by story method of its day.
44030-our-little-danish-cousin:
Our Little Danish Cousin is a volume of the Little Cousin Series, a long line of books that took young readers to visit child life in many lands. The publisher's list at the front names dozens of fellows, from Our Little African Cousin to Our Little Turkish Cousin. Each volume came in cloth at sixty cents, with six or more full-page tinted plates.

The series was written by many hands, among them Mary Hazelton Wade, Mary Nixon-Roulet, Blanche McManus, and Clara Winlow. The Danish volume shows Denmark through a child's eyes, in the series' manner. Such books taught geography as friendship, one small cousin at a time, in the years before the Great War.
44135-albert-ballin:
Albert Ballin is Bernhard Huldermann's biography of the Hamburg shipping magnate. W J Eggers translated it from the German. Cassell published it in London and New York in 1922. Huldermann dedicates it to Ballin's memory in veneration and gratitude. A Hamlet quotation stands for epitaph: he was a man, take him for all in all. Eleven chapters trace the career. An extract annotated by William II is appended.

Ballin was born in Hamburg, in the Steinhöft by the Elbe. Ships then berthed along the northern shore below his father's house. Ballin traced all his later success to that upbringing. The contents climb with him. Morris and Company, the Carr Line, and the Packetfahrt's passenger department come first. The Pool and the Morgan Trust treat his combinations. Politics, the Kaiser, and the war close the public life.
44210-the-angel-of-pain:
The Angel of Pain, a novel by Benson, was published at Philadelphia and London in 1906. Lippincott issued it with copyright taken in 1905 for the work. Benson also wrote Dodo, The Challoners, and The Image in the Sand. The tale opens in a garden dozing in the summer sun of mid June.

Philip Home has moved his chair twice into the shifting shade of the house. Blinds are drawn down on the house, as if it blinked in the brightness. A mowing machine works somewhere on the lawn below the terrace walk. Flower beds hide the sound source from the watcher in that first scene. Quiet country wealth and a slow summer day set the stage for the drama ahead.
44294-the-phantom-violin:
The Phantom Violin is a mystery story for girls by Roy Snell, printed at Chicago by the Reilly and Lee Company with copyright of 1934. Its heroines are Florence and the little French girl Petite Jeanne. The first chapter, The Ship's Ghost, opens aboard a vessel by moonlight. Jeanne bursts through a cabin door and props herself against it: they saw me, she whispers, and thought her a ghost.

Twenty-eight chapters spin the mystery out. Then The Call of the Gypsies, Gold, The Head Hunter and Secret of Greenstone Ridge. The Cavern of Fire, At the Bottom of the Ancient Mine and Mystery from the Sky raise the stakes. Snell wrote shelf loads of such mysteries, and this one mixes wreck, gypsies and buried gold.
44380-the-buccaneer-chief-a-romance-of-t:
The Buccaneer Chief is a romance of the Spanish Main by Gustave Aimard, printed in London in 1864. Aimard also wrote Smuggler Chief and Strong Hand. The tale begins at the Hostelry of the Court of France, with a family scene and an arrest.

From there the chapters run to the Isle of Sainte Marguerite, a council of the filibusters, and a slave sale. An enlistment, an expedition, and the flight from the Hatto carry the action to the West Indies. Port Margot and Fray Arsenio enter late, before the flight and the colony's founding close the arc. The chapter heads promise love at first sight, despair, and a prisoner longing for France. Aimard knew the Americas at first hand, and his sea rovers have the salt of a lived world in them.
44447-fairy-realm-a-collection-of-the-fa:
Tom Hood retells old tales in Fairy Realm, a collection of the favourite old tales told in verse, printed in London in 1865. Ward Lock and Tyler made the book. Gustave Dore draws the plates, five tales' worth of them. Hood signs his first word in November 1865.

His plan, he says, was plain. The five legends are so well known that he chose a simple metre and a most unpretending manner. Ill health kept him from doing more, he owns with regret. The Sleeping Beauty leads, then Little Red Riding Hood and Puss in Boots. Cinderella and Hop o My Thumb close the set. The first tale opens in a dim land where silence reigned, in the days of once upon a time.
44525-report-on-the-radiolaria-collected:
Report on the Radiolaria is a Challenger expedition science volume on tiny sea life. The Challenger sailed from 1873 to 1876 on her great survey of the oceans. Ernst Haeckel worked up the radiolaria gathered on the voyage for this report. A second part carries the subclass Osculosa and the index of the whole.

Plates form a companion Gutenberg volume to the text and its index here. Page numbers in braces tie the text to the index for working use. Addenda and errata from the second part have been applied to the text. Marine biology holds the work as a monument of deep sea science.
44526-report-on-the-radiolaria-collected:
Challenger voyage science reports hold this study of the Radiolaria group. The zoology volume eighteen, second part, came out in 1887. Challenger sailed 1873 to 1876 under Nares and Thomson command. Wyville Thomson and John Murray oversaw the science staff work.

Her Majesty's Stationery Office printed the report for the government. A first part treats Porulosa forms, Spumellaria and Acantharia kinds. A plate volume stands apart as the third part of the work. The tiny shelled sea life forms fill dense Latin named pages. The price for both parts with plates was set in pounds on the title page.
44527-report-on-the-radiolaria-collected:
Report on the Radiolaria holds the sea find notes of a great survey ship. The Challenger roamed the seas in the years eighteen seventy three to seventy six. Her captains names stand on the front of the bound state report. This text is one part of a three part work on those small sea things.

Radiolaria are tiny sea things with shells of glass in strange forms. A first part treats one class, and a last part holds the next class and list. Fine plates show the glass shells in their wild range of shapes. The state paid for the whole set of reports on the great cruise. The work stands as a root text for the lore of deep sea life.
44670-dorothy-dixon-and-the-double-cousi:
A girls' mystery novel by Dorothy Wayne, published at Chicago in 1933. The Goldsmith Publishing Company issued it. Dorothy Dixon is the heroine, an amateur sleuth of school age. Earlier volumes solved the Conway case and a mystery plane case. She also won her wings as a flyer. This adventure turns on a double cousin.

The first chapter is called the Encounter. Dorothy shops for Christmas ties in a crowded store. A tall young stranger whispers urgently at her elbow. He asks how in the world she escaped. Distress fills his brown eyes, and he begs for answers. Dorothy coolly mistakes him for the escapee instead. Sleepwalkers, secret service, and mistaken identity fill the chapter list.
44671-jack-in-the-rockies-a-boy-s-advent:
Jack in the Rockies, or A Boy's Adventures with a Pack Train, is a boys' adventure book by George Bird Grinnell. It was printed at New York by Stokes, with copyright in 1904. The pictures are by Edwin Willard Deming. He also wrote Blackfoot Lodge Tales and The Story of the Indian.

Twenty three chapters carry Jack through the West. The tale opens with the Indians of Fort Berthold and the battle of the Musselshell. Jack starts for the Blackfoot camp and hunts buffalo with the Blackfeet. Then come the wonders of the Yellowstone Park, with its geysers and hot springs. He crosses the Continental Divide and hunts elk under the Tetons. Later chapters trail black-tail deer, follow tracks in the snow, and ask what will become of the elk. Grinnell knew this country and its peoples at first hand.
44731-nabul-our-little-egyptian-cousin:
Our Little Egyptian Cousin is a children's geography book by Blanche McManus, published in 1908 in the Little Cousin series. Each volume carried six or more full-page plates in tint and sold for sixty cents in cloth. The series took young readers country by country around the world.

The publisher's list shows the scale of the scheme. Cousins appear for Africa, Alaska, Arabia, Armenia, China, Cuba, Japan, and dozens more lands. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote most volumes, with McManus and others sharing the work. Through a child guide, in this case an Egyptian boy, American children learned how their counterparts lived, dressed, and played. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
45160-the-shakespeare-expositor-an-aid-t:
Thomas Keightley wrote The Shakespeare-Expositor, an aid to the full grasp of the plays. J Russell Smith issued the book in London in eighteen hundred sixty seven. Keightley had edited the plays and poems of Shakespeare himself. The book was made as mate to that edition of his.

Plain text readers are its first care, Keightley says up front. Few book lovers crave a full grasp of hard lines, he laments. Most glide past a dark phrase on its broad sense alone. His own new readings, found no where else, fill this store. Faults that slipped his edition stand here set right in full. The Globe edition pairs well with it, for its rich word list. His notes and index leave small shade in the plays, he claims. Delay in print did the book good, not harm, he adds at last.
45596-the-insect-world-being-a-popular-a:
The Insect World is a popular account of the orders of insects by Louis Figuier. Appleton published this new edition in New York. Duncan revised and corrected the text for this issue. Five hundred seventy nine illustrations accompany the account. A plate of a dragon fly's life stages fronts the contents. The contents march through the orders of insects in turn. Aptera and Diptera open the systematic survey. Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, and Orthoptera follow in the list.

Hymenoptera, Thysanoptera, Neuroptera, and Coleoptera close the orders. The Lepidoptera section treats larva, chrysalis, and perfect insect in stages. An introduction promises not to investigate anatomy thoroughly. The habits and economy of certain beings are its subject, it says. The principal parts of insect structure are explained simply first. Figuier's book taught natural history to the general reader. Its many pictures made the insect orders familiar at home.
45605-auguste-rodin:
Rainer Maria Rilke meditates on the great French sculptor in a study turned into English by Jessie Lemont and Hans Trausil. The Sunwise Turn issued it at New York in 1919. A photograph of Rodin by Gertrude Kasebier fronts the book.

Rilke's own sonnet on the archaic torso of Apollo opens the volume. Rodin was solitary before fame, the essay begins. Fame only made him more solitary. Fame, Rilke says, is the sum of all misunderstandings that gather round a new name. The work itself grew like a forest. It lost not one hour. A reader walks among a thousand forms, stunned by the craft. Then he looks for the two hands from which the world rose. Rilke had worked as Rodin's secretary. Few poems of praise match this prose.
45616-our-little-czecho-slovak-cousin:
Our Little Czecho-Slovak Cousin is a child's guide to a new land. Clara Vostrovsky Winlow wrote it for the Little Cousin Series of books. Each series volume holds six or more full page plates in tint. Cloth volumes sold at ninety cents each in that uniform series. A list of titles spans cousins from Africa to the Argentine.

Alaskan, Arabian, Armenian, Australian, and Austrian cousins fill that long list. Belgian, Bohemian, Boer, Brazilian, and Bulgarian volumes stand there too. Through one child's daily life, American children met a far country. Home, school, food, dress, and feast days make the portrait concrete. The Czecho Slovak volume came as that new state took its place.
45748-mr-punch-with-rod-and-gun-the-humo:
Hammerton edited this volume of the Punch Library of Humour, gathering the magazine's fishing and shooting jokes from its beginning in 1841. The Educational Book Company published it by arrangement with the proprietors of Punch. It carries 193 illustrations by Charles Keene, John Leech, Phil May, Du Maurier, Raven-Hill, Aldin, Partridge, and others.

An opening survey says the Punch artists have revelled in the sports. The jokes run endlessly on the bad shot who cannot hit the birds and keeps hitting the dogs or his companion guns. Other jokes fall on the lady shooter, and on the Frenchman's alien notion of sport. Short pieces follow, among them observations on ground bait, and an epitaph on an angler that reads Hooked It. The Duffer with a Salmon-Rod comes from the confessions of a duffer, who calls trout-fishing the most sedentary of pursuits and the best to his taste.
45750-our-little-brazilian-cousin:
Our Little Brazilian Cousin is a volume of the Little Cousin Series, a set of children's books about children in many lands. The series list in front runs from an African cousin to a Malay cousin and beyond. Each volume was illustrated with six or more full-page plates in tint and sold in cloth for a dollar.

Volumes like this one introduced American children to the wider world through a child of their own age. The Brazilian volume presents the country's scenes, homes, food, dress, festivals and daily life in simple chapters for young readers. The series, whose authors included travellers and teachers, treated geography as friendship: a cousin in Brazil, a cousin in Japan, a cousin in Egypt. Editions of the series were printed for decades, and this Brazilian number is dated by its copyright to 1907.
45797-jose-our-little-portuguese-cousin:
Jose, Our Little Portuguese Cousin, by Edith Sawyer, belongs to the Little Cousin series for children. Each volume in that series carried six or more full page plates in tint. Cloth copies sold at sixty cents a volume in the series list. Titles by Mary Hazelton Wade lead that roll of cousin books for young readers.

Our Little African Cousin and Our Little Arabian Cousin stand early in the list. Argentine, Armenian, Australian, Belgian, and Bohemian cousins follow in the roll call. A Brazilian cousin and many more lands fill out the shelf of the series. Through Jose a young reader of 1911 met Portugal, its homes, and its ways. Child guides to far lands were a school and home staple in that era.
45844-our-little-persian-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote this volume in the Little Cousin Series, which presents far lands to young readers through the eyes of a child of the place. Each book in the series sold for sixty cents, in cloth, with six or more full-page plates in tint. The roll of titles runs from Africa to Persia and past it, most from Wade's own pen.

The series list shows cousins in Arabia, Armenia, China, Cuba, Egypt, France, Greece, India, Ireland, and many more lands. Blanche McManus, Mary F Nixon-Roulet, and Isaac Taylor Headland wrote a few of the volumes. This one takes its young readers to Persia. It shows home life, dress, and custom as a Persian child would know them day by day.
45845-our-little-russian-cousin:
Our Little Russian Cousin is a children's geography book by Mary Hazelton Wade. The Page Company published it in Boston, with a copyright of 1901. L J Bridgman drew the illustrations. The book belongs to the Little Cousin Series. Each volume in the series sold at 60 cents, with six or more tinted plates. Impressions ran on to a fifteenth by July 1915.

The preface sketches Russia for young readers. The country stretches from the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea. Many of its children, Wade notes, have fair skins and blue eyes. Some live in palaces, and a vast number are very poor. Their parents work hard to keep hunger from the door. A frontispiece shows Petrovna, the little cousin of the title. The series ranged from African and Alaskan cousins to Siamese and Swedish ones. Each volume made a foreign child's daily life familiar to American children.
45995-our-little-porto-rican-cousin:
Our Little Porto Rican Cousin, by Mary Hazelton Wade, is a child geography tale. Page of Boston issued it in the Little Cousin series, rights in 1902. Each series volume sold at sixty cents, cloth, with tint plates inside. Manuel, the little cousin of the title, fronts the book in a plate.

Porto Rico lies near the Gulf of Mexico, that doorway to North America. A Massachusetts child must travel a thousand miles to see this near neighbour. Book excursions have taught readers their Eskimo and other cousins already, Wade says. Cuba, China, Japan, Korea, and more lands fill the same series list. Island home life through a child eyes is the book plan.
46043-vasco-our-little-panama-cousin:
Vasco, Our Little Panama Cousin is a book for young readers by H Lee M Pike. It came out in 1906. The book belongs to the Little Cousin series, which took children to lands round the world.

Each volume in the series came with six or more tinted plates. Through the boy Vasco, readers meet the land of Panama and its folk. The series told the life of one child in each land it chose. Pike also wrote the Korean cousin volume for the same set. Young readers of the day got a first, friendly look at a far canal land. Pike's Vasco stands beside Francisco in the same bright series.
46230-our-little-austrian-cousin:
Our Little Austrian Cousin is one volume of the Little Cousin Series of books for the young. The front matter sets out the line as a whole. Each volume has six or more full-page plates in tint, in cloth, at sixty cents. The list of titles runs through the lands of the world, from an African cousin to a Chinese and a Cuban one.

The names on the series list are Mary Hazelton Wade, Mary F. Nixon-Roulet, Blanche McManus, Clara V. Winlow, Florence E. Mendel, and others. The volume at hand is the Austrian one of that set. The head as shown is the series list and trade matter, so the tale of the Austrian child itself starts past the part in view. The series aim, by its shape, is to bring the lands of the world to young readers at home.
46345-sir-quixote-of-the-moors-being-som:
John Buchan wrote Sir Quixote of the Moors, a Scotch romance. It stands in a buckram series of tales at seventy-five cents each. The Time Machine and The Prisoner of Zenda stand in the same list. The narrative is now presented to the world for the first time. It was written by the Sieur de Rohaine, the account begins.

He wrote it to while away the time during a confinement, it says. Buchan frames his tale as that gentleman's own record of an episode. The moors of Scotland give the romance its ground and weather. A French gentleman adrift among Scots moors is its quixote. Honour, hospitality, and danger meet him on that ground. The tale is an early work of the maker of later adventure. It gives a short, brisk romance in an old narrative dress.
46454-in-vain:
In Vain is an early novel by Henryk Sienkiewicz in English translation. Curtin translated it from the Polish for Little, Brown in 1899. Sienkiewicz later wrote Quo Vadis and With Fire and Sword in fame. Rights rest with Curtin, the translator, in this Boston edition. An introductory note tells the strange youth of this first work.

Sienkiewicz wrote it before he had passed his eighteenth year of life. He was studying at Warsaw when the tale took its shape there. The author left it out of his collected works in later years. Pictures of student life fill the volume, the note promises readers. Warsaw lodgings, lectures, and first loves fill this apprentice tale.
46483-our-little-boer-cousin:
Luna May Innes wrote Our Little Boer Cousin, a book for children issued at Boston in 1915 with pictures by John Goss. It stands in the Little Cousin Series, a long run of small books that take a child of one land as guide. Sister volumes treat African, Alaskan, Arabian, Chinese, Cuban, Dutch, English, Irish, Japanese, Mexican, Russian, and dozens of other folk. Each volume cost sixty cents and held six or more full-page plates in tint.

The plate at the front shows Petrus at work steeping a bullock's hide in water, a farm task of the Boer folk of South Africa. Through a Boer child's daily life, the book shows young American readers how folk of Dutch stock farmed and lived on the far side of the world. Innes had also written Our Little Danish Cousin for the series.
46484-our-little-eskimo-cousin:
Our Little Eskimo Cousin, by Mary Hazelton Wade, belongs to the Little Cousin Series of children's books. Page printed it at Boston in 1902, with pictures by Bridgman and six full page plates. Sister volumes visit Japanese, Indian, Russian, African, and many other cousins around the world.

Baby Etu rides in his mother's hood on a winter morning seventy degrees below freezing, laughing at the starlit dark of the far north. He lives on the shores of northern Alaska, in the frozen zone. Chapters follow his play days, the dog team and sledge, the kayak and harpoon, and the seal hunt. Feast and fun, hard times, an Eskimo Christmas, and summer travels round out his year.
46485-our-little-spanish-cousin:
Our Little Spanish Cousin introduces Spain to young American readers, written by Mary Nixon-Roulet. Page published the book at Boston in 1906, with plates by Blanche McManus. The volume belongs to the Little Cousin series, which covered some thirty lands. Most of the series came from one author's pen, with guests for a few lands.

The book opens on the sunny Iberian shore that sent Columbus out. Its hero, Fernando, shows his home, his donkey, and his daily round. Nixon-Roulet had written With a Pessimist in Spain for grown readers. Here she writes plainly for children about Spanish towns, dress, and feasts. Each volume of the series cost sixty cents in decorated cloth. The set aimed to give American children a friend in every country.
46508-our-little-grecian-cousin:
Our Little Grecian Cousin belongs to the Little Cousin series of children’s geography books, sold at sixty cents a volume. Each volume carries six or more full page plates in tint. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote most of the titles in the long list. Our Little African Cousin and Our Little Alaskan Cousin stand near its head.

Arabian, Armenian, Australian, and Brazilian cousins swell the roll of the series. A child of each land leads young readers through home and school. Greece here gives the cousin his temples, islands, and village days. Such books taught geography as friendship in the age before cheap travel. Sisters and brothers of the series filled whole shelves of home libraries. The Grecian volume is the Greek doorway of that small world tour.
46855-under-the-flag-of-france-a-tale-of:
Under the Flag of France, by David Ker, is a tale of Bertrand du Guesclin for young readers. Blackie and Son printed the book in London in 1908, with drawings by Stanley Wood. Ker gives the tale to his nieces Margaret and Mary.

A front plate shows Bertrand defending the jester, and another shows him grappling with a wolf. The chapters open with a broken bough, a monster faced, and a mysterious message. Bertrand's dream, a timely rescue, and lance-to-lance fighting follow. The Black Death, a midnight battle, and a haunted circle darken the middle. A robber camp, a black wolf, and a clever stratagem fill the later pages. Crescent and cross meet near the close, and the last sunset ends the hero's career on the page.
47198-the-human-boy-again:
Eden Phillpotts, author of The Human Boy, returned to his schoolboys in this second book of stories. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1908, dedicated to Mark Twain, father of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. Quotations from Twain and Nietzsche head the title page, and a frontispiece shows a boy caned for insolence combined with irreverence.

Twelve stories make the contents, from Peters, Detective, and The Doctor's Parrot to The Bankruptcy of Bannister and Tomkins on Tinned Cow. The first is told by Peters's chum, who shared pocket-money with him, the great sign of friendship. Their understanding was that Peters would devote his life to clearing him if he were ever accused of murder or forgery. Peters arrives thin and dark, with a skull pin in his tie, and warms hands so thin the firelight shows through them.
47339-flowers-of-mountain-and-plain:
Flowers of Mountain and Plain, by Edith S Clements, was printed in New York by the H W Wilson Company in 1926, in a third edition. Reprints came in 1945, 1949, and 1955. Clements dated her note at the Alpine Laboratory, Manitou, Colorado, on July 9, 1920. Color plates sort the flowers by family.

Plate one shows the buttercup family, with monkshood, blue columbine, red columbine, and blue larkspur. The text says the flowers of the monkshood are usually deep purple blue, though yellowish white ones are often found. The tall plants, four to eight feet high, grow in mountain meadows and along streams at six thousand to twelve thousand feet. The aconite disguises its kinship to the buttercups by having irregular sepals, shaped by insect visitors in search of nectar. Field fans get a pocket guide.
47626-the-ocean-world-being-a-descriptio:
The Ocean World is a description of the sea and its life by Louis Figuier. A shell lore hand revised and widened the shell parts of the text. Four hundred and twenty seven prints crowd the fat home science book. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

A quote at the front sets two great seas: one at foot, one past head. Calm and storm of the deep, and the lives in it, form the whole theme. Tricks of hunt and flight, work, wars, and loves of sea things fill parts. Plain words keep the lore clear of hard school terms for home minds. The book was a prized shelf work of the age for sea lore.
47628-a-corner-of-spain:
Walter Wood wrote A Corner of Spain as a travel book about Galicia, in the far north-west of Spain. Martin Hume supplied an introduction, and Frank H. Mason made colour and line pictures for the text. Wood states plainly that the book is not a full history of the region.

His aim is to show the life and character of a little-known part of Spain. He writes about things seen and done by a visitor who travels with good guidance. Place names, local speech, and old spellings fill the notes. Readers get a ground-level view of towns, coasts, and customs rather than a formal survey.
47678-remedia-amoris-or-the-remedy-of-lo:
Ovid wrote Remedia Amoris, or The Remedy of Love, shown here in a plain English prose text by Henry T Riley in 1885 with full notes. The poem opens with Cupid reading its title. Cupid cries that war is meant against him. Ovid begs him not to charge his own poet with that crime.

Ovid says he has borne Cupid's flags and loves still. He taught the arts by which love may be won. The new poem does not undo the old, he pledges. Happy lovers should sail on with fair winds, he says. Those crushed by a cruel love should take relief from his skill. He asks why lovers hang or stab themselves for love. The cure is to desist in time, he holds.
48173-practical-carriage-and-wagon-paint:
M C Hillick wrote this treatise on painting carriages, wagons, and sleighs, first copyrighted in 1900 and issued in a third edition in 1903. The title page promises full directions for every kind of work: factory painting, lettering, scrolling, ornamenting, and varnishing, with many tested recipes and formulas.

The preface notes that demand had already worn out two editions, and that twenty years had passed since any such volume appeared in America. In that time, the preface says, painters raised their trade from a simple preserving craft to a fine art. The book is dedicated to the vehicle painters of America and the world. Working painters get a full shop manual.
48203-letters-from-spain:
Letters from Spain presents a Spaniard's view of his own country, by Don Leucadio Doblado. Colburn published this second, revised edition in London in eighteen twenty five. The letters first describe Cadiz from the sea and its life of faith. Religion, the writer says, blends with public and home life at every turn.

Letter two sorts Spaniards into nobles and plebeians, grandees and hidalgos of low life. Spanish pride shows even among the poor, and purity of blood is prized. Seville's day is mapped, from dinner and siesta to the evening public walks. Fans and their many uses, and the character of Spanish ladies, follow. Later letters tell how a clergyman is formed and unformed in Spain. Bull fights, a country journey, and the Inquisition's shadow close the set.
48293-old-quebec-the-city-of-champlain:
Old Quebec, the City of Champlain, by Emily P Weaver, came out at Toronto in 1907, with pictures by Annie E Weaver. Weaver had also written a Canadian history for boys and girls. Her short book tells the story of Quebec from its founder onward, in six chapters.

The chapters move from the founder and the founding of the city to Notre Dame des Victoires. Next come the Plains of Abraham and the fifth siege of Quebec. A last chapter turns to days of peace. Long lists of pictures show gates, churches, falls, and old streets. Young readers get a warm, pictured walk through the old city and the fights that shaped it.
48844-the-story-of-captain-the-horse-wit:
George Wharton James wrote The Story of Captain, the Horse with the Human Brain, published by the Radiant Life Press at Pasadena in 1917. James wrote dozens of books on California and the Southwest, from Indian Basketry to the Grand Canyon. A photograph shows Captain Sigsbee on his educated horse Captain, with Jasper the groom beside them. James dedicated the book to all horses patiently serving man, and to all mankind human enough to love horses.

Educated horses were a stage wonder of the age. Captain could answer questions, spell, and do sums, or seemed to, before crowds across America. James tells the horse's story as evidence of animal intelligence and kindness in training. The Captain book is its curiosity: a sincere tribute to a performing horse, written by a man who believed animals had more mind than his age allowed.
48904-arthur-brown-the-young-captain:
Arthur Brown, the Young Captain is a boys' novel by the Reverend Elijah Kellogg, printed at Boston in the Pleasant Cove series. Kellogg wrote the Elm Island stories, including Lion Ben and Charlie Bell. The preface argues a principle: kindness is sometimes rewarded with ingratitude, but not so often as censorious persons would have us suppose.

Benefits conferred usually excite gratitude, and are sometimes repaid with interest to the donor's posterity. Arthur Brown's story illustrates the principle. Lashed to a raft, perishing with cold and hunger in the edge of the surf, he is rescued by Captain Rhines. The old captain, when a boy poor and unable to read or write, had been instructed and started in business by Arthur's father, afterwards lost at sea. Discovering in the rescued youth the only son of his benefactor, he receives him with open arms.
4907-moths-of-the-limberlost-a-book-abou:
Gene Stratton-Porter's book about the Limberlost Cabin follows moths through their whole lives in a northeastern Indiana swamp. Chapters take up eggs, caterpillars, and winter quarters, then turn to individual kinds: the Robin Moth, the Yellow Emperor, the Lady Bird, moths of the moon, and the King of the Poets.

Stratton-Porter writes as a naturalist who lived beside her subject, and the Limberlost itself becomes a character in the account. Readers learn how to find, raise, and watch moths, and why a swamp's night life rewards patience. The book remains a warm introduction to field study for anyone curious about insects.
49087-the-abbeys-of-great-britain:
H Claiborne Dixon wrote this guide to the abbeys of Great Britain, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York and T Werner Laurie of London. A view of Westminster Abbey from Dean's Yard fronts the book. The tour is sorted by region: northern counties first, then southern, eastern, and western.

Durham, Lindisfarne, Hexham, and Jarrow open the north. Yorkshire fills a long roll: St Mary's at York, Byland, Jervaulx, Rievaulx, Whitby, Fountains, and Kirkstall. Kent, Wiltshire, and Devon follow, then Croyland, Bury St Edmunds, Glastonbury, and Bath. Dixon's introduction praises the monasteries for bringing art, worship, and learning to the doors of rural folk. The book is a compact pilgrim's handbook to ruins and living churches alike.
49121-the-last-days-of-pekin:
Pierre Loti's last days of Pekin were Englished by Myrta Jones and printed at Boston in 1902, from photographs and drawings by Jessie Jones. The emperor's throne in the Forbidden City fronts the book. The book is given to Vice Admiral Pottier, commander in chief of the squadron of the Far East.

The notes which I sent to the Figaro from China are to be collected in a volume published in Paris before my return, Loti writes. It will be impossible for me to look it over. It will doubtless contain much repetition, he owns. You know under what conditions it was written: from day to day during a painful campaign, in the continual excitement of life aboard ship. Loti watches occupied Pekin after the Boxer rising.
50044-romantic-legends-of-spain:
Gustavo Adolfo Becquer wrote Romantic Legends of Spain. Cornelia Frances Bates and Katharine Lee Bates turned them into English. Thomas Y Crowell issued the book at New York in 1909. Toledo Cathedral fronts the volume. Master Perez the Organist opens the tales. That piece is a tale of Seville.

The Emerald Eyes tell a legend of the Moncayo. The Golden Bracelet returns to Toledo's streets. The Ray of Moonshine belongs to Soria. The Devil's Cross rises in the eastern Pyrenees. The Christ of the Skull and The White Doe follow. The Kiss and The Spirits' Mountain stand later. The Gnome and The Miserere close the set. All Souls' Night in Madrid ends the book. Spain's great Romantic poet gave his homeland ghostly tales that still define its legend lore.
50408-jews-and-moors-in-spain:
Rabbi Joseph Krauskopf wrote The Jews and Moors in Spain, published by M Berkowitz and Company at Kansas City in 1887. The copyright stands in 1886. Krauskopf dedicated the volume to his congregation, B'nai Jehudah of Kansas City, Missouri. The lectures were delivered from his pulpit in the fall and winter of 1885-86. They were written as popular discourses, not for print.

Newspaper reports of the lectures spread across the country, and letters urged a book. Jews and Gentiles alike wrote in, the rabbi says. He treats the social, political, religious, and intellectual life of the two peoples in Spain. T T Crittenden, ex-governor of Missouri, heads the letter-writers quoted. The epoch, Krauskopf argues, is highly important and almost neglected in English literature. His Kansas City lectures filled that gap for a popular audience first.
50433-england-and-canada-a-summer-tour-b:
England and Canada is a summer tour book by Sandford Fleming, published at Montreal in 1884. Dawson Brothers issued the tour between old and new Westminster with historical notes. A frontispiece map traces the eastern and western journeys of the route. Fleming, a civil engineer, was the great surveyor of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

He dedicates the record to the Marquis of Lorne as one of Canada truest friends. The journey runs from the imperial capital to the Pacific through Canadian territory. Contents open with an introductory chapter, then Halifax to the west in stages. Dominion building speaks in the engineer own travel narrative of 1884.
50634-among-the-trees-again:
Among the Trees Again is a book of nature poems by Evaleen Stein, issued at Indianapolis by the Bowen Merrill Company in 1902. Stein dedicates the volume to the memory of her beloved brother. The poems take their names from seasons, fields, and quiet waters. April Morning, April Contradictions, and As to the Summer Air stand near the front.

Other pieces sing of the rose, of bindweed, and of the cactus land. A poem goes by the Kankakee, and one rests in the mission garden at San Gabriel. Home fields, fisher folk, and a golden wedding fill out the table. Stein writes short lyrics of Indiana fields and western scenes. Her verse is plain, tender, and close to the ground it praises. The book suits readers who love calm nature poetry.
50654-in-the-wonderful-land-of-hez-or-th:
Street and Smith issued In the Wonderful Land of Hez, or The Mystery of the Fountain of Youth, as number 127 of Brave and Bold in May 1905, at five cents. The weekly promised a different complete story every week, this one by the author of The Wreck of the Glaucus.

One October afternoon in 1880 a sailboat crosses Lake Okechobee in southern Florida, carrying two men as unlike as can be. Professor Remington Easy is short, stout, and good-hearted, hiding his eyes behind blue goggles of extraordinary size. His right-hand man, Martin Haypole, is a lanky Yankee of six feet two and not an ounce of spare flesh. Their boat, the Maid of the Marsh, crawls at twenty miles in two days, to Martin's disgust, while the Everglades wait to the south. Easy is an explorer, and the land of Hez lies ahead.
50824-the-flying-machine-boys-on-secret-:
Frank Walton wrote a boys' aviation novel copyrighted in 1913, subtitled the capture in the air. Walton had written three earlier Flying Machine Boys books. A front picture shows Jimmie lowering himself from one plane to another's top wing. Chapter one, the fall of the bear, opens with two aeroplanes in a green basin in the Rocky Mountains.

Snowy peaks of the Continental Divide lift thirty miles away. Later chapters promise a midnight flight, the loss of the Louise, and the voyage of the Ann. Mysterious signals, a race in the air, and arrests fill the end. The boys serve on secret service, in the new world of flight.
50831-the-river-motor-boat-boys-on-the-y:
The River Motor Boat Boys on the Yukon, by Harry Gordon, bears a copyright of 1915. Gordon had sent the same boys down the Saint Lawrence, the Colorado, the Amazon, and more rivers. This tale adds a sub-title: The Lost Mine of Rainbow Bend.

The motor boat Rambler lies moored in the South Branch of Chicago in late April. She wears fresh paint from cabin top to keelson, with cloth-wrapped lines to guard the shine. A front plate shows a bear knocking a man into rough waters. The chapters promise a mystery, a murderous assault, and the gold fever. Winter quarters, a trade, and a vision fill the Yukon stretch. The lost mine is solved twice over, by the odd doubling of the last chapter heads.
50868-the-highest-mountain:
The Highest Mountain, a science fiction tale by Bryce Walton with drawings by Bob Hayes, ran in Galaxy in June 1952. The blurb warns that the first man up the tallest summit in the solar system was a rotten egg. Bruce, the narrator figure, is caught reading Byron poems he sneaked aboard ship when feet sound on the gravel outside.

Jacobs and Anhauser enter from the icy wind in cold-proof suits. They tease Bruce, the poet, for still being there, and ask where he would run to on a Mars that looks alike in all directions. Bruce climbs into his own suit as talk turns to the climb. Dreams of faces, human and not, haunt his sleep and hint at death.
5087-the-treasure-train:
Arthur B. Reeve's collection presents twelve cases for Professor Craig Kennedy, the scientific detective, and his friend Walter Jameson. Each story turns on a new device or trick of its day: a truth detector, a love meter, a submarine mine, a sunken treasure, and a phantom destroyer, among others.

Kennedy solves crimes with laboratory method rather than simple deduction, testing poisons, codes, and machines to catch the guilty. The stories are brisk pulp mysteries from the early twentieth century, and they show how popular fiction of the period mixed detective work with faith in science and invention.
5092-the-coming-of-cuculain:
Standish O'Grady retells the youth of Ireland's great hero, known in childhood as Setanta, from the Ulster cycle of Gaelic legend. The book follows the boy among the Red Branch knights, through his running away. His feats among the boys of Ulster, his knighting, and his first wars follow, until Setanta becomes Cuculain.

O'Grady drew on old Irish tales and shaped them into a connected narrative for modern readers, keeping their heroic scale and strange magic. The result serves as a clear doorway into Irish myth, introducing the champions, kings. Sacred horses of Ulster join them, in the order a young hero meets them.
51492-armenia-travels-and-studies-volume:
Armenia: Travels and Studies, volume 1 of 2, is H F B Lynch's account of the Russian provinces of Armenia. Longmans, Green published it in London in 1901. The full work carries 197 illustrations. They reproduce Lynch's own photographs and sketches. Numerous maps and plans, a bibliography, and a map of Armenia support the text. Ararat from Aralykh fronts this volume.

Twenty-two chapters cross the country from the Black Sea. Trebizond and the ascent open the route. Akhaltsykh and Akhalkalaki lead to Alexandropol. Erivan, the Persian-facing capital, occupies several chapters. The ascent of Ararat fills chapters twelve and thirteen, heart included. Edgmiatsin and the Armenian Church receive the longest chapter. The consecration of the Katholikos, anointed from a golden dove's beak, is illustrated. Ani, the ruined medieval capital, and Kars follow. Geographical and statistical chapters close the volume. Lynch mixes travel narrative with political survey throughout.
51752-if-you-was-a-moklin:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction tale for Galaxy, where it ran in September 1951, with plates by Harry Rosenbaum. The head note speaks straight to the reader as if he were a Moklin. Earthmen, it says, may look bad to themselves, but not to you.

The narrator swears he cannot think Moklin will be the first planet men quit in haste. Yet the tale's title and note promise love at first sight between men and the folk of Moklin. To a Moklin, Earthmen look so fine that he would even wish to be one. Leinster plays the old star-tale in reverse, with the alien doing the admiring.
51757-samuel-pepys-and-the-world-he-live:
Henry B Wheatley wrote Samuel Pepys and the World He Lived In, issued in London by Bickers and Son in eighteen eighty in a second edition. A plate of Nell Gwyn faces the title page. The Athenaeum in eighteen forty eight praised the Diary of Pepys as a good sirloin that needs just its own juices. Wheatley takes that famed Diary as his core source.

Inside, Wheatley rebuilds the London that Pepys knew, street by street and court by court. He treats the king, the court, the stage, and the taverns of that age. Pepys own words season the tale at each turn. Notes and appendices add lists and rare texts for keen readers. The book suits any reader who loves the Diary and wants its world made plain and near.
51808-the-harvest-of-ruskin:
The Harvest of Ruskin is a study of John Ruskin's teaching by John W Graham, principal of Dalton Hall at the University of Manchester. George Allen and Unwin first published it in 1920, a hundred years after Ruskin's birth. Graham asks what part of the teaching has blown away as chaff and what part stands as good seed.

Graham sets art aside, since Ruskin's art criticism is out of fashion in the age of cubism and futurism, and turns to his teaching on duty and happiness. Chapters weigh the signs of a prophet, Ruskin's road of life, and his uneasy place among the churches. A long chapter works to reconcile Ruskin with John Stuart Mill. Later chapters take up his plan for rebuilding society, his economics for today, usury, war, and machinery. An epilogue and index close the book.
51878-the-city-of-the-sultan-and-domesti:
Miss Pardoe wrote The City of the Sultan, and Domestic Manners of the Turks in 1836, in two volumes. Henry Colburn published the first volume at London in 1837. Pardoe was the author of Traits and Traditions of Portugal. The Chapel of the Turning Dervishes fronts the book as a plate. The Maiden's Tower stands among the illustrations. She dedicated the work to her mother, from whom her sojourn in the East had first separated her.

Her preface owns the difficulties of the work. The Turkish language, wholly unlike every European tongue, raised a barrier between her and her subject. Pardoe writes Constantinople from a woman's access: the homes, visits, and manners closed to male travellers. Her two volumes taught England how Turkish domestic life looked from inside the rooms.
51879-the-city-of-the-sultan-and-domesti:
Miss Pardoe wrote this second volume on Constantinople and Turkish home life in 1836. Colburn printed The City of the Sultan in London, and its plates were drawn by Pardoe herself. Yere Batan Serai, the sunken palace, stands in the list of views.

Volume one holds the first of the two parts; the set stands whole only together. Pardoe was let into houses no man could enter, and she wrote what she saw: baths, weddings, harems, and the round of visits. Her eye was warm and her pen quick, and the books made her name. She writes of the Turks not as foes or riddles but as hosts. A classic of travel into the Ottoman home, read for a century.
52417-legends-from-river-mountain:
Carmen Sylva and Alma Strettell wrote Legends from River and Mountain. George Allen issued the tales at London in 1896. Carmen Sylva was queen of Roumania. T H Robinson drew the pictures. Nineteen legends fill the contents. The Jipi of Roumania opens the set.

The Serpent-Isle and Furnica follow in Roumanian lands. The Caraiman and the Stags' Valley come next. The Witch's Stronghold and Piatra Arsa build the middle. The Cave of Jalomitza tells of a horse turned hawk. That bird bore a maid away in its talons. Saxony and the Hartz hills give the later tales. A Walpurgis-Night legend stands among them. The Little Glass-Man of the Black Forest closes the book. Mountain tales from two lands show how peaks and streams gather stories that mothers pass down.
52558-tubal-cain:
Tubal Cain is a story by Joseph Hergesheimer, printed in New York by Alfred A Knopf in 1922. It first ran in 1918 in a book called Gold and Iron, then was reprinted twice. Sixteen short parts carry the tale.

The tale opens on Alexander Hulings, who sits at a dingy table with green cloth in a small office. His thin, dark face stays still as he stares at a white plaster wall. Spring maple buds split on a calm street past his window, and a door stands ajar on a plank sidewalk. Shelves hold worn law books, a cannon stove stands at the back, and a steel print of Chief Justice Marshall hangs on the wall. Hergesheimer builds mood and doom in fine, slow prose.
52722-an-account-of-the-manner-of-inocul:
An Account of the Manner of Inoculating for the Small Pox in the East Indies is a medical tract by Holwell, a fellow of the Royal Society. Printers in the Strand published the tract at London in 1767, priced at one shilling. Holwell inscribes the work to the president and members of the College of Physicians. Added notes treat how the disease itself was handled in those parts.

Holwell says he gathered his notes after reading recent tracts on inoculation. His subject is the method used from old time by the Brahmins of India. He hopes knowledge of the foreign method will support the practice now spreading at home. He grants that a Dutch work on the theme exists, but in a foreign tongue. He also quotes a saying that medicine owes some of its best gains to chance, and some to rude peoples.
52763-wanderings-in-spain:
Wanderings in Spain, by Théophile Gautier, is a travel book shown here in the London edition of 1853 from Ingram, Cooke and Company, with many engravings. Gautier rides south from Paris through Bordeaux and Bayonne, over the Bidassoa bridge at Irun, and into a Spain of mule carts, beggar children, and slow suppers.

At Burgos he lingers over the cathedral and the coffer of the Cid. Madrid brings bullfights, the Prado, and the water sellers of the Puerta del Sol. A visit to the Escorial follows. Gautier's eye for color made this one of the great French books on Spain.
52974-the-british-army-from-within:
E Charles Vivian wrote this account of the British Army from within, printed by Hodder and Stoughton of London, New York, and Toronto in 1914. Vivian had written Passion Fruit and Divided Ways. His first chapter takes its title from the word Ubique, found on the badges of the Engineers and the Royal Artillery. The word, he says, fits the whole army, which serves everywhere.

Chapters follow the recruit's way, officers and non-commissioned men, and the arms in turn: infantry, cavalry, artillery, and engineers. Camp life, musketry, and the inner workings of the army follow. The new army and active service close the book. Vivian counts the strength of his day: 157 battalions of infantry and 31 regiments of cavalry, with batteries besides.
53038-language-its-nature-development-an:
Otto Jespersen, a teacher at the University of Copenhagen, wrote Language, Its Nature, Development and Origin. George Allen and Unwin in London first issued the book in nineteen twenty two. Jespersen had written many earlier books on speech sounds and on English grammar. He gave this book to Vilhelm Thomsen. Four main parts and an index fill the volume.

Part one traces the study of language from before eighteen hundred to the end of the next century. Part two turns to the child, to sounds, words, and grammar. Part three deals with the foreigner, with pidgin tongues, and with causes of change. Part four takes up word roots, growth or decay, and the start of speech. Students of language will find a broad, clear survey.
5304-my-robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's My Robin answers a question from a young reader of The Secret Garden: did the author own the original of the robin, or was he mere fantasy? Burnett, thrilled to find a reader intimate with English robins, writes of the real robin who visited her garden and of the letters that followed.

The short book, illustrated by Alfred Brennan, tells how a wild robin became a companion. It also tells how a children's author learned from a bird. Readers who loved the robin of The Secret Garden will find here the true story behind him, told with warmth and delight.
53417-the-french-army-from-within:
Ex-Trooper wrote the French Army from Within, in 1914. Doran at New York put out the anonymous account. The constitution of the French army opens its contents. The French soldier at home follows in the second chapter. Higher ranks, infantry, and off duty take the next chapters.

Cavalry and artillery stand in the contents after those. In camp and on the march and manoeuvres fill the middle. With the cavalry scouts and internal economy come later in it. The great garrison towns of France take a chapter of their own. The French army of today dates only from 1871, it says. Changes of government since 1815 remade it again and again there. Every citizen is bound into its principle of service, it holds. A fit young man at twenty owed five years of service. The book gives a British reader the conscript army whole.
53549-i-will-maintain:
I Will Maintain is a tale of the Dutch past by Marjorie Bowen, first out in February of nineteen ten. The book ran past nine prints in three years, a sign of its hold on readers. Its name is the watch word of the House of Orange, in French on the front page. The tale stands in three parts of past a rank of parts each.

The hero of the first part is a statesman of the free Dutch state, a man of tireless work and clean hands. Parts trace plots, a spy of France, a ball at court, and the fall of that man as war comes. The last part takes up a young prince, the will of the folk, and a black date in the year of the fall. War at sea and craft at court drive the whole.
53568-armenia-travels-and-studies-volume:
Armenia: Travels and Studies, volume two, by Lynch, came out in London in 1901. This volume deals with the Turkish provinces. The full work holds 197 plates from the author's photos and sketches, plus maps and plans. A bibliography and a map of Armenia and nearby lands close the set. Chapter heads trace a long route on foot and horseback.

The route runs to Lake Van, across it, and on to Bitlis and Mush. Lynch then goes to Erzerum, Khinis, and Akhlat. He stays in the crater of Nimrud and climbs Sipan. Final chapters turn to geography, figures, and politics. Appendices print the national constitution of the Armenians in the Turkish Empire and notes on lake waters.
53671-modern-poets-and-poetry-of-spain:
Modern Poets and Poetry of Spain, by James Kennedy, came out in London in 1860. Kennedy was a British judge in the mixed court at Havana. A note of thanks to the Earl of Carlisle tells how the book began. Kennedy took up versions from the Spanish to learn the tongue well, and for rest from graver work.

Travel books, he holds, tell much of roads and trade, yet miss the mind of a folk. Verse shows how a people thinks and feels at home, in its hours of ease. A talk with Carlisle in Cuba in 1842 set that view in his mind. His book thus gives Spain in its own songs, turned into English with care. Verse fans get a window on the soul of a land through its poets.
53754-the-captain-of-the-wight-a-romance:
Frank Cowper wrote The Captain of the Wight, a romance of Carisbrooke Castle in fourteen eighty eight, issued in London by Seeley and Company in eighteen eighty nine. Cowper had earlier written Caedwalla, or the Saxons in the Isle of Wight. He made the illustrations himself. A long preface praises the Renaissance. To my mind there is no more picturesque period in Western Europe, he opens.

Among the aspects of that epoch, its influence on chivalry is one of the most interesting, Cowper holds. The rough simplicity of the proud medieval knight yields to the spell of courtly love, he says. However practical the world may grow, minds will always turn with relief to the romantic and the ideal, he adds. A plate shows a page stammering, What art thou. Romance readers get Tudor adventure on the Isle of Wight.
53797-the-dyer-s-guide-being-a-compendiu:
Thomas Packer, dyer and practical chemist, wrote this guide to dyeing cloth. Sherwood, Gilbert, and Piper printed the second edition in London in 1830. It covers dyeing of linen, cotton, silk, wool, and muslin goods. A color plate shows Newton spectrum order at the front.

Simple colors are blue, yellow, red, and black, Packer states. Green comes from blue and yellow, orange from red and yellow. Methods tell how to scour wool and bleach cotton well. Ungumming silk and whitening silk and wool get their own clear directions in full here.
54180-travels-to-discover-the-source-of-:
Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile, volume one, is the great travel work of James Bruce. Ruthven printed it at Edinburgh in 1790. Five volumes cover the years 1768 to 1773. A Latin line from Tacitus serves as motto. The book is dedicated to the king. Bruce praises the new age of humane discovery. Avarice and cruelty ruled the old voyages, he says. His own age, he holds, joins science with humanity.

Volume one sets out his route toward Abyssinia. Bruce of Kinnaird was a Scots laird turned explorer. He reached the Blue Nile's source and claimed the prize. Doubts dogged his tale when he came home. Later travellers confirmed much of what he wrote. The work is a landmark of African travel. Its bulk and colour still draw readers.
54181-travels-to-discover-the-source-of-:
Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile, by James Bruce of Kinnaird, tells of his years in Africa from 1768 to 1773. The work fills five volumes, printed at Edinburgh in 1790. This second volume turns from travel to history. Its third book gives annals of Abyssinia, translated from the original records.

The annals run from the restoring of the line of Solomon under Icon Amlac, from 1268 to 1283. Reign follows reign through Amda Sion, Saif Araad, and many more kings. Wars with Muslim neighbours, dealings with monks, and court deeds fill the summaries. Bruce notes where memoirs of a reign are lost or were cut by churchmen. The volume shows the deep written history Bruce found in Ethiopia. His travels were doubted in his day, yet this history work rests on records he brought home and had translated.
54483-the-rapin:
The Rapin, a novel by Henry de Vere Stacpoole, author of Pierrot, was published in New York in 1899 by Henry Holt. A foreword begins in the rooms of the narrator's friend Otto Struve. There hangs a parrot cage holding a rather dejected lark. The bird came from Gustave Garnier, a painter who took the Prix de Rome and sold a picture of a girl to the state.

A story ties the painter, the picture, and the bird together. Its hero is Celestin, yet the tale must be called Toto, or The Rapin, a rapin being a painter's studio drudge. Three parts follow Toto through Paris art life, with chapter heads on the poetry of hats and the sorrows of art. Stacpoole writes a light, ironic tale of bohemian ambition.
54531-travels-to-discover-the-source-of-:
James Bruce of Kinnaird published travels to discover the source of the Nile in five volumes at Edinburgh in 1790, covering the years 1768 to 1773; this is the third volume. An Ovid motto says the Nile fled terrified to the world's end and hid its head, which still lies hid. Book five of the work fills this volume. It accounts for Bruce's journey from Masuah to Gondar and his transactions there.

Manners and customs of the Abyssinians are described. Bruce claimed to reach the Blue Nile's source in 1770. His vast narrative was doubted, then largely vindicated. Robinson of Paternoster Row sold the London issue. The third volume holds the Ethiopian heart of the journey.
54629-frank-reade-jr-and-his-electric-ic:
Frank Reade Junior and His Electric Ice Ship is a dime novel adventure from Frank Reade Weekly Magazine, number 25, dated 17 April 1903. It was written under the pen name Noname and sold for five cents. The tale opens as the Callisto-bound ship Leo needs a cook. Its regular cook falls ill after tasting his own cooking, just out of Sand City spaceport.

The ship lands on Phobos, the inner moon of Mars, to land the sick man and hire a new cook. But Phobos has few settlers, and war with the Outer Planets makes men wary of a sealed-orders trip. The piping-voiced cook they get proves a Jonah who jinxes the ship straight into chaos, aloft in the frozen sky.
54692-in-the-far-east-a-narrative-of-exp:
In the Far East, published by Nelson in London in 1879, is an illustrated account of exploration in Cochin-China, Cambodia, Laos, and Siam by the unnamed author of The Arctic World. Twenty-eight full-page pictures accompany the text.

Chapters trace the route through Laos toward China, report time spent among the Chinese, and describe the return to Saigon. Other sections cover Morice and the Mekong river and the travels of Mouhot in Cambodia. The opening chapter sets out the ground and waters of Cambodia, giving the country's native name and tracing the Mekong from China through Yunnan and Laos. Books of this kind carried Southeast Asia to British readers who would never see it.
54720-three-years-wanderings-in-the-nort:
Robert Fortune wrote Three Years' Wanderings in China, published by John Murray at London in 1847. Fortune was botanical collector to the Horticultural Society of London. The title promises a visit to the tea, silk, and cotton countries. It also promises an account of Chinese agriculture and horticulture, with new plants. 

The first chapter clears away errors: no correct sources on China exist, he says, and Chinese informants are not to be depended on. He remarks on Chinese character, agriculture, and laws. Hong Kong fills the second chapter, from its harbour and town of Victoria to its unhealthy climate. Amoy and the island of Koo-lung-soo follow. Fortune travelled to steal the tea plant's secrets for British India, and his wanderings record the country trade by trade.
54805-a-servant-of-satan-romantic-career:
A Servant of Satan tells the romantic career of Prado the assassin. Street and Smith published it in New York in June 1889. It stands as number 8 of the Far and Near Series, issued monthly. The subscription price was $3.00 per year. Louis Berard wrote the account. His material came from notes communicated by Prado himself on the eve of his execution.

The title page calls Prado the great riddle the French police were unable to solve. He was reared, it says, in a royal palace. The preface quotes Chief Inspector Byrnes of the New York police. Byrnes calls Prado a wonderful fellow, without a peer for criminal ingenuity. He doubts that cupidity lay at the root of the crimes. Some great wrong, he thinks, embittered Prado against wealthy women.
54904-london-ancient-and-modern-from-the:
London, Ancient and Modern, From the Sanitary and Medical Point of View, by Poore, was published by Cassell in 1889. The book grows out of two talks given that January, one at the Parkes Museum of the Sanitary Institute and one to medical students at University College. A frontispiece map shows the center of London in 1658.

The first half tracks water supply, death rates, and the health of old London against the improved modern city. The second walks medicine from Chaucer's doctor through the plague, the barber surgeons, and the first hospitals. It is public health history told by a working doctor.
55051-rock-blasting-a-practical-treatise:
Rock Blasting, by André, is a practical treatise on the means used to blast rock for industry. Spon printed the book in London and New York in 1878. André was a mining civil engineer and a member of the Society of Engineers.

His preface says the past decade brought great changes to the craft. The machine drill had come in, and hand methods no longer served under machine labour. Stronger agents were needed than the common gunpowder of old. They were found in nitro-cotton and the nitro-glycerine compounds, and in black powder improved and fired by detonation. Electricity gave a quicker and surer means of firing than the old fuse. The book treats each part of the new system in detail, for men who blast rock in mines, quarries, and works.
55118-porcelain:
Edward Dillon wrote a volume on porcelain for the Connoisseur's Library, first published by Methuen at London in 1904. A first plate shows Japanese Imari ware. Contents open with an introductory and scientific chapter. The materials follow: mixing, fashioning, and firing. Glazes and decoration by colour come next. Chinese porcelain then takes two chapters, from the Sung dynasty through the Yuan.

The Ming dynasty continues the Chinese story. A selected list of works on porcelain runs to many pages, with a key to the bibliographical list. Dillon wrote for collectors who wanted history and technique together. Methuen's library gave each art a single expert volume.
55219-the-prose-tales-of-alexander-pushk:
The Prose Tales of Alexander Pushkin was published in 1916. Bell issued the translations in London that year. Keane Englished the tales from the Russian. Eleven stories make the contents. The Captain's Daughter leads, a full tale in chapters. Doubrovsky and The Queen of Spades follow. An Amateur Peasant Girl and The Shot are shorter pieces. The Snowstorm, The Post Master, and The Coffin-Maker fill the middle. Kirdjali and The Egyptian Nights come near the end. Peter the Great's Negro closes the volume. The Captain's Daughter opens in a guards family.

Its narrator's father served under Count Munich in his youth. He retired a senior major to his Simbirsk estate. The boy was enrolled a sergeant before he could study. A gamekeeper taught him letters; a French hairdresser turned tutor followed.
55340-squire-phin:
Holman Day wrote this Maine novel, published by Harper in New York in 1913. Chapter one brings in Hard-times Wharff, who cocks his nose to sniff trouble. A comic song about Miss Lu-ce-e and her parrot, kept in a garret and fed on a carrot, opens the tale as Wharff's favorite.

The village of Palermo drowses on a sleepy afternoon as the story begins. Flies buzz around banana skins curling in the August sun outside Asa Brickett's store. Half a dozen old men sit jack-knifed on a rickety settee in the shade, droning on, while Squire Phin's world takes shape around them.
55415-the-boy-scout-explorers-at-treasur:
Don Palmer wrote a Boy Scout Explorers novel copyrighted in 1955 by Cupples and Leon of New York. A picture shows an old woman stumbling into a room as a door is jerked open. An important assignment opens the contents. Captain Carter and a path to adventure follow. A mission and an ancient manuscript come next. Earthquake tremors and scout cargo build the middle.

Contraband and Captain Carter's deception darken the plot. The fury of a mob and the wilderness follow. A mysterious follower and a poisoned arrow raise the stakes before disaster. Treasure Mountain gives the quest its goal. The Explorers were a senior scouting series of the fifties.
55450-peeps-at-royal-palaces-of-great-br:
Peeps at Royal Palaces of Great Britain, by Beatrice Home, is a guide to the royal homes of Britain for young readers. Adam and Charles Black published it at London in 1913. It holds eight full page pictures in colour and twenty one line drawings. The Tower of London, with the Bloody Tower and the crown jewels, fronts the book.

Chapters walk through Westminster and Windsor first, then the Tower, Kennington, and Eltham. Greenwich, Whitehall, and Hampton Court follow, with Saint James's, Kensington, Kew, and Buckingham Palace. A chapter on vanished palaces gathers the lost ones. Scotland comes last: Edinburgh, Dunfermline, Stirling, Holyrood, Linlithgow, Falkland, and Balmoral. Home begins Westminster with King Cnut, said to be the first king to settle there. The book is a pocket tour of courts and castles, rich in stories of the kings and queens who lived in them.
56012-the-yankee-and-the-teuton-in-wisco:
Yankee and the Teuton in Wisconsin is a history paper by Joseph Schafer. It was reprinted from the Wisconsin Magazine of History in December 1922. Schafer opens with the popular view of Wisconsin as a Teutonic state. German stock, he grants, numerically overshadows other stocks in the blend. Yet he warns that corollaries drawn from that fact can be false.

By census proof Wisconsin began statehood in 1848 as a Yankee state. It stayed Yankee for many years, with deep social consequences in train. Those effects touched land, church, school, and town life for good. Mere racial substitution could not wipe them out, Schafer argues in full. Attitudes toward the land form his first test of the claim.
56196-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
The Three Voyages of Captain James Cook Round the World was printed in London in 1821 for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, complete in seven volumes with map and plates. The copy at hand is volume one, the first part of the first voyage. A portrait of Cook, drawn and engraved by Bond from the picture by George Dance, stands at the front.

A life of Cook opens the set. He was a day-labourer's son, born at Marton in Yorkshire on November 3, 1728, schooled briefly, then apprenticed to a shopkeeper at Snaith. The sea drew him; his master gave up the papers, and he bound himself to a Whitby ship-owner instead. By 1759 he was master of the Mercury at the taking of Quebec, where he charted the St Laurence river.
5621-baron-d-holbach-a-study-of-eighteen:
Max Pearson Cushing wrote Baron d'Holbach as a study of eighteenth-century radicalism in France, submitted for a doctorate in political science at Columbia University in 1914. The book examines Holbach the man through early letters to John Wilkes and his family. It also traces his relations with Diderot, Rousseau, Hume, Garrick, and other leading figures, closing with an estimate of his character and personality.

Later chapters treat Holbach's works, his translations of German scientific books, and the philosophy of his Systeme de la Nature, with bibliographies of editions. Readers get a scholarly life of a radical atheist philosopher, set among the French Enlightenment's salons and debates.
56379-spain-from-within:
Spain From Within, by Rafael Shaw, was printed in New York in 1910. A study portrait of King Alfonso the Thirteenth fronts the book. A note at the start quotes a Madrid paper of February 1910 on truth in politics.

Truth, that paper said, is an exile from the political world, since each faction tells only the part that shames its neighbour. Shaw sets out to show what the people of Spain believe about those who rule them. He gathered the views in talk with Spaniards of all classes, chiefly working folk in town and country. His own reading and watching fill the gaps. He does not pretend to judge whether his informants are right. The weight of the book, he says, lies in the fact that so many hold these views.
565-the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsie:
George Borrow studies the gypsies of Spain, the Zincali, in this work written over five years on the road. Borrow, distributing scriptures in ventas and posadas, gathered lore on gypsy names, language, law, clans, and fortune-telling. Chapters treat colonies, forges, counts, and the Gitana of Seville.

Borrow writes with vivid, partisan energy, mixing travel, philology, and anecdote. An introduction surveys gypsies from Russia to England. The book endures as a pioneering, if prejudiced, portrait of a people Borrow knew by campfire talk and long road days, not by library alone.
56502-travels-to-discover-the-source-of-:
Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile, volume four, continues James Bruce's Abyssinian narrative. Bruce had reached the source of the Blue Nile. This volume covers the return from the source to Gondar and the civil wars that trapped him there.

The contents are a chronicle of battles. Bruce joins the king's army at Mariam-Ohha, watches rebels apprehended and executed, and describes three battles of Serbraxos in detail, with the king's rash conduct and narrow escapes. Ras Michael is carried away prisoner, Gondar is invested, and at last Bruce obtains leave to depart. The volume is travel narrative swallowed by war reporting: the explorer as unwilling courtier and eyewitness in a kingdom tearing itself apart.
5663-the-prose-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein's short prose gathers sharp, unsettling pieces from a German writer of the early twentieth century, including a fragment from an unfinished novel. The opening piece, called The Winner, follows Max Mechenmal. He runs a newspaper kiosk, eats and drinks well, and keeps careful control of his many affairs. Quietly, he also takes money from Ilka Leipke. His comfort rests on calculation, not on luck.

The prose is blunt about greed, fear, and the wish to look grand without being caught. Lichtenstein watches people who dream of fine clothes and fine company yet shrink from the risk their schemes would need. Readers looking for polished heroes will not find them here. Instead they meet vivid, flawed figures drawn in a few hard strokes. Their city world pulls desire one way and caution the other.
56648-memoirs-of-the-distinguished-men-o:
Memoirs of the Distinguished Men of Science of Great Britain treats the men of science living in the years 1807 and 1808. William Walker Junior gathered the lives, and Robert Hunt wrote the opening. Spon printed the book in London in 1864, in a second edition. A Shakespeare line stands at the front, that the evil men do lives after them.

The short lives run from William Allen and Francis Baily to Sir Joseph Banks, Matthew Boulton, and Joseph Bramah. Robert Brown, Sir Mark Isambard Brunel, Edmund Cartwright, and Henry Cavendish follow. Samuel Crompton, John Dalton, Sir Humphry Davy, and Peter Dollond stand in the mid list. Walker says the lives were first made to go with an engraving of the men gathered at the Royal Institution. Science fans get a group portrait of a great age in brief lives.
57100-the-clue-of-the-gold-coin:
Helen Wells wrote a Vicki Barr mystery copyrighted in 1958 by Grosset and Dunlap, with a picture showing a case holding a clue to the gold coin theft. A sunshine assignment opens the contents. A strange trip and an odd offer follow. Pirate gold appears by chapter four, and the FBI takes over in chapter five. A New York interlude and Ybor City set the Florida scenes.

Skull and crossbones, a torchlight parade, and the French sand continue. Havana enters near the end. Vicki Barr, a flight stewardess, solved mysteries along her airline routes. Wells created the series for postwar girls. The gold coin ties Tampa's pirate lore to a modern theft.
57201-seventeen-years-among-the-sea-dyak:
Edwin Gomes wrote Seventeen Years Among the Sea Dyaks of Borneo, described on the publisher's list of new and recent books at the front of the hosted copy. The entry calls it a record of intimate association with the natives of the Bornean jungles. Gomes had written The Sea Dyaks of Borneo before it. An introduction by John Perham, formerly Archdeacon of Singapore, goes with the book. Forty illustrations and a map fill the volume, the entry notes.

The same list offers companion works of travel and study from the same house. Baring-Gould's Cliff Castles and Cave Dwellings of Europe stands there, and Fraser's record of thirty-seven years among the rajahs and ryots of northern India. Swann's account of fighting the slave-hunters in Central Africa is praised by the Athenaeum as extraordinarily fascinating.
57246-rifles-and-riflemen-at-the-battle-:
The National Park Service issued this short study as History number twelve in its Popular Study Series. It was reprinted in 1947 and sold for fifteen cents. Its theme is the part played by the rifle in the Battle of Kings Mountain.

Kings Mountain, A Hunting Rifle Victory leads the book, by Roger Young of the Branch of History. A second part treats the American rifle at the battle in more depth. A third tells how a modern marksman shot a Ferguson rifle of 1776 with high skill. Major Patrick Ferguson, the British chief at the battle, fronts the book in a plate. He devised the breech-loading rifle that bears his name.
57341-my-year-in-a-log-cabin:
My Year in a Log Cabin is a bit of autobiography by William Dean Howells, printed at New York in 1893. It stands in Harper's Black and White Series, small cloth books priced at fifty cents. Howells, by then a famed novelist, looks back to a boyhood year that shaped him.

In the fall of 1850 his father moved the family from a city to a property on the Little Miami River. The father was to run a saw mill and grist mill and oversee their hoped-for change into paper mills. The property was held by the father's brothers, doctors and druggists. Howells tells the year plainly, as a seed time for the writer he became.
57502-the-observations-of-sir-richard-ha:
