Sir Richard Hawkins set down his Observations of a voyage to the South Sea. The Hakluyt Society reprinted the work in London in eighteen hundred forty seven. C R Drinkwater Bethune shaped the old text of sixteen hundred twenty two. Hawkins sailed in fifteen hundred ninety three under the Queen’s own warrant.

Sea rovers of those years stood half accused as pirates, Bethune owns. Drake himself bore that stain till Elizabeth’s honors cleared his name. Hawkins bears no such blame in his editor’s firm defense here. Kindness and mercy marked his whole course on that far coast. Small ships and slight stores made such voyages feats of nerve. Spain’s rich towns on the Pacific shore drew the bold English crews. Murchison heads the Society list, with Darwin among its council. Their aim: print the great sea tales of England’s first age of sail.
57683-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of William Harrison Ainsworth is a catalogue compiled by David Widger. It lists Ainsworth's historical novels held in that digital library, title by title. Windsor Castle heads the contents, followed by Old Saint Paul's and the Star Chamber volumes. The Lancashire Witches, Rookwood, and Guy Fawkes stand in the same roll of famous tales.

Jack Sheppard fills three volumes in the list, a mark of his fame as a highwayman hero. The Tower of London, The Miser's Daughter, and Cardinal Pole round out a huge shelf. Tables of contents for each volume follow the index proper. Readers can map a vast Victorian storyteller's output at a glance here.
57716-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Samuel Merwin is a reference volume compiled by David Widger. It gathers the works of the novelist Samuel Merwin available in Project Gutenberg. For each book it reproduces the table of contents. Readers can survey Merwin's whole shelf at a glance. The list opens with The Short Line War and The Road to Frontenac.

Calumet K, written with Henry Kitchell Webster, follows. Drugging a Nation, Merwin's study of the opium trade in China, stands among the novels. The Road Builders, The Merry Anne, and Henry Is Twenty come next. The Trufflers, In Red and Gold, and Anthony the Absolute continue the run. Hills of Han and His Little World close the list, with The Whip Hand last. The index serves readers who want Merwin's plots and chapter shapes before choosing a book.
58400-hans-holbein:
Arthur B Chamberlain, deputy keeper of the Birmingham Art Gallery, wrote a short life and study of Hans Holbein for Bell's Miniature Series of Painters in 1902. The volume carries eight illustrations. Contents divide the book into the life of Holbein and the art of Holbein. The life begins with early days in Augsburg and Basle.

Holbein was born in 1497 at Augsburg in southern Germany, the text states. Sections follow his first visit to England, return to Basle, and second residence in England. The art section treats wall paintings, religious paintings, book illustration, and designs for goldsmiths. Portrait painting gets its own chapter. A list of chief works and a chronology close the book.
58468-sun-and-shadow-in-spain:
Maud Howe, author of 'Roma Beata' and 'Two in Italy,' wrote this travel book on Spain, published in Boston in 1908. Pictures from photographs and color plates support the text throughout. A front view shows the Arab quarter of Tangiers, across the strait from Spain itself.

Howe dedicates the book affectionately to Isabel Anderson by name at the front. An opening piece called 'Child's Play' starts far from Spain, on First Beach in Rhode Island. Children there dig foundations and raise forts in the sand while the tide comes in, a small parable Howe uses to open her Spanish journey.
58685-the-privilege-of-pain:
Everett wrote The Privilege of Pain, published in Boston by Small, Maynard in 1920, with a contribution by Kate Douglas Wiggin, dated from New York in May 1920. The opening essay, Health and Strength, begins in anger at a famous doctor's interview.

The doctor had favored drafting women for war. A good many would perish, he allowed, but from the standpoint of race their perishing would not be regrettable. A sick race, he argued, goes to the wall. Wiggin calls the statement outrageous, printed at the war's height, when men without arms, legs, or eyes were crawling home in hordes. And nearly everybody, she charges, agreed with him. The book argues the other side: what pain and broken bodies are worth. Invalid readers of 1920 got a brief against the worship of health.
58762-the-new-year-s-bargain:
Susan Coolidge tells a year of tales in The New-Year's Bargain, from Roberts Brothers of Boston, with pictures by Addie Ledyard. A child coaxes the stories out, and the contents show the plan: the children meet the Months in the wood and strike a bargain. Each chapter is a month's tale, from The Bear Story to May's Garden.

Little housekeepers, the last of the fairies, a desert island, and Nippie Nutcracker fill the middle months. How the Cat Kept Christmas closes the year, and a conclusion tells what was on the tree. The frame poem mourns one lost listener.
58923-select-books-published-by-mr-t-fis:
Select Books is a trade catalogue sent out by London publisher T. Fisher Unwin from Paternoster Square. Unwin asks buyers to order through their local bookseller. The list sorts his stock by kind, from fine writing and history to books for children.

Each entry gives the author, the look of the book, and its price in plain terms. One top item is English Wayfaring Life in the Middle Ages, turned from French and shown with prints from old hand written books. Other entries cover old Chelsea, tales, church sketches, travel, and lives of note. The catalogue is a window on what a London house chose to push and how it sold books in its day. Book trade fans will value the prices and blurbs.
59194-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index volume gathering the tables of contents of Alexander Pushkin's works as issued by Project Gutenberg, compiled by David Widger. Nine works are listed, from Marie and Boris Godunov to Eugene Oneguine and the prose tales.

The contents are reproduced in full. Marie shows its chapters of Pougatcheff, the fortress, and the siege; Boris Godunov lists its scenes from the Kremlin palace to the tavern on the Lithuanian frontier. Eugene Oneguine appears in eight cantos, in the Spalding verse translation. The poems volume prints Ivan Panin's introduction, sorting the lyrics into poetic ideal, inner life, and general characteristics. Readers get Pushkin's English-language shelf mapped at once.
59392-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of John Ruskin is a guide compiled by David Widger. It lists the Ruskin books held by Project Gutenberg and gives the table of contents for each in turn. A reader can scan the whole shelf at once, from The King of the Golden River to the five volumes of Modern Painters.

Among the heads stand The Seven Lamps of Architecture, The Stones of Venice in three volumes, and Unto This Last. Smaller works appear too, such as Ruskin Lilies, Hortus Inclusus, and The Harbours of England. The index serves as a map to a vast body of writing on art, building, nature, and society.
59439-tom-slade-on-overlook-mountain:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh sends his boy hero to the Catskills in a scout tale issued by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1923. Howard L Hastings drew the pictures. The Boy Scouts of America approved the book.

Fitzhugh dedicates the tale to his mother. It recalls an afternoon spent on the summit of Overlook Mountain. Thirty-four chapters crowd the list. Hervey wanders in and out early. A stranger, a cup of sorrow, and an unknown friend follow. Tom gets his wish and a job on the mountain. Voices, an accident, and a face in the storm raise the stakes. A criminal and a confidence close the run. The opening warns New York drinkers with the strange tale of old Caleb Dyker. Fitzhugh's scout books preached woodcraft and good turns.
59450-an-attempt-to-explain-the-origin-a:
Gilbert French of Bolton wrote this attempt to explain the origin and meaning of early interlaced ornament, printed at Manchester in 1858. The work studies the woven, knot like carving found on the ancient sculptured stones of Scotland, Ireland, and the Isle of Man. It was printed for presentation only, not for sale.

French traces the style through the Roman time in Britain, the Saxon period, and Norman building work. He notes its return in printed capital letters, in bone lace patterns, and on Highland dirks, targets, and brooches. His plea is modest: even if his theory fails, close looking at these stones may one day prove or refute it.
59847-rainbolt-the-ranger-or-the-aerial-:
Rainbolt, the Ranger is a dime novel in the Beadle line of cheap tales. Its full title adds a claim of an aerial demon of the mountain. The house sold each such book for ten cents by post to any home. Hand book ads in the front list dime guides for speech and song.

The ranger tale forms the core fare of the small cheap book it fronts. Scout craft, horse chases, and high hill perils drive the stock pulp plot. Ads for school books, joke books, and song books fill the front pages. The line served boys and camp men who craved the west in print. Bold types and swift turns mark the whole dime book trade mode.
59853-a-young-hero-or-fighting-to-win:
Edward Ellis wrote a boys tale held under an 1888 right, of school fights and wild scrapes. A front print shows a lion in mid spring in a ring of scared folk, a hint of risks to come. First pages drop in on a road fight by school boys from Tottenville, home from class at noon.

Sam McClay and Joe Hunt trade blows while their friends shout for blood and urge them on. Girls watch in fright and vow to tell the teacher and both mothers of the pair. The first chapter takes its name from a peace maker, and pluck with a good heart is the mark set for its young hero.
59885-wild-animals-of-the-rockies-with-a:
Wild Animals of the Rockies, by James Gilligan, is a short guide with a full list of mammals found in Rocky Mountain National Park. Copies could be had by writing to the author at Boise Junior College in Boise, Idaho. Early pages treat wildlife of the last hundred years, game care, and life zones.

Species notes move from hoofed beasts such as elk, mule deer, and mountain sheep to flesh eaters such as black bear, mountain lion, coyote, and fox. Rodents, hares, shrews, and bats each get short entries. Photos and mark guides help readers tell like beasts apart, such as marten, mink, and weasel. The book serves as a handy field list for park guests and students.
59944-impressions-of-spain:
Impressions of Spain, by Albert F Calvert, came out in London in 1903, with a portrait of Alfonso the Thirteenth at its head. Calvert had written on the finding and survey of Australia. He gives the book to a Spanish friend whose kind help taught him much on his trips.

His preface is plain about the book and its limits. It is no deep or full study of Spain and its people. It is a set of notes on folk met and places seen, over years of trips. Loose chapters grew from a note book, and a rich stock of photos grew with them. Granada and the Alhambra fill much of that stock. Travel readers get warm, frank sketches of a land Calvert calls much misread.
60076-an-englishwoman-in-utah-the-story-:
An Englishwoman in Utah is the autobiography of Fanny Stenhouse, the story of a life's experience in Mormonism. It was published in London in 1880, with a preface by Harriet Beecher Stowe. Stenhouse was for more than twenty-five years the wife of a Mormon missionary and elder in Salt Lake City. Her book promises a full account of the Mountain Meadows massacre and of the life, confession, and execution of John Lee.

Stowe's preface states the book's claim. A woman, a wife and mother, speaks the sorrows and oppressions of which she has been both witness and victim. Her sorrows, Stowe says, are those of thousands who suffer like her and dare not speak. The tale is offered as plain, unvarnished truth, stranger than fiction. Stenhouse dedicated the volume to her children. It remains one of the most read accounts of early Utah by a woman who left the faith.
60109-floyd-s-flowers-or-duty-and-beauty:
Floyd, a Georgia school principal and minister, wrote this book of one hundred stories for colored children. Hertel, Jenkins published it in 1905, with illustrations by John Henry Adams, professor of art at Morris Brown College in Atlanta. The stories are gleaned, the title page says, from the storehouse of human knowledge and experience, and are meant to be simple, amusing, and elevating. President Garfield's words stand at the front: he felt a profounder reverence for a boy than for a man.

The publisher's note gives Floyd's record. He graduated from Atlanta University in 1891, taught and kept school at Augusta, and worked three years as a Sunday-school field worker across the South. He pastored the Tabernacle Baptist Church at Augusta, among the largest in the South. Duty and beauty are his twin themes, and the flowers of the title are the stories themselves, planted for the children.
60269-along-the-mohawk-trail-or-boy-scou:
Boy Scouts on Lake Champlain is the tale inside this scout novel, Along the Mohawk Trail. A letter from the Boy Scouts of America, dated July 31, 1913, heads the book. It states why the tale was made, in the movement's own words.

The leaders learned, the letter says, that a boy must be shaped in his rest hours too, not just in camp and drill. At such times tales of daring deeds catch him whole. So tale writers were set to feed that hunger with clean, stirring stuff. The book that follows sends its patrol up the old Mohawk trail to the lake. War paths, portages, and scout craft fill its road.
60319-jerusalem-the-city-of-herod-and-sa:
Walter Besant and E H Palmer wrote Jerusalem, the City of Herod and Saladin. Bentley published it at London in 1871. A photograph of the Dome of the Rock fronts the book. Palmer held the Arabic chair at Cambridge. Their preface is brief.

The volume gives a history of Jerusalem from about the year 30 to the present time. That span holds the siege and capture by Titus and the last revolts of the Jews. Christian occupation follows. Then come the Mohammedan conquest and the Dome of the Rock. The Crusades, the Christian kingdom, and the reconquest fill the middle. A long Mohammedan occupation closes the story.
60328-the-boy-travellers-on-the-congo-ad:
Thomas Knox wrote The Boy Travellers on the Congo, dated eighteen eighty-seven, as one of his travel books for boys. Two youths, Frank and Fred, cross the sea with Henry M. Stanley, the famed explorer of Africa, and on board they form a small club to study lands and maps. Knox had used the same pair in books on the Far East, South America, and Russia.

The boys read Stanley's Through the Dark Continent as they sail, and it tells how two news firms joined to fund his trip and ready his ship, the Lady Alice. From there the pair follow his route into the heart of Africa. Drawings and plain facts mix with the tale to teach as it moves.
60570-court-life-from-within:
Court Life from Within, by the Infanta Eulalia of Spain, was published at New York in 1915. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the royal memoir in that year. A photograph of the Infanta by Manuel of Paris fronts the volume. The seeds of revolt opens the contents as chapter one of the book.

Irksome duties of a princess and pulling the strings of sovereignty follow in the list. Love and ennui, then my marriage in mourning, fill the personal chapters. England and the English, the Kaiser and his court, and the Tsar and his people come next. The regal pose, Scandinavian democracies, and the courts of Italy round out the survey. Adventures in America and after the war close the contents of the memoir. A princess who chafed at court tells Europe courts from inside the palace.
60725-not-snow-nor-rain:
Not Snow Nor Rain is a science fiction story by Miriam Allen DeFord, taken from Worlds of If for November 1959. A blurb says Sam should have let the twenty two nixies go to the dead letter office, or gone there himself for sanctuary. Sam Wilson is a mail carrier on his last round.

On his first day as a carrier, Sam noted the inscription cribbed from Herodotus on the General Post Office. It vows that not snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night stays these couriers from their rounds. Through the years Sam had been as faithful as any Persian messenger. Now the long years had galloped by, and this was the very last time he would walk his route before retirement. Tale fans get a gentle retirement fantasy.
60802-colin:
Colin, a novel by Benson, was copyrighted in 1923 and issued at New York by Doran. A long list of his earlier books stands at the front. Miss Mapp, Queen Lucia, and David Blaize are among those titles. The author warns that Colin is only the first part of the romance.

A second volume will tell of the final fading of the legend, he says. The story opens with that legend, neither superstition nor its opposite. Benson wrote society novels of wit and quiet malice. Colin stands apart as a darker, stranger tale of his. A family curse and a beautiful, doomed hero shape its course. Readers of Lucia meet a very different Benson in these pages.
60809-gravy-train:
Daniel Galouye's Gravy Train ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in March 1960. Titus McWorther, aged one hundred and thirty, lives retired with his wife Edna on a small planetoid. McWorther's World sits hidden behind a dark nebula, complete with gravity machine, air, soil, and chosen plants and animals. Wanting one last comfort, he orders an automatic bather with a back-scrubbing attachment and toy boat docks. His message crosses in transit with a state paper from Gauyuth-VI through a fault called message interfusion.

The two texts swap signatures on their way through the relay. A bath machine order thus travels under a prime minister's name, while a pledge of interstellar aid bears McWorther's. Undersecretary Wharton Hoverly receives the crossed traffic at Hub City. The tale builds its comedy on the machinery of far-future mail. One old man's small wish sets off a chain no one planned.
61118-westy-martin:
Westy Martin is a scout tale by Percy Fitzhugh, of the Tom Slade line. The scout corps of America gave the book its seal of praise. A gift page sends the tale to a club of men who aid boys. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty four.

A shot, a vow, and a parting open the tale in swift scout mode. First aid, small drops of grace, and a trail hunt fill the early parts. A guilt charge and its price test the young scout in the mid run. A lost son comes home, and a pal named Pee Wee lends noise and aid. One good turn and kin scenes at home close the warm tale.
61146-retief-of-the-red-tape-mountain:
Keith Laumer wrote Retief of the Red-Tape Mountain, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction for May 1962. Consul Passwyn had asked for a small post, he tells Vice-Consul Retief. He had in mind a charming resort world with an occasional visa problem. Instead he keeps zoo for confounded settlers on eight worlds at once. He hates travel, and this backwater system most of all. 

The situation on Adobe nears crisis, he explains at the wall-screen. A handful of Terrestrial settlers has stirred up trouble with the Jaq, the planet's intelligent natives. Sector Headquarters has authorized action at last. Passwyn sends Retief in under sealed orders to work a miracle: peace between settler and Adoban, and a division of territory. Retief knows the use of sealed orders, and the need to keep them that way.
61208-sydney-lisle-the-heiress-of-st-que:
Dorothea Moore wrote Sydney Lisle, the Heiress of St Quentin, printed at Philadelphia. Wal Paget drew the pictures. Contents run to twenty-eight chapters. A wonderful guinea opens the tale, then her own people and uprooted. The first night and the first morning follow. Lord St Quentin, Miss Morrell, and school accomplishments come next, with the heiress-apparent after.

A meeting, on the church tower, and a merry Christmas fill the middle heads. Hugh's battle, at the deanery, and a proposal lead on. St Quentin's story, the chain broken, and Pauly's birthday follow. Hugh to the rescue, fever, given back, and a home-coming close the tale. The first chapter opens on a rainy November afternoon in a dull old square not far from Euston Station. From one house, the last in the square, much more light than usual streams into the dark.
61267-the-surgery-of-the-skull-and-brain:
Surgery of the Skull and Brain is a medical work by Bathe Rawling. Rawling was surgeon at Saint Bartholomew's Hospital in London then. Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton issued it at Oxford in 1912. It forms one of the Oxford Medical Publications for practitioners. Contents open with cranio cerebral topography at page one in detail.

The special technique in operations on the skull and brain follows. Cephaloceles and birth fractures take the third chapter of the work. Rawling had been Hunterian professor and taught operative surgery in London. Tumours, wounds, and pressure on the brain fill his later chapters. Surgeons of 1912 got plates, cases, and hard method in one volume.
61338-moments-with-mark-twain:
Albert Bigelow Paine chose the pieces in Moments with Mark Twain, issued at New York and London in 1920, with roots in a 1907 photo book. Twenty four parts draw on Twain's books and short works. Sketches New and Old leads the set. The Innocents Abroad and Roughing It come next.

Parts draw on Tom Sawyer, Huckleberry Finn, and The Prince and the Pauper too. A Connecticut Yankee, Life on the Mississippi, and Joan of Arc pieces fill the middle. Late parts treat the Jews, Christian Science, and Eve's Diary. One part holds notes from his last days and one holds the death of Jean. The set gives a short path through a long and varied life in print.
6136-bars-and-shadows-the-prison-poems-o:
Ralph Chaplin's Bars and Shadows gathers prison poems with an introduction by Scott Nearing. Chaplin was serving a twenty-year sentence in the Federal Penitentiary, not for violence against person or property, but solely for expressing opinions, accused with fellow prisoners of conspiracy to obstruct the war.

The introduction notes the government produced no single witness to show the war had been obstructed in the relevant way. Poems titled Mourn Not the Dead, Taps, Night in the Cell House, Prison Shadows, and Song of Separation follow. Chaplin writes from a cell about freedom, comrades, and the cost of dissent.
61441-the-little-green-goblin:
James Ball Naylor wrote a tale of a small green goblin for the young. Harry Miller drew its plates for the book of 1907. The book came out in New York, Akron, and Chicago. A front plate shows a fair town: a most fair sight, it says. A broad band of moon light streams in a pane at page 36.

A man takes a great knot pole for a cane at page 82. Two giants grin down in triumph in a late plate's scene. Moon roads, giants, and a fair town give the tale its wild scope. Naylor's verse hand keeps the pace light for young ears. Each plate marks a fresh turn in the goblin's road. Gay and strange it runs.
61657-pathfinding-on-plain-and-prairie-s:
Pathfinding on Plain and Prairie recounts stirring scenes of life in the Canadian North-West. John McDougall wrote the memoir. William Briggs published it at Toronto in 1898. Laughlin supplied the illustrations. McDougall had earlier written Forest, Lake and Prairie.

The contents trace years of mission and travel. Early chapters describe the work of Indian women and the hunts of the men. Winter camping and dog teams follow. An epidemic breaks out among the Indians. McDougall takes a wife and builds at Pigeon Lake. Cree guests steal the horses in one chapter. The Stonies ride in hot pursuit. Later chapters treat the Thirst Dance and its lodges. Buffalo herds frame much of the tale.
61703-a-collection-of-seven-and-fifty-ap:
Printed in London in 1665, a small book of plague cures gathers seven and fifty approved receipts for poor readers. The writer signs as W J and says the receipts come from the five books of secrets by Don Alexes. His long preface tells why he trusts them.

He recalls wounds in 1642, a long gut sickness in 1649, and plague in his house in 1663. One man died, yet the rest of the house lived. He then found the works of Don Alexes in English dress and chose the best cures. Readers get short, plain receipts meant for home use in a plague year.
61719-food-and-flavor-a-gastronomic-guid:
Food and Flavor, a gastronomic guide to health and good living by Henry Finck, was published at New York by the Century Company in 1913. A saying of Brillat Savarin on the destiny of nations heads the book. Pictures by Charles Chapman go with the text. Finck dedicates his work to Luther Burbank and Harvey Wiley.

Those two men, he says, did most to make daily food palatable and honest. The first chapter is called Ungastronomic America, a rebuke to his country. Mark Twain and his patriotic palate enter that chapter early. Food missionaries in the far west and the danger in food follow. Wiley’s poison squad and the fight over preservatives fill the tale. Finck writes as a lover of flavour with a reformer’s zeal.
61808-tales-about-birds-illustrative-of-:
Tales About Birds, by Thomas Bingley, teaches young readers the nature, habits, and instincts of birds. This second edition was printed in London in 1840. Bingley had written stories about dogs and horses in the same vein.

An Uncle Thomas tells the tales to a circle of children. He begins with the golden eagle and stories of its strength and ferocity. The osprey and the bald eagle of America follow, then the vulture and its greed. Falcons and the old sport of hawking fill a chapter, and owls get one on their night hunting gear. The heron, the stork, and the crane close the run shown here. Drawings by Scott, cut by Landells, picture the chief scenes for young eyes.
61865-the-master-of-man-the-story-of-a-s:
The Master of Man is a novel by Hall Caine, subtitled the story of a sin, published by Lippincott in 1921. Caine sets the tale in the Isle of Man, whose law he studied with the island's attorney-general. Its hero, Victor Stowell, rises toward the deemster's seat, the Manx judgeship, with a secret sin behind him.

The contents lay out a seven-book moral architecture: the Sin, the Reckoning, the Consequence, the Retribution, the Reparation, the Redemption and the Resurrection. Chapter titles follow Victor from boyhood and temptation through a trial and a verdict to the grave of a sin and victory through defeat. In a note Caine credits conversations with the writer Franzos for incidents in the book, and reports that Tolstoy found the seed of Resurrection in similar events in Russia. The novel is Caine's last great exercise in the Manx melodrama of guilt and law.
62095-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
Volume five of The Three Voyages of Captain Cook Round the World opens the third voyage. Longman and partners printed the set in London in eighteen hundred twenty one. Maps and plates go with the text. A view of Christmas Harbour in Kerguelen’s Land faces the title page.

Two ships, Resolution and Discovery, sail from England in this part. Omai, a guest from the South Seas, ships out with them. Tenerife and the Cape of Good Hope mark the long road south. At Kerguelen the crews land in a bleak port at Christmas. Van Diemen’s Land and talks with its folk come next. Notes on plants, beasts, and shore life fill the gaps in the log.
62401-mason-s-norwich-general-and-commer:
Mason's Norwich General and Commercial Directory and Handbook is a city directory of 1852. It covers Norwich and the hamlets round it: Earlham, Eaton, Heigham, Hellesdon, Lakenham, and more. The proprietor published it in London and sold it through all booksellers. Subscribers paid two shillings and sixpence; others paid three.

The preface argues the immense utility of a directory in a city of Norwich's importance. Only those who have felt the want, it says, can fairly estimate the worth. Directories listed tradesmen, gentry, carriers, and public offices street by street. They were the search engines of the Victorian city, bought by commercial travellers and counting houses. Mason's volume preserves Norwich at mid century in its most practical form: names, trades, and addresses, arranged for daily use.
62650-the-little-dauphin:
The Little Dauphin is a story for young people, translated from the German of Franz Hoffmann by George Upton. McClurg of Chicago published it in 1905, with four illustrations. Hoffmann's title was Ein Königssohn, a king's son.

Upton's preface calls the Dauphin's story one of the most pathetic in the history of royalty. The boy was Louis Charles, son of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette. His life is measured by the Revolution and the Reign of Terror. Hoffmann follows the accepted version: the child was confined in the Temple. After his parents' execution he was left to waste away under cruel keepers. The brutal cobbler Simon, his keeper, stands out in the narrative. Doubts about the boy's fate, and the pretender Naundorff, add a mystery.
62683-the-camp-fire-boys-at-log-cabin-be:
Camp Fire Boys at Log Cabin Bend is a boys camp tale by Clifton. Oliver Lee Clifton wrote it for Barse and Hopkins in nineteen twenty three. Charles Wrenn drew the pictures of the four chums in tall timber. Clifton also wrote Camp Fire Boys in Muskrat Swamp and at Silver Fox Farm.

Chapters open at nightfall in the big woods with the first campfire lit. The chum beloved, surprise visitors, and busy beaver work fill the early days. A beech tree climber and Amos strange actions stir the camp peace. Traps are set, a storm catches them, and woodcraft pays in need. Elmer plan, a long long night, and sun breaking through end it.
62820-the-fire-within:
Patricia Wentworth wrote The Fire Within, a novel issued by Putnam in New York and London in 1913. A line from Matthew Arnold gives the book its name and its theme: quench the fires of old gods, but not the fire within. The tale opens with old Edward Mottisfont giving his blunt view of his nephew to a friend named David Blake.

The nephew Edward is, in his uncle's word, a prig, and his dead mother's pride is blamed for the flaw. Twenty four parts bring in David Blake, a girl named Elizabeth Chantrey, songs, dreams, a grey wolf, and a lost name. Love must go to school, one part title says, before hearts can be set right.
62843-georgia-s-stone-mountain:
Willard Neal wrote Georgia's Stone Mountain, a book on the Confederate memorial cut into the great granite mount. The carving shows Jefferson Davis and Generals Robert Lee and Stonewall Jackson on horseback. It is the world's largest sculpture, cut into the world's biggest mass of granite: ninety feet tall, one hundred ninety feet wide, rising four hundred feet above the ground.

No hammer blow fell for thirty-six years, from 1928 to 1964, though fifty-five years ran from the plan in 1915 to the finish in 1970. The plan traces back to Helen Plane of the United Daughters of the Confederacy, who raised it in 1909 and 1915. Gutzon Borglum, fresh from praise for his Lincoln, took fire at the sight of the stone. Neal tells the tale of the carving, with a plate of chief carver Roy Faulkner.
62974-benjamin-franklin:
Benjamin Franklin is a biography by Robin McKown, published by Putnam's Sons in New York in 1963 and here in its third impression. Seventeen chapters carry Franklin from a boyhood in Boston to his closing years. The middle chapters treat the birth of Poor Richard, the civic-minded citizen, and the thunder giant of the electricity experiments. Later ones take up the Stamp Act, the Hutchinson letters, and independence.

The opening chapter sketches the Franklins of Boston: poor, numerous, lively, and intelligent. There were seventeen children in all, seven by Josiah Franklin's first wife and ten by his second, Abiah, Benjamin's mother. Suggested reading and an index close the volume, told plainly for the general or younger reader.
63085-the-music-of-spain:
The Music of Spain is a book by Carl Van Vechten, published in New York by Alfred Knopf in 1918. Van Vechten had written on music after the Great War and on interpreters before turning to Spain. A photograph of Mary Garden in the role of Carmen forms the frontispiece.

The book is built in three main parts. The first, Spain and Music, is the long study. The second is called The Land of Joy. The third runs from George Borrow to Mary Garden, joining the great English writer on Spain to the great singer of Carmen. Notes on the text close the volume. Van Vechten writes as a critic and a lover of Spanish art, and the contents promise a survey that moves from folk roots to the opera stage.
63126-royal-palaces-of-spain:
Royal Palaces of Spain is a tale and guide of the seven chief houses of the kings of Spain, by Calvert. He shaped a whole set of books on that land, told of at its front. A hundred and odd prints fill this book, put out at London and New York in the year cut in Roman marks.

His set takes the great paint men of the land, its old towns, its great church store, and its famed drear house of kings. This part starts with that drear house, the vast pile of stone in the hills. Then come the rest of the kings seats: hunt lodges, town houses, and isle homes of the crown.
63136-valencia-and-murcia-a-glance-at-af:
Calvert wrote on Valencia and Murcia for the Spanish Series, printed at London and New York in 1911 with two hundred eighty eight plates. Albert Calvert edited the series, which also holds Goya, Toledo, Madrid, Seville, Murillo, Cordova, El Greco, and Velazquez. The old kingdom of Valencia opens the book, then Saguntum and Castellon, then the kingdom of Murcia.

A general view of Valencia is the title plate. Views from the Puente del Mar, the Puerta de Serranos, the market place, the Puente Real, and the Paseo de la Glorieta fill the picture list. Valencia is shut in between the barren range of the Sierra Molina on the north and the arid plains of Murcia to the south. It is one of the regions of Spain least visited by the tourist, he begins. Orange groves and Moorish towers fill this glance at African Spain.
63287-i-d-like-to-do-it-again:
Owen Davis wrote I'd Like to Do It Again, his life tale, for Farrar and Rinehart at New York in 1931. Davis had won fame as a maker of plays, among them Icebound, The Detour, and The Nervous Wreck. A photo from the White Studio fronts the book. Chapters named False Starts and Selling the First One open his account. A cry of Hold, Villain points to his years in melodrama, the school he rose from.

One chapter claims to tell how to write three hundred plays, his own vast count. The dramatist's profession gets a full part, and Hollywood closes the main tale. Plates show Davis at Harvard in 1889, and stage folk such as Maurice Barrymore.
63322-the-philosophy-of-earthquakes-natu:
The Philosophy of Earthquakes, Natural and Religious, was written by William Stukeley and printed in London in seventeen fifty. C Corbet published this second edition, with a second part added. Stukeley was rector of St George's, Queen Square, and a fellow of the Royal Society and the College of Physicians.

London had just been shaken by two earthquakes in the spring of seventeen fifty. Stukeley delivered the philosophical part to the Royal Society that March. The theological part he preached in his own church. His dedication to Martin Folkes marvels that the shocks moved the whole city yet damaged no building and took no life. The treatise joins natural inquiry to providence, insisting that philosophy without religion is vain curiosity.
63449-the-story-of-the-bank-of-england-a:
Henry Warren's The Story of the Bank of England, published in London in 1903, pairs a history of English banking with a sketch of the money market. Warren had already written Your Bankers' Position at a Glance. His first chapter takes the bank's years of sole rights, from 1708 to 1826, and starts with its founding in 1694.

William Paterson, the Scotsman who put the bank forward, gets a hard look for his Darien scheme and its ruin. Later chapters work through the Act of 1844, the bank's weekly return, its two departments, and its work for the Mint. Credit, the bank rate, the Stock Exchange, and the panic years each get their own study.
63580-the-loot-of-cities-being-the-adven:
Arnold Bennett wrote The Loot of Cities, the adventures of a millionaire in search of joy, a fantasia. Thomas Nelson and Sons published it at London, Edinburgh, and New York. Bennett was the author of The Old Wives' Tale. Six shorter stories stand behind the title piece. Mr Penfound's Two Burglars and Midnight at the Grand Babylon come first. The Police Station and The Adventure of the Prima Donna follow.

The Episode in Room 222, Saturday to Monday, and A Dinner at the Louvre close the set. The Loot of Cities opens on a Friday evening. Bruce Bowring, managing director of a two-million mining corporation, brushes his hair before a Florentine mirror. The telephone calls him into the cabinet. A nameless friend whispers that a determined robbery will be tried at his Lowndes Square house before nine.
63831-queens-of-old-spain:
Martin Hume's Queens of Old Spain was published by Grant Richards in London in October nineteen six and reissued in July nineteen eleven. Hume edited the Calendars of Spanish State Papers and lectured in Spanish history at Pembroke College, Cambridge. A frontispiece shows Mary Tudor, queen of England and Spain, after a painting by Antonio More.

The reissue opens with a grave meditation addressed to the severe but honest public. The books left by a man whose every thought was about books, it argues, are even more himself than his actions in life. A friend's name on a tombstone stirs revolt, since death feels like a cheat even when everyone calls it natural. The Greeks felt it too, the writer says, when they invented Nemesis.
63858-story-telling-ballads-selected-and:
Story-Telling Ballads is a set of ballads chosen by Frances Jenkins Olcott. Olcott selected and arranged them for telling aloud and for young readers. Houghton Mifflin issued the book at Boston and New York in 1920. Colour illustrations from the first printing enrich this text in full. Olcott dedicates the volume to her sister Virginia Olcott by name.

A front picture shows a lift gone dark as wind blows loud at sea. Ballads of storm, love, battle, and ghostly return fill the collection. Each piece is shaped for the voice, with pace and refrain intact. Teachers and parents could read them to boys and girls at home. Olcott, a librarian, knew what tales hold a young audience fast.
64046-home-made-toy-motors-a-practical-h:
Home Made Toy Motors is a practical handbook by A P Morgan, published in New York with copyright in nineteen nineteen. It belongs to an Arts and Sciences series for home builders. Its subtitle promises detailed instructions for building simple but operative electric motors. Chapter one explains how an electric motor works, starting with some principles of magnetism.

The difference between a shunt and a series motor is set out for the beginner. Coils, magnets, wire, and batteries that a boy or hobbyist could find are the materials in view. Morgan wrote to make electricity a bench craft, not a mystery. Step by step builds turn theory into a toy that actually runs.
64300-task-of-kayin:
Task of Kayin is a science fiction tale by William Morrison. It was put out in Planet Stories in July 1953. The head note sets the scene: from out beyond a second sun came a fugitive from a dead and barren world. He sought comfort, friends, and a home on Earth, a planet of still greater terrors.

The tale opens with the lone state of its lead figure. He is no longer much afraid, and at times he thinks his foes back home have ceased to hunt him. Yet among these strange beings he learns that one thing is worse than open hate, and that is cold neglect. They have no more care for him than they have for each other, the tale says, though that neglect adds to his chance of safety.
64308-the-ethic-of-the-assassin:
The Ethic of the Assassin is a science fiction story by Hayden Howard, first printed in Planet Stories in July 1953. It opens on a colony world five light-years from Earth. A young doctor wakes in the night when the cry of the kri-kri falls silent. His wife Kit sleeps beside him, three months from bearing their first child.

Something is wrong outside the dome of the city. A skar comes sputtering toward the window screen, and a spear glints quivering in the wire. The story's title names its theme: an assassin bound by a code, and a death that can be bought. Howard builds the tale from the colony's strange beasts and moons. The doctor must face what the night has brought to his home. The piece is pulp science fiction of the early fifties, tense and strange.
644-the-haunted-man-and-the-ghost-s-barg:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas ghost tale in this novella, where a learned chemistry teacher is haunted by more than a ghost. The haunted man, hollow-cheeked and grizzled, lives in a chamber part library and part laboratory, where students hang on his lips. A spirit offers him a bargain: to forget his sorrows and lose the power to recall pain.

Dickens writes with rich, somber prose, full of fog, bells, and inner echoes. The gift proves a curse, as a man without memory loses pity too. The tale endures as a lesser-known Christmas book, where Dickens warns that sorrow, rightly borne, keeps the heart human.
6446-greifenstein:
F. Marion Crawford opens Greifenstein with Frau von Sigmundskron, called the old baroness though not really much past middle age. Her hair is very white, she is thin and pale, and her bold, almost emaciated features show the framework of departed beauty. She carries her head erect and walks with firm, elastic step, though her looks promise little strength, and she has never been ill in her life.

Her leanness has the most natural of causes, the narrator hints, but she herself would be last to mention it. A mid passage turns to Rex, an enlightened man, learned and cultivated, scorner of old prejudices and cheap theories. He yet trusts astrology enough to risk serious personal interest on what he pretends to foretell. Crawford writes a German castle novel of pride, family, and a rational man caught by an irrational faith.
64496-moses-not-darwin-a-sermon-preached:
Moses, Not Darwin, a sermon by the Reverend B G Johns, was preached at Saint Mark's, Surbiton, Kingston on Thames, on Friday, March 31, 1871. Rivingtons of London printed it at one shilling. Its text is Genesis, chapter two, verse seven: and the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.

Johns preaches against the new teaching that man descends from the ape. He grants that man's body is of the dust, like the beasts that perish. But the sermon holds that man was formed at once by God's own hand, not raised by slow degrees. He is fallen, Johns says, but not utterly debased, and the breath of God in him remains his glory. The sermon is a parish answer to Darwin from a Surrey pulpit.
64535-a-record-of-buddhistic-kingdoms-be:
A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms is the travel account of the Chinese monk Fa Hien, translated by James Legge. Fa Hien travelled in India and Ceylon from the year three ninety nine to four fourteen in search of Buddhist books of discipline. Legge, professor of Chinese at Oxford, translated and annotated the text. The Clarendon Press published it in eighteen eighty six.

A Korean recension of the Chinese text is printed with the translation, as the title states. An introduction covers Fa Hien's life and the soundness of his narrative. Chapters then follow his road from Chang an to the sandy desert and on through Buddhist lands. Pilgrim, scholar, and geographer meet in one early record.
64687-to-be-talked-about-use-cookie-n-cr:
To Be Talked About: Cookie 'n' Cracker Cookin' is a recipe book from a biscuit firm. The United Biscuit Company of America held its rights in 1959. It sold for thirty five cents, to cover handling, by mail. A preface promises recipes that make the hostess talked about for skill. Not hard or costly recipes, the preface stresses, make that fame.

A contents index sorts recipes by type and by page number. Appetizers, soups, snacks, entrees, and vegetables fill the early pages. Salads, pies, cakes, frostings, and desserts fill the later pages. Foods pictured on the cover list a mystery cheese ball and vichyssoise. Steaks Continental, oven fried chicken, and pecan pie tempt the buyer.
6475-facts-and-arguments-for-darwin:
Fritz Muller, translated from German by W. S. Dallas in 1869, offers Facts and Arguments for Darwin after reading On the Origin of Species. One mode of testing Darwin seemed most certain. Apply his views as specially as possible to some particular group of animals, building a genealogical tree for families, genera, or species. Pictures of common ancestors should be as complete as possible. If Darwin were false, detailed application should breed irreconcilable contradictions.

Muller tests, chapter by chapter, whether the tree holds or breaks. A mid passage treats a worm of the Amphinomidae family, guest in the floating Lepas. Its place is intelligible at once from the Darwinian standpoint, while its relation to free living sea worms stays unintelligible otherwise. Muller writes natural history as evidence, where small sea creatures argue a great theory.
64879-the-spiritual-improvement-of-the-c:
Baker, vicar of Fulham, preached a sermon in the parish church of All Saints on March 30, 1851, on the census. His text tells how Davids heart smote him once he had counts made of the people. David owned his act as a great sin and begged God to take the guilt from his servant.

Baker asks what good faith can draw from a head count of the realm, held that same year. Notes back the talk, which was sold in Fulham by Lavis in a cheap print form. Youth, faith, and trust mark Davids rise in the tale, from sheep folds to throne, as a foil for his late lapse.
65177-come-into-my-brain:
Alexander Blade wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Imagination in June 1958. Dane Harrell volunteers to enter a captured alien's brain with a new thought helmet. The head note calls it a fast way to commit suicide. Doctor Phelps asks if he is sure, and Harrell answers that he volunteered. If he is not back in half an hour, Phelps should come get him.

Psionic current surges as the switch is pulled. Harrell glides out of his body and drifts into the alien's skull. Terran patrol ships caught the Dimellian spy near Planetoid 113 a week before. The Earth Dimell war is four years old. Harrell seeks fleet deployment data.
65193-the-frozen-north-an-account-of-arc:
Frozen North, by Edith Horton, tells Arctic exploration tales for school use. Heath issued the revised edition, with rights held in nineteen o four and nineteen eleven. Chapters run in date order from Franklin early voyages to Peary triumph. Maps and views of polar scenes support the school text throughout.

Franklin land trips and the lost Erebus and Terror fill early chapters. Kane, the Eskimos, and hunting in the icy north follow in turn. Nordenskjold northeast passage and the Jeannette voyage come later in line. Greely, Nansen in the Fram, and Andree balloon trip build toward the close. Peary discovery of the North Pole in nineteen o nine ends the book.
65509-the-adventures-of-peterkin:
Gilly Bear tells fairy fun in The Adventures of Peterkin, printed in New York with copyright in 1916. Helen Ohrenschall draws the plates, and Gabriel Sons made the book. The tales first ran in The Evening Sun of New York, by kind leave, the front pages say.

Peterkin Pumperkin heads the cast, with a house of pumpkin shell. Heads send him afloat, to a whale, and to a palace in turn. His appetite and his cooking get heads of their own. He meets a toothless foe, drinks the water of bounceability, and walks the vale of the blind. Valleys of silence and of dancing legs stretch his road. Child readers get brisk, silly peril and safe returns.
65754-the-middleton-place-privy-house-an:
Helen Woolford Haskell wrote a dig report on a privy house at Middleton Place. The report came out in Columbia, South Carolina, in 1981. It sits in a plain series from a state dig and lore unit. A short past of the great house leads the book. Lists of plates and marks close it.

Diggers found china, glass, and drug jars in the privy soil. Wine, beer, and food jars tell what the house used and ate. Lamp glass and lab glass add more small facts. Haskell dates finds by maker marks and known glass dates. Readers learn how trash pits speak of daily life on a farm estate.
65791-tri-nitro-glycerine-as-applied-in-:
Geo M Mowbray wrote on tri-nitro-glycerin as used in the Hoosac Tunnel. James T Robinson and Son printed the work at North Adams in 1872. Mowbray gives the book to Walter Shanly, who saved the tunnel project. A paper read at the Albany Institute grew into these pages.

Underwater blasting and firing mines by electric spark stand among the uses. Mowbray made the fluid's making a trade success at the tunnel works. He hopes to clear errors about its risks and past mishaps. Engineers gain a maker's own account of the strongest blasting agent then known.
65877-destiny-uncertain:
Destiny Uncertain is a science fiction story by Rog Phillips, taken from Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy for May 1952. A blurb asks if fate is a robot typing out the destiny of the world. Lin knew it was true, and with his own future at stake, he stole a page from history.

Lin says with a gloating tone that he is never going to take his last breath. He waits for the remark to land, then adds that he is simply going to take his next to last breath and hold it. Jerry Myer voice emerges from the wave of laughter, serious. There does often seem to be something predestined about death, he says, even seemingly accidental death. Phil Arnoff cries nonsense and points to surgery, serums, and safety devices. Space tale fans get a fate debate.
65910-norse-mythology-or-the-religion-of:
Norse Mythology, or The Religion of Our Forefathers, is a handbook of the myths of the Eddas by Anderson, professor of the Scandinavian languages in the University of Wisconsin. Griggs of Chicago published the second edition in 1876. Its frontispiece shows Thor fighting the giants. Anderson dedicates the book to Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, who had communed with Brage the god of poetry and drunk from the wells of Urd and Mimer.

The myths are systematized and interpreted, with an introduction, vocabulary, and index. The introduction, in a passage preserved in the copy, argues the past's value. The whole past, Anderson writes, is the possession of the present. It had always something true in it, and is a precious possession. In a different time and place, another side of our common human nature was developed. His opening pages call Scandinavian paganism the latest of the old creeds.
65968-the-house-we-live-in:
Vesta Farnsworth wrote this book for home reading. The Pacific Press Publishing Company entered it at Washington in 1900. It helps mothers teach their children how to care for their bodies and the evil effects of narcotics and stimulants. Its title figure is the body as a house, backed by scripture: the body as the temple of the Holy Ghost.

Chapters tour the house part by part. They cover the frame of bones, the walls of muscle, the weatherboards and roofing of skin, the cupola, and the telephone system of the nerves. The kitchen and eating room of digestion and the pumping engine of the heart follow. The lessons come as talk between a mother and children named Helen, Percy, and Elmer, starting with houses of many lands, from wigwams to snow houses. Later chapters name a wicked thief and a cruel murderer among the house's enemies.
66031-the-rise-progress-and-phases-of-hu:
Rise, Progress, and Phases of Human Slavery is a history by James Bronterre O'Brien. William Reeves published it in London in the year 1885. A poem by William Maccall fronts the book in praise of O'Brien. It calls him a man who lived for truth and truth alone. His heart, the verse says, was rent by each slave's moan.

An address to the people says the work appears complete for the first time. In life O'Brien was blocked from finishing his history by exploiters. Editors built the whole from his various writings kept in print. His own words, ungarbled by foreign pens, form the rule of the edition. The title states his arc: how slavery came, and how it shall go out.
66116-modern-greek-folklore-and-ancient-:
John Cuthbert Lawson wrote Modern Greek Folklore and Ancient Greek Religion, a study put out at Cambridge in 1910. Lawson was a fellow and a teacher at Pembroke College in that town. His short title calls the work a study in things that live on past their age. The book grew from two years of work in Greece.

Lawson held a post for study from 1898 to 1900, by the gift of Lord Craven of old. He thanks that gift for his chance to roam and learn. His first plan was to study the ways and fears of the Greeks of his day. He sought what light those ways cast on the faith of the Greeks of old. The book weighs tales, rites, and fears that held on through long years of change. It shows a past faith at work in the life of a new land.
66364-guide-to-the-norris-geyser-basin:
Guide to the Norris Geyser Basin is a fifteen-cent trail pamphlet for Yellowstone National Park. The basin is named for Philetus W Norris, the park's second superintendent, from 1877 to 1882. He did not discover it, the guide owns. His explorations and reports called attention to the area. Norris is considered the hottest and most active geyser basin in the park. Its features change faster than anywhere else in Yellowstone.

A new hot spring may come into being literally overnight here. It may last a few days, a month, or many years. The ground is unstable and hazardous in many places. Visitors must stay on the trails and boardwalks at all times. Nothing may be thrown into the pools, since debris can clog a vent and kill a spring. Pets are barred from the trails.
66434-let-space-be-your-coffin:
Tenneshaw wrote a tale of a space freight man who plots a clean kill. The tale ran in Imagination in November 1954. Bert hates Miles and holds that Miles stole his due. Their freight line is the best in the whole star set, Bert claims. Miles has his eyes on Carol, Bert's own girl, as well.

I shall kill you, Miles Berendt, Bert thinks in cold wrath. Miles lorded it over him since both were mere kids, he holds. Now Miles has all but seized the firm Bert helped build. A tally book and a desk talk start the last day's calm. No atoms of Miles shall be found, Bert vows in thought. Crime in the void takes new forms here.
66439-on-strike-or-where-do-the-girls-co:
On Strike, or Where Do the Girls Come In, is a novel by Glenfield, made out to all his sisters of the south land. It came out at Sydney in the year of the great sea strike of that land. Its hero is a rich young heir.

He was born, the text says, with the stock spoon of gold in his mouth. How his house got its wealth the book will not say. At one and twenty he was worth a vast sum in gold coin of the realm. He was deep in love with a girl born in a town by his own lands. His love was no swift craze. He had borne her in his arms as a babe and prized her as a child of twelve.
66519-the-power-of-music-in-which-is-sho:
The Power of Music is a set of tales of tone force on man and beast. A Harris house of London brought it out in eighteen fourteen. A front plate shows the Ox Minuet from a page deep in the book. Its first tale tells of fits eased by tone play in a sick girl. Grief in her youth broke her frame health and brought on fall fits.

Fits came first each month, then day by day in worse count. Drugs made the ill worse, and no cure held the fits at bay. A concert by chance left her free of fits while it played. Fits came late that round, so tone play was tried once more. Her sire in the end kept tone at hand as her chief cure.
66564-the-heart-s-domain:
Georges Duhamel, a French writer, set down a set of essays on the good life called The Heart's Domain. Eleanor Stimson Brooks turned the work into English, and it came out in New York in 1919. Duhamel had won note for a book on the war years. He gave this book to his son Bernard.

Ten parts treat the hope of happiness, wealth and want, the hold we have on others, and the finding of the world. Later parts sing the lyrics of life, treat sorrow and giving up, and seek a shelter for life. The first essay grants that he had to pass middle age to see that happiness is the aim of all life. Friends he asked gave wild, split answers, which the book works through.
66651-meadowlark-basin:
Meadowlark Basin is a Western novel by Bower, author of Chip of the Flying U. Little, Brown held the rights in 1925, and Grosset and Dunlap issued this printing. A frontispiece by Gage shows a rider's amazement. The contents run to twenty four chapters of range intrigue.

Lark rides to a hill brow and stops, as habit bids him, to gaze below. Four hundred feet down lies Meadowlark Basin, the stronghold of old Bill Larkin. The Little Smoky River races past the meadows like a millrace. Chapter titles promise rustling, branding, and a sign of the golden arrow. Butch Cassidy himself gives advice in one chapter. Stolen money is found, and shots are asked after in another. Snowball testifies at the close. Bower wrote knowing Westerns for a wide public.
66864-moving-the-mountain:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote a novel printed at New York in 1911. On a gray, cold, soggy Tibetan plateau, two white people glared at one another, a man and a woman. With him stood a group of peasants in peasant dress. With her stood the guides and carriers of a well fitted exploring party. The woman's eye caught sunlight on a belt buckle of twisted initials.

Where did you get that belt, she cried. The man threw back his hood, and the bearded face under it was white. John, she cried, John, my brother, and he answered Nellie and fell. A brother lost for years wakes in an America remade by his sister's faith. Gilman builds her case for a saner world inside a homecoming tale.
67451-minor-tibetan-texts-1-the-song-of-:
Johan van Manen prepared this first part of Minor Tibetan Texts for the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Its press at Calcutta printed it in 1919 in the Bibliotheca Indica line. The text it presents is The Song of the Eastern Snow-Mountain, a Tibetan song in print for students of the tongue.

Van Manen opens by showing how little was then known of spoken Tibetan. He quotes Lewin's manual of 1879 and the great Jäschke word book to make the point. Songs and folk tales of the people, he notes, stayed almost unknown to the West. A printed song with a scholar's care helps fill that gap for those who read Tibetan.
67580-under-the-skin:
Leslie Perri wrote Under the Skin, illustrated by Engle, printed in Infinity Science Fiction for June 1956. The narrator runs the Martian desk of Universal News. He tells of okaying a picture of a Martian diplomat's wife at a tea. In her Rio couture she looked a carbon copy of every other woman. What was different about her was no longer very different, he says. The thought saddens and frightens him. It takes him back to his Marsport days.

He and Deborah pioneered the bureau there in the gloomy early days. The biggest story they ever covered is the one they never wrote. A news flash came in from Faleeng, a hill community in the Ul Mountains. Disaster had struck the remote mining settlement. Power failure threatened the community, and the official call for help reached Marsport with the flash.
67768-hand-book-of-sanitary-information-:
Roger Tracy wrote a home hand book on health in the house. Tracy was a health scout for New York City's board. Appleton of New York put the book out. Its themes are air, drains, and the care of those with catching ills. Clean-up, food, and water each take their own part.

Back parts deal with the stuffs that kill germs in a home. A list of plumber's goods and their worth ends the book. Tracy writes for house folk, not for men of the cure art. Plain rules tell how to vent a room and guard a well. Sick room care is spelled out step by step. Town homes in that age had much need of such a guide.
67959-on-the-preparations-of-the-indian-:
W B O'Shaughnessy, a doctor in the Bengal Army, wrote on Indian hemp, or gunjah, in work reprinted from Calcutta and London journals. His paper dates from eighteen thirty-eight and eighteen forty-three. He had taught chemistry and drugs at the Medical College of Calcutta.

He notes that hemp was widely used in Africa, Asia, and South America, yet little known in Europe. He asks if the hemp of cold lands is the same plant as that of India. The resin, he argues, gives the drug its strength. He then tests its use for tetanus and other spasm ills, where pain and cramp stand out.
68491-the-improved-antidote-supposed-to-:
A Dublin pamphlet of 1820 answers the Reverend Sir Harcourt Lees and his Antidote, an anti-Catholic tract. The improved antidote of the title claims to be more active in expelling poison than that late invention. Its purpose is plain on the title page: the Catholics are vindicated from his abuse, and their claims for unrestricted emancipation are considered. A saying of Basil in Greek heads the address to the public.

The writer begins with the nation: decay of trade, a long ruinous war, lavish expenditure, and an oppressive debt have sunk a great commercial people to distress. The people murmur and rise; the administration reaches for coercion. In such a crisis, remedies are every man's business. Lees's remedy, the pamphlet argues, would cherish the malignancy of the disease rather than eradicate its cause. Emancipation, argued in the language of physic nine years before it passed, is the counter-prescription.
68725-snap-a-legend-of-the-lone-mountain:
Snap, a Legend of the Lone Mountain, by C Phillipps Wolley, was printed in a new edition in London in 1892, with thirteen plates by H G Willink. Wolley had written Sport in the Crimea and Caucasus. He gives the book to small Clive, his three year old son.

A verse to Clive jokes that the boy will cost him a lot, and warns him to be brave and go straight. Chapters open with a cricket match, Fernhall against Loamshire, and a ghost at Fernhall. Later heads take the cast out of Liverpool to bear hunts, scrub cattle, and branding in the wild west. A firm called Bull Pine is founded, then lost. The close climbs Lone Mountain to the end of the rope. Boys got sport at home and abroad in one tale.
6873-mark-twain:
Archibald Henderson writes Mark Twain with photographs by Alvin Langdon Coburn. He opens with Bliss Carman's verse on Twain jesting in Avalon, isle of dreams. Chaucer, Shakespeare, Molière, and Cervantes listen and smile there. Henderson's preface speaks of a debt of personal gratitude owed by men, women, and children worldwide for Twain's humor and charm.

From childhood, Henderson says, his feeling for Twain was warm and personal, drawn first from the books alone, from Tom, Huck, Jim, and Brer Rabbit. The biography that follows traces that beloved life. Mark Twain is a fond, early life of America's great humorist, full of affection and anecdote.
68896-cat-o-mountain:
Cat O Mountain is a tale of hill crime by Arthur Friel. Donald Humphreys drew the prints that dress the text. The author had past fame with a tale of a king of the north hills. The book came out in Philadelphia in the year nineteen twenty three.

A panther in the hills gives the tale its name and first dread. Parts track a run man, a knock out, a death, and a scrap of paper. Law men come, a hill code rules, and a stab falls in the night. A gift page thanks a kind pair who fed a stray cat at their door. Man hunts and ghost hands drive the swift pulp chain to its close.
69131-the-northmen-in-britain:
Eleanor Hull wrote The Northmen in Britain, for Crowell at New York, with sixteen full-page plates. Meredith Williams drew the pictures for the book. An old English poem, The Seafarer, stands at the front in Hull's English. It tells of a heart that yearns ever for sea-faring and the rolling of waves. Hull had written on the Gael, Cuchulain, and early Ireland before this work.

Contents open with the age of the Vikings and the first coming of the Northmen. The saga of Ragnar Lodbrok, called Hairy-Breeks, and a call for help follow. Alfred the Great, Harald Fairhair of Norway, and the Orkney settlements take their turns. The Northmen in Ireland, Athelstan, Brunanburh, and Hakon the Good fill the close. Hull gives young readers the Viking age in Britain in saga tone and plain fact.
69244-via-berlin:
Crittenden Marriott wrote this spy novel, copyrighted in 1917, by the author of Sally Castleton, Southerner. It opens in the Secretary of State's office, where a young naval officer named Topham is studied in silence before being told to sit down.

Topham is posted as naval attaché to Tokyo, and the Secretary has something else in mind. Rather than the direct route by San Francisco, he is to travel by Europe and the Suez Canal, indicating a desire to go by Berlin. An old Annapolis chum at the Berlin embassy gives him his excuse. Orders will send him onward to join a battleship at Brindisi. The illustration promises two men waiting with baited breath. Readers get American espionage fiction from the year of intervention.
69610-robin:
Mary Grant Bruce wrote a girls book printed at Sydney in 1926 by the Cornstalk Publishing Company. Bruce had written A Little Bush Maid, Mates at Billabong, and Norah of Billabong. The first edition of four thousand copies in June 1926 was followed by a second of three thousand in August. Robin flung the gate open, a picture shows from page two hundred seventy five.

Calton Hall opens the contents, then next day, Merri Creek, and plans and problems. Two months later, Robin finds stranded wayfarers, and a business arrangement follows. Making friends, the Merri Creek falls, the hut in the scrub, and concerning the end of a pig fill the middle. Strangers, Black Sunday, and the last chapters close an Australian tale. Bruce's bush girls ride, work, and laugh through hard seasons.
698-memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this memoir of Fleeming Jenkin, the Scottish engineer and teacher who was his friend. Jenkin worked on telegraph cables, taught at Edinburgh, and wrote on many topics, from drama to trade. Stevenson draws him as a man of restless mind, warm talk, and strong views, liked by students and peers alike.

The memoir first served as an introduction to a set of Jenkin's papers, and it stands alone here. Stevenson blends fact with fond recall, showing Jenkin's work, his home life, and his talk. It gives a vivid portrait of a Victorian man of science who was also a man of letters, seen through the eyes of a novelist who knew him well.
69834-seven-years-in-vienna-august-1907-:
Seven Years in Vienna, August nineteen oh seven to August nineteen fourteen, a Record of Intrigue, was issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in nineteen seventeen. The book was printed in Great Britain. A front plate shows the German Emperor and the Emperor of Austria driving in Vienna in nineteen oh eight. More than twenty chapters fill the volume. Courts, counts, and Balkan plots drive the tale.

Chapter one treats King Edward at Ischl and a parting of the ways. The Emperor illness and Archduke Francis Ferdinand follow, with Countess Chotek. Kaiser Wilhelm in Vienna, affairs in Turkey, and the annexation fill the middle. The Great Servia idea, the Balkan War, and King Ferdinand of Bulgaria add fuel. Berchtold and Tisza, called the men who decided on war, stand near the end. Readers get an insider tale of the road to the Great War.
70154-murderer-s-chain:
Wenzell Brown's Murderer's Chain ran in Fantastic Universe in March 1960, a crime tale told by the murderer himself. The narrator wants money, and his rich mother-in-law Maudie will not give it to him.

He complains that Maudie refused him ten thousand dollars for a Martian mining venture that proved sound. Now she will not stake five thousand dollars on the Balsavius Six Mining Corporation, a secret deal offered by his friend Sylvester. His wife Isabelle would inherit everything at her mother's death, so he turns over ways to kill her. Shooting or stabbing seem vulgar to him; he hunts for a subtle poison instead. The story's chill comes from his calm, whining voice as he plans.
70287-algeria-from-within:
Bodley wrote Algeria from Within after living in the country, and the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis published it in 1927. He dated his thanks from Laghouat in November 1926, and dedicated the book to his many friends of all nationalities in Algeria. Maps and photographs fill the volume.

The contents show a full survey. A little geography and a little history lead to the French conquest and the inhabitants of today. Then come the French administration and the Arab administration side by side, the marabouts or holy men, and the Arab character. Life among the Arabs, Arab women, music and dancing, and religion take the middle chapters. Superstitions, the hero Abd-el-Kader, education, and sport follow, with the nomads and sheep breeding toward the end. English readers got the colony explained by a man who had friends inside it.
70375-discoveries-in-egypt-ethiopia-and-:
Richard Lepsius wrote Discoveries in Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Peninsula of Sinai, in a second English edition of eighteen fifty-three. Kenneth R H Mackenzie edited the text with notes. Frederick William the Fourth of Prussia had sent the mission out.

The party worked from eighteen forty-two to eighteen forty-five, by the king's rich funding. Its aim was to study and gather the old monuments of the Nile valley and Sinai. Alexander von Humboldt backed the work, and Lepsius gave him the book. A great work of plates, with more than eight hundred plates planned, was to follow. Front pictures show Mount Barkal in Nubia and Meroe. Topography and carving lead.
7046-annals-and-reminiscences-of-jamaica:
Harriet Manning Whitcomb prepared her annals and reminiscences of Jamaica Plain at request, to be read before the Jamaica Plain Ladies Tuesday Club. A wish to preserve the paper led her to print it for sale at a fair for the Jamaica Plain Indian Association, though she felt reluctant to appear in public print. She drew on the Memorial History of Boston, Drake's Town of Roxbury, Doctor Thomas Gray's Half Century Sermon, and the memory of older residents.

If any date or incident proves wrong, she begs readers charity and courtesy for indulgent criticism. The sketch that follows collects and reviews the circumstances and events of a Boston neighborhood, from early days to the author's own time. It is a local history written by a neighbor for neighbors, plain, fond, and careful.
70562-be-young-again:
Be Young Again is a feature novel by Murray Leinster. The tale ran in a science fiction magazine in the summer of 1950. Its blurb sets an elixir of youth pitch against an old bootlegging baron. The narrator is a boy of sixteen who works with a very old partner.

Old Jode, the narrator's friend, is a prince among swindlers. He once sold a gold brick to the Denver mint, the boy boasts. He also emptied a bank by mailing its cash to himself from inside. Now Jode means to crown his career by fleecing Vachti, a rich old liquor baron. A professor named Barr has a fake youth cure to sell the old man. But Buck, the boy hints, has the real goods. Leinster tells the con in slangy first person.
708-the-princess-and-the-goblin:
George MacDonald wrote this fairy tale about Princess Irene, a small girl who lives in a mountain house watched over by her nurse. Below the mountain live goblins, who plot to steal her and marry her to their prince. Curdie, a miner's boy, hears their plans in the mines and warns the household.

Irene finds help from a mysterious great-grandmother, who gives her a thread to follow through dark halls. Courage, trust, and kind deeds guide the children past traps and tunnels. The tale blends wonder with moral weight, and it has long been a favourite first fantasy for young readers.
70803-darwin:
Gamaliel Bradford wrote a study of Charles Darwin dated 1926, as one of his soul portraits of famed lives. A time line at the front runs from birth at Shrewsbury in 1809 to death at Down in 1882. Sea years on the Beagle, wed life with Emma Wedgwood, and the books of 1859 and 1871 mark the span.

Chapters name Darwin in turn as observer, thinker, and the man who found a great truth. Later parts call him loser, lover, and wrecker of old faith, then close on the temper of science itself. Prints show the child, the ship laid ashore, the study at Down, and the man in age.
70882-the-clue-of-the-new-pin:
The Clue of the New Pin is a mystery novel by Edgar Wallace, with rights dated nineteen twenty three. Burt published the New York edition by arrangement with Small, Maynard and Company. Chapter one sets out Yeh Ling's restaurant between theatreland and a rough street. The Golden Roof, as it grows to be called, gleams with tiles and rosewood.

Yeh Ling began with strange Chinese dishes at the street's respectable end. House by house his place crept toward the lights and grew rich and sedate. A French chef and Italian waiters serve the fine diners in its rooms. But one back room, number six, is never let to any diner at all. It keeps its old plain look and its soft footed waiters from Han Kow. A hidden patron's will keeps that room apart for darker business.
71029-jasper-s-old-shed-and-how-the-ligh:
Jasper's Old Shed is a religious tale by Coker, published in London by the Religious Tract Society. A picture shows a girl saying she has come for the goods. The first chapter presents the shed and its master. Jonas Jasper's sign-board has swung over his entry for more than forty years, the tale says.

Jasper is a general and marine store dealer who gives best prices and refuses no reasonable offer. Everyone in the poor neighbourhood knows him, the oldest inhabitant of the street. Chapters follow his troubled thoughts, lessons from rags, and Phil's start in life. The Christmas message and the home call bring the light of the title into the old shed.
71100-memoirs-of-a-griffin:
Captain Bellew tells the tale of a young cadet in his first year in India. The book came out in a new form in London in 1891. Bellew says he mixed fact and tale on purpose. He drew the scenes from life he knew well.

A griffin was a new hand, fresh and green to the work. The tale shows the men, ways, and small shocks such a youth met. Bellew wrote for readers who liked a light, true tone. The book gives a clear view of army life in India in that age.
7112-erema-or-my-father-s-sin:
R D Blackmore's Erema, or My Father's Sin, opens with a biblical curse that has followed the heroine always. It speaks of the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation. If she had not known her father, loved him, and closed his eyes in desert silence deeper than the grave, her path might have differed. The common business of the world might have led her down the general track that leads to nothing.

Until her father fell and died, she never dreamed he could die, so resolute was he in seeing her safe in a new home before starting again for remoter solitudes. His mind once made up, no one had ever known him fail of it, and he showed that resolve in the last and fatal act of his fatal life. The novel that follows is a daughter's reckoning with a father's sin.
71674-less-than-kin:
Alice Duer Miller wrote a novel published by Henry Holt at New York in May 1909. Chapter one opens as a theater curtain rolls down and the horns give a final blare. The whole house rustles with returning self consciousness. Mrs Raikes and Miss Lewis have always had orchestra seats for Monday nights. Their jeweled collars and little bare backs are familiar to opera goers.

They have the reputation of being musical, the narrator notes dryly. Miller wrote society fiction before her verse narrative White Cliffs made her famous. Less than kin treats family claims and social rank in New York. Holt published several of her novels in these years.
71687-the-art-and-mystery-of-curing-pres:
A wholesale curer of meats wrote a plain manual of his trade for Chapman and Hall in 1864. The title page keeps his name hid. The book treats curing, preserving, and potting for meats, game, and fish. It adds the arts of pickling and of keeping fruits and vegetables, and it aims at dealers and housekeepers alike.

In his preface the author sets out his whole field. Light and heavy salting, drying by soft heat and moving air, and smoking with woods, peat, and turfs all stand there. He treats the marinating of fish and the bucaning of meats, a way of part drying and part smoking. He blames poor fuel for many spoiled hams and tongues. A cheap curing and smoking device is described at the back. He pledges that no harmful stuff is urged in his pages to please the eye at the cost of the stomach.
72165-memoirs-of-the-lady-hester-stanhop:
Volume one of the Memoirs of the Lady Hester Stanhope, in their second edition, was published by Henry Colburn in London in 1846. The memoirs are her own telling, taken down from her conversations with her physician, and comprise her opinions and anecdotes of some of the most remarkable persons of her time. Three volumes hold the whole.

A preface to the second edition answers the critics. The author will not reply to desultory reviews, but he takes up one point of fact: the Quarterly Review had claimed that Earl Stanhope flatly contradicted part of the Conversations. What his lordship denied, the preface says, was no part of those conversations at all, but an extract from a letter of Lady Hester's own to the Duke of Wellington. The answer the review left out is printed here, to set the record right.
72166-memoirs-of-the-lady-hester-stanhop:
Memoirs of the Lady Hester Stanhope lets a famed exile speak for herself. Her talk was set down in long visits with her own physician. Henry Colburn put out the second edition in London in 1846. Three volumes hold her views and tales of the great of her age. This hosted text is the second of those three volumes.

Chapter one starts with her birth line and her flight from England. She went to live with her uncle, Prime Minister Pitt, in time. Pitt trusted her sense and praised her grasp of state craft. Tales of George the Third, General Moore, and great lords fill the talk. Her scorn of doctors and her views on prudery spice the pages. Stowe visits and Walmer work show her in Pitt's last years.
72167-memoirs-of-the-lady-hester-stanhop:
Memoirs of the Lady Hester Stanhope holds her talk as set down by her doctor. The hosted text is the third volume of the three volume set. A print shows her home at Joon on Mount Lebanon in the east. This copy is a second run, set in London in eighteen forty six.

Parts trade tales of a Prince who roamed the east in those years. A cave of snakes, a ride to Sayda, and court ways fill the talk. Her money woes are owned: rich rooms kept though funds ran low. Restless moods and sharp views of famed men mark her late voice. The book is a chief well for her odd fame in the east.
