Benjamin is the tribe of Israel named for Jacob’s youngest son by Rachel. Alone among the brothers he was born in Palestine itself, between Bethel and Ephrath. His dying mother called him Ben-oni, “Son of my sorrow,” and his father changed it to Benjamin, likely “Son of the right hand.”

Jacob’s blessing calls Benjamin a tearing wolf, and the tribe’s fighters kept that fierce name: Ehud, Saul and Jonathan came from it. Its slingers were famed as left-handed, some even skilled with both hands. In the days of the judges the tribe was nearly wiped out, six hundred men escaping, then rebuilt. Bethel and Jerusalem both lay in its story, giving the least of the tribes an odd weight in Israel’s religion.
britannica-1911-bennett-charles-edwin:
Charles Edwin Bennett (born 1858) was an American classical scholar born at Providence, Rhode Island. Brown University graduated him in 1878, and he studied further at Harvard and in Germany. After school teaching in Florida, New York and Nebraska, he held Latin chairs at Wisconsin, Brown and, from 1892, Cornell.

Bennett’s studies of Latin syntax, above all his papers on the subjunctive, rest on counting through texts, a fresh method with new names for its findings. He led the “New American School” of syntax scholars, who demand a fresh look at all the evidence first. His Latin Grammar of 1895 recast the short scholarly school grammar for America, and he edited school texts of Tacitus and Cicero.
britannica-1911-benzoin-resin:
Benzoin, also called gum Benjamin, is a balsamic resin drawn from Styrax benzoin, a fair-sized tree of Sumatra and Java, and from other Styrax kinds. The name may come from an Arabic word for frankincense, its first syllable lost in European mouths. The resin is not secreted freely: it forms as the tree’s answer to cuts in its bark.

Siam benzoin is the finest sort, small “tears” of resin with a sweet smell owing partly to vanillin, rich in benzoic acid. Sumatra benzoin comes in dull red masses holding white tears and carries cinnamic acid too. Palembang benzoin ranks lowest of the three. Much benzoin is burned as incense, and its medical uses rest on the benzoic acid inside it.
britannica-1911-berlin:
Berlin, capital of Prussia and of the German Empire, receives one of the longest city articles in the 1911 Britannica. It lies on both banks of the Spree. The ground is flat and sandy, 110 feet above sea level. The city is the seat of the emperor, the Reichstag, and the imperial offices. It also hubs a great railway network and busy waterways.

The article covers the site, quarters, public buildings, industry, trade, and growth of the city. Its history runs from medieval trade through occupation in the Seven Years' War. It also covers the French occupation of 1806 to 1808. The hosted text adds a companion account of the Congress and Treaty of Berlin of 1878. That treaty redrew the Balkan settlement after war.
britannica-1911-bertin:
Bertin is a family name of weight in French journalism. Its head was Louis François Bertin (1766–1841), called Bertin aîné and born in Paris. He wrote for papers during the Revolution. After the 18th Brumaire he founded the Journal des Débats. The consulate suspected his royalist views and exiled him in 1801. He returned in 1804 to run the paper under censorship.

Napoleon renamed the paper Journal de l'Empire in those years. In 1811 the government took its conduct and profits over entirely. Bertin regained it in 1814 and restored the old title. He is often called the father of modern French journalism. His brother and his two sons carried the paper on after him.
britannica-1911-bilin:
Bilin, in Czech Bilina, is a town of Bohemia in Austria, 90 miles north of Prague by rail. Its 1900 population was 7,871, chiefly German. The town is very old and stands on the river Biela. A castle of the 17th century, held by Prince Lobkowitz, stands in it. Large lignite mines work in the ground nearby. Basalt rocks ring the town on every side.

Bilin is famous above all for its mineral springs, the Biliner Sauerbrunnen. Their water holds a large share of bicarbonate of soda, at a temperature of 45.6 degrees Fahrenheit. About four million bottles of the water are exported every year. Salt recovered by evaporation is a second export of the town. The 1911 Britannica entry also praises the Biliner Stein, a phonolite crag south of town. Rare plants grow on it, and the view is fine.
britannica-1911-bin:
Bin is a word for a receptacle of various kinds, first made of wicker or basket-work. The word appears in most European languages, the 1911 Britannica entry says. The Italian benna and the German Benne match it closely. Etymologists trace the family to a root meaning to plait. That root fits the woven basket the first bins plainly were.

The entry lists the forms the word keeps in daily speech. A dust-bin holds refuse, and a wine-bin holds bottles in a cellar. Hop-bin, coal-bin, and corn-bin name store boxes for farm and fuel use. Each keeps the old sense of a fixed container for loose goods. The entry is a short glossary note of a few lines.
britannica-1911-bisharin:
Bisharin are a nomad tribe of African Arabs, of Hamitic origin, in the eastern Nubian desert. The ancients knew them as the Ichthyophagi, the fish-eaters. In the middle ages they were known as the Beja. The 1911 Britannica entry calls them the most characteristic of the Nubian Arabs. With the Ababda and Hadendoa they stand for the Blemmyes of classical writers. In language and geography they link the Hamitic peoples with the Egyptians.

Nominally the Bisharin are Muslims, the entry says. Yet they keep some non-Islamic practices alive beside that faith. Traces of animal worship show in one firm rule: they never kill the serpent or the partridge, holding both sacred. The entry is a short ethnographic note of a few lines. It gives the tribe's desert home, its old names, and that striking custom. No numbers or chiefs are named.
britannica-1911-bissell-george-edwin:
George Edwin Bissell (1839– ) was an American sculptor, born at New Preston, Connecticut, on 16 February 1839. His father was a quarryman and marble-cutter. During the Civil War Bissell served as a private in the 23rd Connecticut volunteers. That service ran in the Department of the Gulf in 1862 and 1863. On mustering out he became an acting assistant paymaster in the South Atlantic squadron. After the war he joined his father's business at home.

He studied sculpture abroad in 1875 and 1876. He lived much in Paris from 1883 to 1896, with visits home between. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his chief works across two countries. They include the Waterbury soldiers' and sailors' monument, a Lincoln statue at Edinburgh, and Burns and Highland Mary at Ayr. A statue of President Arthur stands in Madison Square, New York. Chancellor Kent's statue went to the Congressional library in Washington.
britannica-1911-black-mountain:
Black Mountain is a range and border district on the Hazara side of the North-West Frontier Province of India. The range runs 25 to 50 miles and averages about 8000 feet high. It rises from the Indus basin. Yusafzai Pathan groups lived on its western face. Among them were the Hassanzais, the Akazais, and the Chagarzais.

Most of the entry lists four British expeditions into the district. Forces went in during 1852–53, after two customs officers were murdered. They went again in 1868, after a police post at Oghi was attacked. The Hazara expeditions of 1888 and 1891 followed years of raids. Each time, large forces crossed the tribal country. The tribes then submitted and agreed to keep the peace.
britannica-1911-bloemfontein:
Bloemfontein is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes the capital town of the Orange Free State in South Africa. The town lies on open grass veld, ringed by low round hills. Streets cross at square angles round a large market square at its heart.

The entry tells how a stream runs through the town from end to end. A great flood led men to straighten its course and bridge it in stone. Fine halls of red brick and pale stone face the square in rows. One hall held the old state council and now holds the province one. A plain hall in town saw the pact that freed the Boer state.
britannica-1911-bodkin: Bodkin is a small tool of needlework, defined in a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In old English the word meant a dagger, from a source no one has fixed, though a Gaelic word for a short sword may be kin. The tool is a slim, needle like piece of steel or bone. It has a flat knob at one end and one or more eyes, through which cord, tape or ribbon can be drawn along a hem.
britannica-1911-bodmin:
Bodmin is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a market town and borough in Cornwall, England, and the county town. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred one. It lies between two hills in a short valley at the south edge of Bodmin Moor.

The text describes the large church of Saint Petrock, with older parts and a late Norman font. Near it stand a ruined chapel and a Tudor tower in the burial ground. Parts of an old Franciscan friary live on in the market house. The entry also notes the town prison and its rail links to Plymouth.
britannica-1911-bonnat-leon-joseph-flore:
Léon Joseph Florentin Bonnat (born 1833) was a French painter famed for strong, lifelike portraits. Born at Bayonne, he was schooled in Spain under Madrazo at Madrid. His long line of portraits shows the mark of Velasquez and the Spanish realists, the entry says.

At Paris he won the medal of honour in 1869 and became one of the leading artists of his day. In 1888 he took the painting chair at the École des Beaux Arts. In May 1905 he followed Paul Dubois as its director. Portrait painting in a vivid manner is called his most characteristic work. His subject pictures also won fame, among them the Martyrdom of St Denis in the Panthéon.
britannica-1911-boos-martin:
Martin Boos (1762–1825) was a German Catholic priest whose warm, inward piety won him followers and enemies in turn. Born at Huttenried in Bavaria on Christmas Day 1762, orphaned at four, he was raised by an uncle at Augsburg and sent to the university of Dillingen. There he formed the modest piety that marked his whole life.

After serving in Bavarian towns he moved in 1799 to Linz in Austria, welcomed by Bishop Gall, and in 1806 became pastor at Gallneukirchen. His movement spread among Catholic laypeople and drew some fifty or sixty priests. When Gall and other protectors died, persecution began about 1812, with endless charges in the church courts. Prussia sheltered him at last, with a Düsseldorf professorship in 1817 and the pastorate of Sayn in 1819.
britannica-1911-brierley-benjamin:
Benjamin Brierley (1825–1896) was an English weaver who became a popular writer in Lancashire dialect. Born near Manchester to humble parents, he started work in a textile mill and taught himself in his spare time. At about thirty he began placing pieces in local papers, and sketches gathered as A Summer Day in Daisy Nook in 1859 won him notice.

In 1863 he turned fully to writing and journalism, bringing out Chronicles of Waverlow that year and the long tale The Layrock of Langley Side in 1864, later put on stage. He ran Ben Brierley's Journal, a weekly, from 1869 to 1891, and gave public readings of his work, touring America in 1880 and 1884. His Ab-o'-th'-Yate sketches and scenes of Lancashire common life sold widely. A building society failure cost him his savings in 1884, a fund was raised for him, and a statue rose in Queen's Park, Manchester, two years after his death.
britannica-1911-bruce-alexander-balmain:
Alexander Balmain Bruce (1831–1899) was a Scottish divine born at Aberargie near Perth on 31 January 1831. His father suffered for holding to the Free Church at the Disruption of 1843 and moved to Edinburgh, where the son was educated and showed exceptional ability from the first. Early religious doubts, stirred above all by Strauss's Life of Jesus, made him lifelong sympathetic to others under the same stress.

After serving as assistant at Ancrum and Lochwinnoch he was called to Cardross in 1859 and to Broughty Ferry in 1868. He published his first considerable exegetical work, The Training of the Twelve. His Cunningham Lectures of 1874 became The Humiliation of Christ. In 1875 he took the chair of Apologetics and New Testament exegesis at the Free Church College, Glasgow, holding it twenty-four years.
britannica-1911-bucer-martin:
Martin Bucer (1491–1551) was a German Protestant reformer. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born at Schlettstadt in Alsace. In 1506 he entered the Dominican order. He studied at Heidelberg and read Erasmus and Luther. In 1521 he left the order by papal dispensation. He married a nun and preached the new doctrine. After his excommunication in 1523 he settled at Strassburg.

Bucer worked hard for Protestant unity. His views on the Lord's Supper leaned toward Zwingli. Still, he sought a formula to unite Lutherans and Swiss. That effort brought him charges of ambiguity. In 1548 he refused the Interim agreement at Augsburg. Cranmer then invited him to England. In 1549 he became regius professor of divinity at Cambridge. He advised on the revision of the prayer book. He died on 27 February 1551. Mary later had his body dug up and burnt. Elizabeth had his tomb rebuilt. The entry credits him with ninety-six treatises.
britannica-1911-buchez-philippe-joseph-b:
Philippe Joseph Benjamin Buchez (1796–1865) was a French author and politician. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his ideas and career. He was born on 31 March 1796 at Matagne-la-Petite. He finished his schooling in Paris. He then studied natural science and medicine. In 1821 he helped found a secret society. It copied the Italian Carbonari. Its aim was an armed rising against the government.

Buchez took his medical degree in 1825. He joined the Saint-Simonian society for a time. He left it over its strange religious turn. He then built his own Christian socialism. His journal L'Européen spread those views. His Introduction to the science of history appeared in 1833. It divided the past into four great epochs. Each epoch rested on a universal revelation. Later works include a Traité de politique, published in 1866. He died on 12 August 1865.
britannica-1911-buckstone-john-baldwin:
John Baldwin Buckstone (1802–1879) was an English actor and playwright. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his stage career. He was born at Hoxton on 14 September 1802. He was articled to a solicitor at first. He soon left the law for the stage. After years in the provinces he reached London in 1823. He played Ramsay at the Surrey theatre. In 1827 the Adelphi took him on as leading low comedian.

Buckstone later joined the Haymarket theatre. He was its lessee from 1853 to 1878. There he acted in his own plays and farces. Luke the Labourer was one popular piece. As manager he built a strong company. It included Sothern and the Kendals. He staged plays by Gilbert, Planché and Robertson. He wrote 150 plays in all. Some of them stayed popular for years. He died on 31 October 1879.
britannica-1911-bussy-roger-de-rabutin:
Roger de Rabutin, count of Bussy, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the thirteenth of April 1618 at Epiry, near Autun, he was a French writer of memoirs. His family held high rank in Burgundy, and his father led troops in the Nivernais.

The article follows a soldier whose wit kept undoing him. He entered the army at sixteen and fought through many campaigns. Richelieu sent him to the Bastille for a spell in 1641. A bid to carry off a rich widow cost him a large sum to settle. In the civil war he changed sides and won back royal favour. Falls from grace still dogged him. His famed book of court love tales, written in forced rest, sealed his ruin at court.
britannica-1911-butler-benjamin-franklin:
Benjamin Franklin Butler, an American lawyer, soldier, and politician who lived from 1818 to 1893, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Deerfield, New Hampshire, and graduated at Waterville College in 1838. He joined the Massachusetts bar in 1840 and won early fame as a lawyer at Lowell, above all in criminal cases.

A Democrat, Butler campaigned hard for a law to set a ten hour day for labourers. He sat in the state house in 1853 and the state senate in 1859. At the Democratic convention of 1860 he backed Jefferson Davis and opposed Stephen Douglas. After the Baltimore riot at the start of the Civil War, he led state troops to reopen the road to Washington. At Fortress Monroe he refused to return fugitive enslaved people who reached his lines, holding them as contraband of war.
britannica-1911-cain:
Cain, in the Bible the eldest son of Adam and Eve, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. He tilled the ground while his younger brother Abel kept sheep. Angry that God took Abel's gift and not his own, Cain killed his brother in the field. A curse was laid on him for the deed.

Cain was doomed to roam the earth as a fugitive. A mark was set on him so no one who found him would kill him. He settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden, and built a city named for his son Enoch. The piece then weighs hard points in the tale. It links the mark to tribal signs and the name to the Kenites.
britannica-1911-captain:
Captain is a rank and title in the army and navy. The word comes from the Latin caput, meaning head. It passed through the late Latin capitanus. This 1911 Britannica article explains its many uses. At sea, anyone who commands a ship is called captain. That holds even without the substantive rank. A lieutenant in command is addressed as captain.

The master of a merchant ship is her captain too. On a warship, petty officers also carry the title. There are captains of a top, of the forecastle and of a gun. A post captain in the British navy is a full captain. The name comes from being posted on the captains' list. Admirals are chosen from that same list. The captain of the fleet serves as an admiral's chief of staff. The article then turns to the army rank. It gives the French, German and cavalry forms of the title.
britannica-1911-carpenter-william-benjam:
William Benjamin Carpenter (1813–1885) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English physiologist and naturalist born at Exeter, the eldest son of Dr Lant Carpenter. He studied medicine at University College, London, and took his M.D. at Edinburgh in 1839. His thesis dealt with the nervous system of invertebrate animals, a line of work that grew into his Principles of General and Comparative Physiology.

The Royal Society elected him in 1844 and gave him a Royal medal in 1861, and he became Fullerian professor of physiology at the Royal Institution in 1845. The entry stresses his gift as a lecturer when popular science was young. His deepest research lay in marine zoology, above all the Foraminifera and Crinoids. That work helped spur deep-sea exploration, leading to the Lightning expedition of 1868 and later the famous Challenger voyage.
britannica-1911-cartagena-spain:
Cartagena is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a fortified seaport of south-eastern Spain, in the province of Murcia, on the Mediterranean. Its population in 1900 was 99,871. The city holds an arsenal and naval dockyards, and an admiral with the title of captain-general governs it, as at Ferrol and San Fernando. It is also an episcopal see and the end of a branch railway from Murcia.

The city stands on a hill above its harbour, with a fertile valley to the north and east and high mountains closing the south and west. Its grey houses look neglected, being built of a friable, crumbling stone. The harbour, the largest in Spain after Vigo and the finest on the east coast, is a deep bay guarded by four hills and a narrow entrance with forts on either hand. Tramways run through modern suburbs to the mining district about two leagues inland.
britannica-1911-castelsarrasin:
Castelsarrasin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of south western France. It is capital of a district in the department of Tarn-et-Garonne. Montauban lies twelve miles to the east by rail. Counts from 1906 give the town 3189 people. The wider commune held 7496 in that count. The town stands on the left bank of the Garonne canal. 

Promenades ring the town on the site of old fortifications. Its chief building is the church of Saint Sauveur. That brick church dates from the thirteenth century. The town holds a sub-prefecture and a court of first instance. A communal college stands among its buildings. A metal foundry is the principal industrial works there. Copper, tin, and other metals are worked in it. Flour mills, saw mills, and dye works add to the trade. The town trades in cattle, farm produce, and wine.
britannica-1911-cautin:
Cautin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a province of southern Chile. Arauco, Malleco, and Bio Bio bound it in the north. Argentina lies to the east. Valdivia lies to the south. The Pacific washes its west. Its area is officially put at 5832 square miles. The province sits in the temperate farming and forest belt. It produces wheat, cattle, lumber, tan bark, and fruit.

The state railway from Santiago to Puerto Montt crosses Cautin north to south. Two rivers cross it east to west. Both give good transport. The province once formed part of Araucanian land. Its political existence dates only from 1887. Its people in 1905 numbered 96,139. Many of them were European settlers, chiefly Germans. The capital is Temuco, on the Rio Cautin. Lautaro and Nueva Imperial are the other chief towns. Both were Spanish outposts in the long Araucanian struggle.
britannica-1911-chadwick-sir-edwin:
Sir Edwin Chadwick, an English reformer of public health who lived from 1800 to 1890, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Longsight, near Manchester, in January 1800. Called to the bar with no means of his own, he lived by writing. His essays won the notice of Jeremy Bentham, who took him on as a literary helper.

In 1832 Chadwick was hired by the royal commission on the poor laws, and in 1833 he became a full member. With Nassau Senior he drafted the famed report of 1834 that reformed the old poor law. His own mark was the union as the unit of management for relief. He wanted a far more central system than the law gave, run by paid officers from a central board. That quarrel with his chiefs helped end the poor law commission in 1846.
britannica-1911-chain:
Chain, a set of links joined so the whole bends like a cord, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. Chains serve to bind, to join, to lift weights, and to pass on power. They also serve as dress, as a collar, a badge of office, or a chain of knighthood. Fine chains take many link forms for show.

Work chains fall in two chief types, the piece shows. Stud chains have a brace across each link, which raises the safe load by half. Open link chains have no such brace. Small chains are made by machine, while large links are cut, bent hot, and welded by a smith. Chains with no weld are also made, and pitch chains drive machines such as bikes.
britannica-1911-chamberlain:
Chamberlain is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a court post of old roots. The word comes from terms for a chamber or room in French and German. At its root it names a man in charge of house affairs. Such men served in abbeys and great churches as well.

In a cloister the chamberlain held the funds and called chapter meets. He also got the goods needed for each rite and service. The pope's own chamberlain took his title from court use, the text says. A royal chamberlain attends the king's person and runs court form. A second old line of the post ran the royal funds. That line is traced back to the Carolingian court.
britannica-1911-champlain:
Champlain is a long lake between New York state and Vermont in America. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that it pokes a few miles into Canada. It runs about 130 miles from north to south in length. Its width shifts from a mile or less to some eleven miles. The lake covers about 500 square miles of water in all.

Its surface lies 96 feet above the level of the sea. In the north the water runs 200 to 300 feet deep in places. Near its middle the depth grows to a full 400 feet down. Isles large and small crowd the north end of the lake. From its west arm the Richelieu river flows out to the St Lawrence.
britannica-1911-chaplain:
Chaplain is an office article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about clergy who serve outside a parish. In the strict sense, a chaplain conducts services in a chapel. He is a priest or minister with no parish charge of his own. He is attached for set duties to a ruler, a bishop, a noble house, or an institution.

Schools, colleges, workhouses, and burial grounds all have chaplains, as do the army and the navy. A parish priest may hold a chaplaincy too, but as chaplain he has no parish duties. The article notes the examining chaplains who test candidates for holy orders. The British sovereign keeps thirty-six chaplains in ordinary, who serve at Saint James's in turn. There are also royal chaplains in Scotland and Ireland. The entry maps a flexible office across church and state.
britannica-1911-charcot-jean-martin:
Jean Martin Charcot, a French doctor who lived from 1825 to 1893, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Paris on November 29, 1825. He took his medical degree in Paris in 1853. Three years later he joined the Central Hospital Bureau as a doctor.

In 1862 Charcot began his long link with the Salpetriere hospital in Paris. His work there shaped the study of nerve disease. His talks on such ills, first printed in 1873, marked a large step in sorting them out. He also studied hysteria and hypnotism, the work that made his name most widely known. He taught with great success.
britannica-1911-charles-ii-king-of-spain:
Charles the Second, king of Spain who lived from 1661 to 1700, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Spaniards knew him by names meaning the Desired and the Bewitched. He was the son of Philip the Fourth by a second marriage. Born in November 1661, he was the only son of his father's two marriages to survive.

The entry paints a bleak picture of his childhood. Constant marriage within the Habsburg house had bred the family type to deformity in him, it says. His birth was greeted with joy, since Spain feared a fight over the succession. The boy was so feeble that he was fed at the breast until age five or six. For years it was not thought safe to let him walk, and he was left wholly uneducated.
britannica-1911-chartier-alain:
Alain Chartier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French poet and political writer. He lived from about 1392 to about 1430. He was born at Bayeux about the year 1392. He belonged to a family marked by considerable ability. His eldest brother Guillaume became bishop of Paris. Another brother, Thomas, became notary to the king. Alain studied at the university of Paris, like his elder brother.

His earliest poem is the Livre des quatre dames. He wrote it after the battle of Agincourt. Other debates and poems followed from his pen. La Belle Dame sans merci is named among them. None of these poems show very patriotic feeling, the entry says. But his prose shows he was not indifferent to his country's woes. He followed the fortunes of the dauphin in those years. That dauphin afterwards became king of France.
britannica-1911-chatelain:
Châtelain is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French feudal title, from the medieval Latin castellanus, the commander of a castle. In England the word stayed at that plain sense. In France it gained a special weight. It came to imply the jurisdiction of which the castle was the centre. The châtelain began, in Carolingian times, as an official of the count.

With the growth of feudalism the office became a fief and then hereditary. In rank the châtelain usually matched the simple sire, between the baron and the chevalier. In the Low Countries some were great nobles with wide jurisdiction. In the towns their power turned on their struggle with superiors and, from the twelfth century, with the rising communes. The châtellenie, the district under their justice, survived the office itself and lasted until the Revolution.
britannica-1911-chindwin:
Chindwin is a river of Burma and the largest stream that feeds the Irrawaddy. The 1911 Britannica article says its whole course lies in Burmese land. The Manipuris call it the Ningthi. Three streams join to form it, and which one is the true main source is not sure. The Tanai has long been held the chief source. It rises on a peak of the Kumôn range, north of Mogaung.

From the Hukawng valley the river turns south and keeps a southward course. It passes through the Upper and Lower Chindwin districts. It then enters the Irrawaddy, with mouths spread some twenty-two miles apart. Low islands fill the gap between those mouths. By old tale the most southern mouth is a cut made by a king of Pagan. Floods in 1824 cleared it after it had been choked for ages.
britannica-1911-chlorpicrin:
Chlorpicrin is a chemistry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chlorpicrin, also called nitrochloroform, is a sharp-smelling liquid. It is made by treating certain nitro compounds with bleaching powder. Strong nitric acid acting on chloral or chloroform can also yield it.

The entry gives a worked recipe from the chemist Hofmann. Bleaching powder is mixed into a paste with cold water, and a strong solution of picric acid added. A violent reaction follows, and the chlorpicrin distils over with little or no added heat. The liquid is colourless and barely mixes with water, though it dissolves freely in alcohol. Its vapour attacks the eyes with great force. Other reagents turn it into further compounds, which the article names. The piece is a practical note for the laboratory of its day.
britannica-1911-church-frederick-edwin:
Frederick Edwin Church was a painter of land views in the United States, who lived from eighteen twenty-six to nineteen hundred. He was born at Hartford and learned his craft past a famed master in the north. From the first he sought the great sights of the wild for his themes. Falls, high peaks, and rain woods drew his hand.

He roamed to the south main land twice and caught fire hills, ice hills, and sun sets in his work. His paints drew wild praise and vast sums in his day, though that craze has past. He was the chief man of a famed school of land painters. His house on a great stream shore was his home and work shop for years.
britannica-1911-clavecin: Clavecin is the French name for the harpsichord, as a short note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The word is a short form of names in Flemish and Italian for the same instrument. On this keyboard instrument the strings are not struck but plucked. A quill on a small jack does the plucking when a key is pressed. The note sends the reader on to the main entries on the harpsichord and the pianoforte for the full account.
britannica-1911-clinchant-justin:
Justin Clinchant lived from 1820 to 1881 and served as a French soldier for most of his life. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his rise from cadet to senior general. He joined the army from Saint Cyr in 1841 and fought in Algeria and then in the Crimea. At the storming of the Malakoff he led a battalion with clear skill.

Later posts took him to war in Mexico and then to command in the war of 1870. His troops were shut up in Metz, and he was held and then got free. He took command of the Army of the East in 1871 after its leader broke down. He then led troops against the Paris Commune and died as the city governor.
britannica-1911-cochin-denys-marie-augus:
Denys Marie Pierre Augustin Cochin (born 1851) was a French politician born at Paris. He studied law and entered the chamber of deputies in 1893. Over time he rose to lead the Conservative party in debate. The entry marks him as one of that party's main speakers.

His public stands give the shape of his career. He fought the income tax plan in 1894 and the reopening of the Dreyfus case in 1899. He also fought the split of church and state in 1905. The entry lists his books as well. They run from L'Évolution de la vie in 1895 to Ententes et ruptures in 1905.
britannica-1911-coffin:
A coffin is the box or case in which a corpse is confined. The word comes from a Latin term for a basket or chest. That older word never held the present sense. Greeks and Romans both buried and burned their dead. Greek coffins took the shape of an urn, a plain box or a triangle. The body in the last kind sat upright.

Burnt clay was the common Greek stuff, at times moulded round the body and then baked. Rome burned its dead until the Christian era brought stone coffins. Stone finds in London and other English towns fill much of the entry. In early England only the rich used stone. The poor were wrapped in cloth or laid under hay and flowers. By the late 1600s coffins served all ranks. Notes on American Indian practice close the account.
britannica-1911-coin:
Coin names, at root, the wedge-shaped die used to stamp money. The word comes through French from the Latin cuneus, a wedge. In time the name passed from the die to the money it stamped. A coin is thus a piece of money. Older English forms of the word are coyne, quoin and coign.

Those old forms live on in split uses. Quoin names the outer angle of a building. Coign also names a jutting angle. Shakespeare's phrase, a coign of vantage, keeps that sense alive. The entry is short and word-based. It gives no account of how coins are made or used. A reader gains the root, the shift in sense and the two building terms. That is the whole scope of the piece.
britannica-1911-conradin:
Conradin, also called Conrad the Younger (1252–1268), is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was king of Jerusalem and Sicily, son of the German king Conrad the Fourth. He was born at Wolfstein in Bavaria in March 1252. His father died in 1254, and the boy grew up at the court of his uncle Louis, duke of Bavaria. Pope Innocent the Fourth chased him with deep hate and sought to give Sicily to a prince from abroad.

After Manfred fell in 1266, envoys from the Ghibelline towns begged him to come and free Italy. He pledged his lands, crossed the Alps, and put out a claim to Sicily at Verona. His cause grew fast. His envoy was cheered in Rome, and he was cheered at Pavia and Pisa. In 1267 he was cast out of the church.
britannica-1911-conrart-valentin:
Valentin Conrart was one of the founders of the French Academy, born in Paris of parents of the reformed faith. Trained for trade, he turned to the world of letters on his fathers death. He soon won a name in that world, though he wrote nothing for print for many years.

Made a royal clerk and aide, he threw his house open as a meet place for men of letters. There they talked of books and read and judged each others work. A great cardinal took the group under his wing, and from it the French Academy was born. Its first meets were held in Conrarts house. Picked by all as its clerk, he did that work for more than forty years, till his death. His chief book is a tale of his own times.
britannica-1911-constant-benjamin:
Benjamin Constant, a French painter of scenes and portraits, gets a brief art note in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Paris in eighteen forty five, he learned his craft with Cabanel. His first Salon picture, a Hamlet scene, was hung in eighteen sixty nine. At once he stood as a known master of his day in France. Scene works drawn from trips to Morocco stand in his list.

Face work made him just as famed as his scene work in the text. Men and women of high place sat for his brush in those years. One of his last such works was a portrait of Queen Victoria in nineteen hundred. He held a seat in the Institut de France by then. Marks of honor from France and from lands abroad came to him as well.
britannica-1911-constant-de-rebecque-hen:
Henri Benjamin Constant de Rebecque is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French writer and politician. He lived from 1767 to 1830. He was born at Lausanne on the twenty fifth of October 1767. His mother, Henriette de Chandieu, died at his birth. His father commanded a regiment in the Dutch service. After a good private education at Brussels, he went to Oxford. He went thence to Erlangen for further study.

A residence at Edinburgh followed those university years. Relations formed there with prominent Whigs influenced his views deeply. He returned to Switzerland in the year 1786. In the next year he visited Paris for the first time. There he met Madame de Charriere, a Dutchwoman by birth. She had married into a Swiss family allied to his own. Though twenty seven years older, she became his mistress.
britannica-1911-conway-sir-william-marti:
Sir William Martin Conway (1856- ) was an English art critic and mountaineer, and this 1911 Britannica entry covers both halves of his career. Born at Rochester, the son of a clergyman, he was schooled at Repton and at Trinity College, Cambridge. He grew keen on early printing and engraving and toured the great libraries of Europe in 1880. The fruit was a history of the Dutch woodcutters of the fifteenth century, printed in 1884.

More books on art followed, on Flemish and Tuscan artists and on the art of the ancient world. He held art chairs at Liverpool and later at Cambridge and was knighted in 1895. As a climber he led the way: in 1892 he reached twenty-three thousand feet in the Himalayas, a record at the time. He crossed Spitsbergen, climbed in the Bolivian Andes and Aconcagua,.
britannica-1911-cousin:
Cousin is a term of kinship that comes through French and Italian from a Latin root. Children of brothers and sisters are first cousins to each other, or cousins-german. Children of first cousins are second cousins to each other. The count runs on in that same step pattern. A child of a first cousin stands as first cousin once removed to that cousin's kin.

A second use of the word sits far from the family tree. Since the 1500s sovereigns have used cousin as a style of honour in speech. It fits persons of high rank who are not equal sovereigns. Brother is kept for one sovereign to a second. In Britain the sovereign calls dukes, marquesses and earls cousin in royal writs. In France the style went to princes of the blood, cardinals and marshals. In Spain it forms a set right of the grandees.
britannica-1911-craufurd-quintin:
Quintin Craufurd (1743–1819) was a British author born at Kilwinnock on 22 September 1743. In early life he went to India and entered the service of the East India Company. He came back to Europe before he was forty with a handsome fortune in hand. Paris became his home from that point. There he gave himself to letters and art.

He built a good library and a rich collection in that city. Paintings, coins and other objects of old interest filled his rooms. He stood on close terms with the French court, most of all with Marie Antoinette. He was one of the men who arranged the flight to Varennes. He fled to Brussels when that flight failed in its aim. In 1792 he came back to Paris in hope of saving the royal prisoners. Through Talleyrand's sway he kept his Paris home when war broke out anew. He died there on 23 November 1819.
britannica-1911-cumin:
Cumin, an annual herb of the carrot family, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It probably came from some part of western Asia. It is scarcely known in a wild state today. Early growers raised it in Arabia, India, and China, and around the Mediterranean Sea.

The plant stands about a foot high, with a slender branching stem. Its leaves are deeply cut into thread-like parts, and its flowers are small and white. The fruits, sold as seeds, are the cumin of the pharmacy trade. They are hotter to the taste, paler, and larger than caraway seeds. Nine fine ridges run along each half, over as many oil channels. Their strong scent and warm, bitter taste come from an essential oil. The piece notes cumin in the Bible and in Greek medical writers. Pliny reports the ground seed taken with bread or wine as a medicine.
britannica-1911-custrin:
Custrin is a town of Germany in the kingdom of Prussia, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is a fortress of the first rank, at the confluence of the Oder and the Warthe. It lies 51 miles north east of Berlin by rail in its province. Its count in 1900 was 16,473, including the garrison of the fortress.

Custrin consists of the town proper within the strong fortifications, a suburb on the left bank of the Oder, and one on the right bank of the Warthe. There are three Evangelical churches and one Roman Catholic church, and a handsome town hall. Bridges cross both rivers at the town in its plan. Custrin has manufactories of potato meal, machinery, pianos, furniture, and cigars. About 1250 a town was erected on the site, where a fishing village originally stood.
britannica-1911-daly-augustin:
Augustin Daly, an American stage manager and playwright born in eighteen thirty eight, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Plymouth, North Carolina, he was a stage critic for New York papers from eighteen fifty nine. He wrote and reshaped a number of plays. His first hit came in eighteen sixty seven.

In eighteen sixty nine he took charge of the Fifth Avenue stage house. Ten years later he built and opened his own house in New York, and in time one in London too. At the New York house he built a troupe led by Ada Rehan that won high fame. For them he reshaped plays from abroad and staged the comedies of Shakespeare in a fresh way new to America. He took the whole troupe on tour to England, Germany, and France. Many top stage names learned their craft with him.
britannica-1911-dammartin:
Dammartin is a small town of France in the department of Seine et Marne, 22 miles north-east of Paris. It stands well on a hill of the Goële plateau. Its weight in the entry is historical, not modern. Dammartin was the seat of a countship whose holders played a large part in French history. A certain Hugh first made himself master of the town in the 900s.

Reynald I, count of Dammartin, fell with the coalition crushed by Philip Augustus at Bouvines in 1214. His two heiresses carried the countship into other houses by marriage. Through Fayel and Nanteuil it reached Antoine de Chabannes, a favourite of Charles VII. He founded the town's collegiate church in 1480, and his tomb stands in its chancel. Sold to the Montmorency dukes in 1554, the countship was seized by Louis XIII in 1632 and given to the princes of Condé.
britannica-1911-de-costa-benjamin-frankl:
Benjamin Franklin De Costa, an American clergyman and historical writer who lived from 1831 to 1904, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Charlestown, Massachusetts, in July 1831, he graduated in 1856 from the Biblical Institute at Concord, New Hampshire. He became an Episcopal minister in 1857. He served as rector at North Adams and then at Newton Lower Falls.

During the first two years of the Civil War, De Costa served as a chaplain in two Massachusetts regiments. He then edited church and history journals in New York. He was rector of St John the Evangelist in New York from 1881 to 1899. He left that post after becoming a Roman Catholic. The article also notes his temperance work and his standing as an expert on early maps of America. His books treat the Northmen and the age of exploration.
britannica-1911-delessert-jules-paul-ben:
Jules Paul Benjamin Delessert (1773-1847), a French banker, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Lyons, he was the son of Etienne Delessert, who founded the first fire insurance firm and the first discount bank in France. The young man was in England when the Revolution broke out. He rushed home, joined the Paris National Guard in 1790, and became an artillery officer in 1793.

The article says his father bought him out of the army in 1795 to run the family bank. Full of energy, he started the first cotton factory at Passy in 1801 and a sugar works in 1802, which won him a baron's title. He sat in the chamber of deputies for years. There he backed humane causes, such as ending the death penalty and making prisons better.
britannica-1911-demmin:
Demmin is a town of Prussia on the navigable river Peene, where the Trebel and Tollense join it, 72 miles west-north-west of Stettin on the Berlin-Stralsund railway. Its people numbered 12,541 in 1905. Textiles, breweries, distilleries and tanneries employ the town, and an active trade in corn and timber passes through it.

The town is Slavonian in origin and of great age, already a place of weight in Charlemagne's time. A German army besieged it in 1148 and Henry the Lion took it in 1164. The Thirty Years' War brought repeated fights over it, and Swedes and the electoral prince took and retook it after the peace. It passed to Prussia in 1720, and its walls were dismantled in 1759.
britannica-1911-elgin:
Elgin is a royal burgh and county town of Elginshire, Scotland, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells its long story. It stands on the river Lossie, five miles south of its port, Lossiemouth, with 8,460 people in 1901. Alexander I made it a royal burgh, and Alexander II gave its charter in 1234.

The entry notes Edward I's stays at the castle in 1296 and 1303, and the castle's destruction once Scottish freedom was won back. Fire gutted half the town in 1452, and Montrose plundered it twice in 1645. In 1746 Prince Charles Edward lodged there for a few days. The entry closes with the town's quiet cathedral-city character giving way to a modern spirit.
britannica-1911-estebanez-calderon-seraf:
Estébanez Calderón, Serafín (1799–1867), was a Spanish author best known by his pen name “El Solitario.” He was born at Málaga on 27 December 1799. His first literary effort was El Listón verde, a poem signed “Safinio” and written to mark the revolution of 1820. He was called to the bar and settled for a time at Madrid.

At Madrid Estébanez published a volume of verses in 1831 under the name “El Solitario.” He died at Madrid on 5 February 1867. His most interesting work is Escenas andaluzas of 1847. It is written in a curiously affected style, its word-hoard part archaic and part provincial. Yet, for all its odd mannerisms, the entry calls it a vivid record of picturesque scenes and local customs. He also left an unfinished history of the conquest and loss of Portugal, printed in 1883 under his nephew's editing.
britannica-1911-ettingshausen-constantin:
Constantin, Baron von Ettingshausen (1826–1897), was an Austrian geologist and botanist born in Vienna on 16 June 1826. He took a medical degree there. In 1854 he became professor of botany and natural history at Vienna's medical and surgical military academy. In 1871 he moved to the botany chair at Graz. He held that post until his death at Graz on 1 February 1897.

His name rests on work with fossil plants. He studied the Tertiary floras of many parts of Europe. He also worked on the fossil floras of Australia and New Zealand. His books include a study of living ferns as a key to fossil kinds, issued in 1865. His Physiographie der Medicinal-Pflanzen appeared in 1862. With J. Starkie Gardner he produced a monograph of the British Eocene flora, whose fern volume came out in 1879–1882.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-vi-of-spain:
Ferdinand the Sixth of Spain is a royal life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Madrid on the twenty-third of September 1713 and died in 1759. He was the second son of Philip the Fifth, founder of the Bourbon line in Spain. His youth was a depressed one, the article says.

His stepmother, Elizabeth Farnese, was a managing woman with love only for her own children. She saw her stepson as a block to their fortunes. His father's low spirits left her mistress of the palace. Ferdinand wed in 1729 a daughter of John the Fifth of Portugal. Observers thought her plain looks shocked the prince at their first meeting. Yet he grew deeply attached to her. By nature he was gloomy, shy, and unsure of his own powers.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-vii-of-spain:
Ferdinand the Seventh, king of Spain from 1784 to 1833 in life span, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the eldest son of Charles the Fourth and Maria Louisa of Parma. He was born at the palace of San Ildefonso in the Somosierra hills in October 1784.

The article presents a youth shut out of rule by jealous parents and a royal favourite. It tells how unrest in 1808 forced his father's abdication and put him on the throne. He then spent years as a prisoner of Napoleon while Spain fought in his name. On his return in 1814, he held that full power lay in his person alone, and fresh revolt came in 1820.
britannica-1911-feval-paul-henri-corenti:
Paul Henri Corentin Feval (1817-1887), French novelist and dramatist, was born at Rennes in Brittany on 27 September 1817, and much of his best work draws on his native province. Trained for the bar, he left law after his first brief and gained a footing in Paris with the Club des phoques in 1841. His Mysteres de Londres of 1844, where an Irishman plots England's ruin to avenge his countrymen, appeared under the pen name Sir Francis Trolopp.

The entry lists a long shelf of novels: Le Fils du diable, Les Compagnons du silence, Le Bossu, Les Habits noirs and others. Some were staged, Le Bossu with Sardou as collaborator most successfully. His crime chronicles, the entry says, did harm that he himself later saw. In old age he turned ardent Catholic, revising his early books and writing religious pamphlets. Overwork broke his health, and he died in Paris on 8 March 1887.
britannica-1911-flavin: Flavin, from Latin flavus, yellow, is the commercial name for an extract or preparation of quercitron bark, from the tree Quercus tinctoria. It serves as a yellow dye. Growers and dyers use it in place of the ground and powdered bark itself, which the entry points to under the head Quercitron. The hosted text is a genuine short article of a few lines. It gives the name, its Latin root, the bark it comes from, and the dyeing use that made it an article of trade.
britannica-1911-flint-austin:
Austin Flint (1812–1886) was an American doctor, born at Petersham, Massachusetts, on 20 October 1812. He took his degree at the medical school of Harvard in 1833. From 1847 to 1852 he taught the theory and practice of medicine at Buffalo Medical College. He was one of the founders of that school. He then held the same chair at the university of Louisville from 1852 to 1856.

From 1861 to 1886 Flint taught at Bellevue Hospital Medical College in New York. His chair covered the rules and practice of medicine and care at the bedside. He wrote many text-books on health and disease. They include Diseases of the Heart, Principles and Practice of Medicine, and Clinical Medicine. He also wrote on the study of the lungs by sound and touch. Flint died in New York on 13 March 1886. The article then turns to his son.
britannica-1911-florin:
Florin is a name used for scores of coins of the main land and for two coins struck in England. The word comes from an Italian term for flower. That name first marked a gold coin struck at Florence in twelve fifty-two. A lily on its face gave it the name of the flower.

That coin was held in high trade grace past all Europe, and like coins were struck in scores of lands. An English gold form came in thirteen forty-three but was ill priced and dropped in a year. A coin of the same name in white metal came in the last age but one.
britannica-1911-fluorescein:
Fluorescein, or resorcin-phthalein, C20H12O5, is a chemical compound discovered in 1876 by A. von Baeyer. He made it by joining phthalic anhydride with resorcin at about 195 to 200 degrees. The entry describes the making in detail. The two substances are heated, the melt is boiled out and washed, then dissolved in sodium hydrate. Acid throws the product down again. Repeated two or three times, the process yields fluorescein pure.

The pure compound is a yellow powder that will not dissolve in water but dissolves in alcohol, crystallizing in small dark red nodules. In caustic alkali it gives a dark red solution. Diluted, that solution shows a brilliant green fluorescence, the trait that gave the substance its name. Brominating it yields eosin, a dye that colours silk, wool and cotton a fine pink.
britannica-1911-folkes-martin:
Martin Folkes (1690-1754), English antiquary, was born in London on 29 October 1690. He was educated at Saumur and at Clare College, Cambridge. There he so excelled in mathematics that at only twenty-three he was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society. He joined its council in 1716, and in 1723 Newton, the society's president, made him a vice-president. On Newton's death Folkes stood for the presidency but lost to Sir Hans Sloane, whom he succeeded in 1741.

In 1733 Folkes toured Italy and composed his Dissertations on the Weights and Values of Ancient Coins. He was president of the Society of Antiquaries from 1749 to 1754. Before it he read papers on the Trajan and Antonine pillars at Rome, among other studies of coins, weights and antiquities. The French Academy made him a member in 1742, and Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1746. The entry traces a life at the centre of learned London.
britannica-1911-formalin:
Formalin, or formaldehyde, is a chemistry article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The substance is the first member of a series of fats based aldehydes. It is most readily made by passing the vapour of methyl alcohol, mixed with air, over heated copper or platinum. The vapour is then condensed and taken up in water or alcohol.

At common temperatures formaldehyde is a gas with a pungent smell, the entry says. It is a strong antiseptic and disinfectant. A solution of forty parts in a hundred, sold as formalin, serves as a deodorant, a killer of fungi, and a preservative. The pure substance cannot be held, since it readily joins with itself into larger forms. It also makes glue or gelatin insoluble in water.
britannica-1911-fountain:
Fountain, from late Latin fontana, from fons, a spring, names outlets of water that bear the work of human art where the water emerges. An early example is the carved Babylonian basin of about 3000 B.C. found at Tello. Layard also found an Assyrian fountain in a gorge of the river Gomel. It was a series of basins cut in the rock, stepping down to the stream, the lowest carved with two rampant lions.

The word covers simple gear that lets water gush into an ornamental basin, and grand gear that forces it into high jets. A fountain may be the basin or the jet itself. The long article follows fountains through history, from market-place columns with masks at their spouts to ornate Gothic structures with figures of virgins, saints and warriors. The hosted file opens with the end of the Foundling Hospitals article before reaching this survey.
britannica-1911-fouquier-tinville-antoin:
Antoine Quentin Fouquier-Tinville (1746-1795), French revolutionist, was born at Herouel, a village in the department of the Aisne. He was first a procureur attached to the Chatelet at Paris. He sold that office in 1783 and became a clerk under the lieutenant-general of police. He seems to have taken up revolutionary ideas early, though little is known of his part at the Revolution's outbreak. His name was made by the tribunal that judged the Terror's victims.

When the Revolutionary Tribunal of Paris was set up on 10 March 1793, Fouquier-Tinville was made its public prosecutor. He held the post until 28 July 1794. His work was less to convict the guilty than to carry out, in due form, the proscriptions ordered by whatever faction held power. That work earned him a name as one of the most sinister figures of the Revolution. The entry follows him to his own trial and execution.
britannica-1911-frahn-christian-martin:
Christian Martin Frahn (1782-1851), German numismatist and historian, was born at Rostock. He began oriental studies under Tychsen at the university of Rostock and continued them at Gottingen and Tubingen. In 1804 he became a Latin master in Pestalozzi's famous institute. He went home in 1806, and the next year he was chosen for the chair of oriental languages in the Russian university of Kazan. A German coin scholar was thus planted deep inside the Russian empire, among Tatar and Mongol money.

In 1815 Frahn was invited to succeed Tychsen at Rostock, but he chose St Petersburg instead. There he became director of the Asiatic museum and a councillor of state, and there he died. He wrote over 150 works. The entry names his studies of oriental coin cabinets and of Bulgar coins. It also names his work on the Mohammedan coins of the St Petersburg Academy.
britannica-1911-franklin: Franklin is a short word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Late Latin francus, meaning free, and at first meant simply a freeman. In England it later named a landholder who was free born but not noble. Some older writers also used it for a free or liberal host. The Latin form given is franchilanus. The entry runs to a few lines only and gives no more than these senses and the word origin.
britannica-1911-frobisher-sir-martin:
Sir Martin Frobisher (about 1535-1594), English navigator, was born at Altofts in Yorkshire and went to sea young, sailing to Guinea in 1544. By 1560 or 1561 he had fixed on the great aim of his life: a North-West Passage to Cathay and India. For fifteen years he sought backing in vain.

In 1576, helped by the earl of Warwick, he sailed with two tiny barks and a pinnace and 35 men. The pinnace was lost and one bark deserted. Alone, he reached Labrador and entered Frobisher Bay, losing five men to capture there. A lump of black earth brought home was rumoured to be gold ore. In 1577 a far larger expedition sailed with a royal ship and a Company of Cathay. Later he served as Drake vice-admiral in the West Indies and won his knighthood against the Armada. He died at Plymouth in November 1594 of a wound taken at Fort Crozon.
britannica-1911-galicia-spain:
Galicia is a region in the north-west of Spain, bounded by the Bay of Biscay, Leon and Asturias, Portugal and the Atlantic. It held 1,980,515 people in 1900 over 11,254 square miles, divided since 1833 into Corunna, Lugo, Orense and Pontevedra. Mountains cross it, reaching 6593 feet in the Peña Trevinca, and the Miño runs 170 miles to the Atlantic. The coast, 240 miles, is bold and cut, with Ferrol among Europe's best harbours and the port of Corunna.

The coast climate is mild, the interior colder and rainy. The soil is fertile, with grain crops in the lowlands and cattle herds on the pastures. The Galicians resemble the Portuguese in speech and habits, and Gallego has become in Madrid almost a synonym for a labourer. Corunna is the largest town; Santiago de Compostela is the capital. The Suevian kingdom fell to the Visigoths in 585, and after 1072 Galicia remained part of Castile or Leon.
britannica-1911-garnier-germain:
Germain Garnier is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Garnier was a French statesman and writer on wealth who lived from 1754 to 1821. He was born at Auxerre and trained for the law. He held a law post in Paris while still young. He won a seat linked to Paris when the states general were called.

The article follows his safe path through stormy years in France. He left the country in 1792 and came back in 1795. He later served as prefect, senator, and count. After the old kings returned he became a peer and a marquis. His fame rests on his works on wealth and money. Chief among them is his translation, with notes, of Adam Smith's great work on the wealth of nations. He also wrote a history of money in two volumes.
britannica-1911-gastein:
Gastein is a side valley of the Pongau in Salzburg, Austria, famed for its mineral springs. The 1911 Britannica entry describes a valley some 25 miles long, set between 3,000 and 3,500 feet, with the Tauern peaks behind it. The river Ache runs through it, forming great waterfalls near Wildbad-Gastein. The Tauern railway reached the valley in 1905, through a tunnel over five miles long.

Two watering places share the waters. Hof-Gastein, the valley capital, receives thermal water by a five-mile conduit built in 1828, and was once rich from gold and silver mines worked since Roman times. Wildbad-Gastein, or Bad Gastein, draws over 8,500 guests a year to springs of 77 to 120 degrees. The entry also records the Gastein Convention of 1865 and Bismarck's 1879 talks there, which led toward the Triple Alliance.
britannica-1911-gawain:
Gawain, in the 1911 Britannica, is the most famous hero of Arthurian romance. The entry opens with his many name forms, from the Welsh Gwalchmei to the Latin Walganus. He is made son of King Loth of Orkney and nephew to Arthur through his mother.

The article traces his figure through the early records. William of Malmesbury tells of his tomb found in the Welsh province of Ros, and calls him a king over Galloway. In Geoffrey of Monmouth and in Wace he acts as Arthur's envoy to the Roman emperor and dies fighting Mordred's landing. English poems make him the model of chivalrous courtesy, 'the fine father of nurture.' The entry notes that before Malory, Gawain, not Arthur, was the typical English hero, and contrasts his smaller place in Chretien de Troyes.
britannica-1911-gedymin:
Gedymin (died 1342) was grand-duke of Lithuania. The 1911 Britannica entry questions the old chroniclers who made him a servant of Prince Witen, and makes him more probably Witen's younger brother. He inherited a vast domain: Lithuania proper, Samogitia, Red Russia, Polotsk and Minsk.

Around him stood greedy foes, above all the Teutonic Knights, whose raids under colour of conversion had united the Lithuanian tribes. Gedymin aimed higher, at a dynasty that would make Lithuania mighty, not merely safe. In 1322 he wrote to Pope John XXII seeking protection, and in 1325 he invited settlers of every rank from the Hanse towns, with free choice of settlement and their own laws. The entry then follows his gains in the Russian principalities, Kiev among them, his marriage alliances, and his even-handed rule over Catholic and Orthodox clergy.
britannica-1911-gelatin:
Gelatin, the clear substance that sets into a jelly, is explained in a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms when collagen, the base stuff of bone and skin, is boiled in water or weak acid. The mix turns to liquid when hot and sets again as it cools. The word comes from Latin and French roots that mean frozen or stiff.

Inside, the entry sorts where collagen and its kin are found in the body. Tendons, the eye, fish scales, and cartilage are all covered. Bone collagen, called ossein, sits with calcium salts in bone. Pure gelatin is shown as pale, brittle, and clear, with no taste or smell. Its rough mix of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen is given. Study of which animals hold the tissue is also reported.
britannica-1911-gerbert-martin:
Martin Gerbert, a German theologian who lived from 1720 to 1793, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He came from a noble family and was born at Horb on the Neckar. He was educated at Freiburg, at Klingenau, and at a Benedictine abbey in the Black Forest. There he took his vows in 1737 and was ordained priest in 1744.

He was made professor at once, first of philosophy and later of theology. From 1754 to 1764 he issued a run of theological works. They sought to soften the rigid school system by an appeal to the early Fathers, above all Augustine. His travels through monastic libraries in three lands woke a taste for history in him. In 1764 he was elected prince abbot, and proved a model ruler.
britannica-1911-gerolstein: Gerolstein is a village and health resort in the Prussian Rhine Province of Germany. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it on the river Kyll in the Eifel range. It stands 1,100 feet above the sea, 58 miles west of Andernach by rail. Its count in 1900 was 1,308 people. A ruined castle from 1115 looks down on the valley, and the village is famed for lithia waters that are shipped far and wide.
britannica-1911-gin:
Gin, a spirit flavored with the juniper berry, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word gin is short for Geneva, and both stem from a French word for juniper. Early makers of crude spirits threw in strong spices to mask a foul taste. Ginger and grains of paradise were used for that end.

Some one then tried the juniper berry in their place, by the tale told here. Its taste pleased, and it was held to add worth for health as well. From then on, makers of flavored spirits used it as a rule. The entry clears modern gin of old charges of foul dosing with lead or acid. Two great types are set apart, Dutch geneva and British gin. They part most in how far the base spirit is refined.
britannica-1911-gitschin:
Gitschin, in Czech Jicin, is a town of Bohemia, Austria, 65 miles north-east of Prague by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 9,790 people in 1900, mostly Czech. Its parish church was begun by Wallenstein on the model of Santiago de Compostela, and its castle, finished in 1630, stands beside the church.

Wallenstein made the town capital of his duchy of Friedland, and in 1813 the emperor Francis I signed there the treaty joining the Allies against Napoleon. The entry recalls his murder and the town's fall in the Thirty Years' War, and its later passage to the Trauttmannsdorf family. On 29 June 1866 the Prussians won a great victory there over the Austrians. That win let two Prussian armies join, leading on to the Austrian defeat at Koniggratz.
britannica-1911-glycerin:
Glycerin, also called glycerine or glycerol, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name comes from a Greek word for sweet. In the science of drugs it bears a Latin form of the name. The stuff is an alcohol made from most natural fatty bodies.

Alkalis and like agents break fats apart, take up water, and form glycerin. The same act forms the alkaline salt of an acid that shifts with the fat in use. Bodies that act this way with alkalis are known as glycerides. In the common making of soap, glycerin stays dissolved in the watery liquors. The soap parts from those liquors as it forms. Scheele found glycerin in 1779 and called it the sweet principle of oils. Chevreul later gave it the name in use.
britannica-1911-gmelin:
Gmelin is a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a line of German men of science from Tubingen. The line starts with Johann Georg Gmelin, a drug seller and skilled chemist who died in 1728. His three sons all took up science or healing.

The article follows the family branch by branch. One son spent ten years touring Siberia and wrote books on its plants. A grandson died in 1774 after being seized on a trip near the Caspian Sea. Best known of all was Leopold Gmelin, who taught at Heidelberg. He found a new salt of iron and cyanide in 1822. His handbook of chemistry ran through four versions and was put into English.
britannica-1911-gobelin:
Gobelin began as the name of a family of dyers in Paris. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them in the Faubourg Saint Marcel by the Bièvre river. Jehan, the first head of the firm, found a prized scarlet dye. He spent so much on his works that locals called the place la folie Gobelin.

A tapestry works joined the dye works in the next century. Wealth grew fast, and some in the family bought noble titles and state posts. In 1662 Colbert bought the works for Louis XIV. They became a royal shop for tapestry and fine furnishings, and the work still went on under the state.
britannica-1911-grain:
Grain is a word most used for the seed of cereal plants. Its word entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from the Latin granum, meaning seed. As a joint term it covers cereal plants as a whole group.

Grain also names the malt waste left from brewing and distilling work. Small hard round bits like sand, salt, and gold are called grains too. Grain is the smallest unit of weight in Britain and America both. Its source is said to be the weight of a dry wheat grain. From dye use, ingrained came to mean dyed through and hard to shift.
britannica-1911-grand-rapids-wisconsin:
Grand Rapids is a city and county seat of Wood county, Wisconsin. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on both sides of the Wisconsin river, north west of Milwaukee. Counts rose from forty four hundred in nineteen hundred to sixty five hundred in nineteen ten.

Four rail lines serve Grand Rapids as a rail and shipping centre. Mills make lumber, doors, paper, wood pulp, furniture, and flour there. Public buildings hold a post office, court house, city hall, and hospital. The Scott Free Public Library dates from eighteen ninety two in the city. The city runs its own water works for homes and shops.
britannica-1911-great-basin:
Great Basin names a vast dry tract in the west of the United States. The Britannica entry of 1911 gives its size as some 200,000 square miles. No stream in it flows out to the sea. All its waters drain inward and end in lakes or dry flats. High ranges mark its rim on most sides.

Its shape is close to a long triangle with a sharp point in the south. The tract takes in most of Nevada and the west half of Utah. Parts of Idaho, Oregon, Wyoming, and California also fall inside it. The land is not one smooth bowl, as the name might suggest. It holds many small closed basins, each with its own drain.
britannica-1911-griffin:
The Griffin, Griffon or Gryphon, from the Greek gryps, was in the natural history of the ancients an imaginary creature of the eagle kind. The 1911 Britannica entry describes it with four legs, wings and a beak: eagle in front, lion behind, and in some writers a serpent's tail. It watched over gold mines and hidden treasure.

Consecrated to the Sun, whose chariot the ancient painters showed drawn by griffins, it was said to inhabit Asiatic Scythia. There gold and precious stones abounded, and the griffins tore apart strangers who came to gather them, chastising human greed. The one-eyed Arimaspi warred with them constantly, Herodotus is cited as saying. Mandeville made the griffin eight times a lion's size. The entry then follows the beast into heraldry and architecture, from Persepolis capitals to the table supports of Pompeii.
britannica-1911-groin:
Groin carries several distinct meanings. One old sense comes from the Latin grunnire. It meant the grunting of swine, and hence a pig's snout. That sense probably gave rise to groyne. A groyne is a small coastal breakwater of timber or masonry. It checks the drift of sand and shingle. A second sense names part of the body. It is the fold between the lower abdomen and the thighs.

Architecture takes its meaning from that fold. A groin is the angle where two vaults cross. Equal vaults meet in a vertical plane. Unequal vaults produce winding curves. Those curves were hard to centre without ribs. The entry also explains the Welsh groin. There the main vault stands higher than the cross vaults. It explains groin centering too. That is the timber support used while vaulting is built.
britannica-1911-grossenhain:
Grossenhain is a town in the kingdom of Saxony, 20 miles north of Dresden on the main railway line to Berlin, with 12,015 people in 1905. It has an Evangelical church, modern and commercial schools, a library and an extensive public park. Its industries are important, covering woollen and cotton cloth, buckskin, leather, glass and machinery.

The town began as a Sorb settlement, was held and strongly fortified by the Bohemians, and then passed to the margraves of Meissen, from whom Brandenburg took it in 1312. It suffered in all the great German wars and was nearly destroyed by fire in 1744. On 16 May 1813 French and Russian forces fought a battle there during the Napoleonic wars.
britannica-1911-guest-edwin:
Edwin Guest (1800–1880) was an English antiquary. He was educated at King Edward's school, Birmingham. At Caius College, Cambridge, he graduated as eleventh wrangler. He became a fellow of his college. He was called to the bar in 1828. After some years of legal practice he turned to research. Antiquarian and literary studies filled the rest of his life.

In 1838 he published his History of English Rhythms. That exhaustive work made his name. He also wrote many papers on Roman-British history. Dr Stubbs edited them after Guest's death as Origines Celticae (1883). Fresh material for a history of early Britain joined them. Guest became master of Caius College in 1852. He served as vice-chancellor in 1854–1855. He died on 23 November 1880.
britannica-1911-harrison-benjamin:
Benjamin Harrison, twenty third president of the United States, born at North Bend, Ohio, in eighteen thirty three, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His great grandfather signed the Declaration of Independence. His grandfather, William Henry Harrison, was ninth president. His father sat in the national House for a term.

The boy grew up on the family farm and went to a log school house nearby. A private tutor fit him for college. He studied two years at a farm college, then graduated from Miami University in eighteen fifty two. He was a keen student and a great reader, with a marked gift for speaking on the spot. He read law in a judge's office and was admitted to the bar in eighteen fifty three. At twenty one he moved to Indianapolis.
britannica-1911-hasan-and-hosain:
Ḥasan and Ḥosain is a joint life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the sons of the fourth caliph Ali. Their mother was Fatima, daughter of Mahomet. On Ali's death Ḥasan was proclaimed caliph, but the strength of Moawiya, who had rebelled against Ali, forced him to resign his claim. The terms gave him the treasure stored at Kufa and the revenues of Darabjird.

The article then follows his brother's fate. Ḥasan retired to Medina and died there about 669. Ḥosain was later invited by partisans in Kufa to revolt against Yazid, Moawiya's successor. He was defeated and killed at Kerbela on the tenth of October 680. He is the hero of the passion play performed each year by the Shi'ites of Persia and India.
britannica-1911-hoadly-benjamin:
Benjamin Hoadly (1676-1761) was an English divine known for church controversy, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his rise. He was born at Westerham in Kent and entered Catharine Hall, Cambridge, in 1691. After two years as a tutor he held a London lectureship from 1701 and a city rectory from 1704. His first big fight as a controversialist ran from 1703 to 1707, over conformity.

He then clashed with Francis Atterbury, first over the reading of certain texts and then over the whole doctrine of non-resistance. His main treatises set out the limits of obedience to rulers and the ground of civil government. The Commons were so pleased that in 1709 they asked the queen to give him some church dignity for his service. She answered kindly, the entry notes, but the dignity was not then conferred.
britannica-1911-hohenstein:
Hohenstein, or Hohenstein-Ernstthal, is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Saxony, on the slopes of the Erzgebirge, 12 m. N.E. of Zwickau. Its population was 13,903 in 1905. It has two fine Evangelical churches, a town hall restored in 1876, and monuments to famous men. Cotton spinning and weaving lead its industries, with machines, stockings, gloves, woollen and silk fabrics, printing and dyeing.

Many townsfolk also work in the copper and arsenic mines nearby, and a mineral spring with baths lies close. Hohenstein is the birthplace of the physicist G. H. von Schubert and of C. G. Schröter, an inventor of the pianoforte. The town joins two older towns, Hohenstein and Ernstthal, united in 1898. A second Hohenstein, in East Prussia, founded by the Teutonic Order in 1359, is noted at the end.
britannica-1911-holguin:
Holguín is a town of the high plateau country in the interior of Oriente province, Cuba, about 65 m. N.W. of Santiago de Cuba. Its population was 7,592 in 1907. It stands near the Marañon and Jigüé rivers, on a plain ringed by hills except to the east, where it lies open to the plateau winds. For long it was the chief station where Spanish troops were acclimatized.

The town's oldest public buildings are two churches, built in 1800 and 1809. Its trade is in cabinet woods, tobacco, Indian corn and cattle products, exported through Gibara, its port some 25 m. N.N.E., linked by railway. Holguín was settled about 1720 and became a city in 1751. In the Ten Years' War of 1868–1878 and the revolution of 1895–1898 it was an insurgent centre.
britannica-1911-huntsman-benjamin:
Benjamin Huntsman, who lived from 1704 to 1776, was an English steel maker. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how he beat poor steel. Born in Lincolnshire to German parents, he made clocks and tools at Doncaster. He also won local fame for science and skilled hand work.

Bad steel for springs and edges hampered all his trade. He set out to make a purer and harder steel himself. After years of trials near Sheffield he reached his goal. Town cutlers refused the new steel as too hard to work. For years his whole output shipped to France instead. French knives from his steel at last forced Sheffield to yield. A rival stole the secret by posing as a tramp at the works.
britannica-1911-idrialin: Idrialin is a brief mineral note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a mineral wax found with the mercury ore at Idria. Goldschmidt showed it can be drawn out with xylol, amyl alcohol, or turpentine, or distilled whole in a stream of hydrogen. The stuff is a white crystal body, very hard to melt, boiling above 440 degrees. Treated with chromic acid in acetic acid, it yields a red powder and a fatty acid much like a mix of palmitic and stearic acids.
britannica-1911-isnard-maximin:
Maximin Isnard lived from 1758 to 1825 and was a French revolutionary leader. The 1911 Britannica life opens with his trade in perfume at Draguignan. Voters of the Var sent him to the Legislative Assembly as their deputy. There he joined the Girondist party in the hall of law. He attacked the court and the so called Austrian group at the Tuileries.

He called for the king's guard to be broken up at once. Yet when a mob burst into the palace in June 1792, he stood by the king. He placed his own body by Louis to shield him from harm. Sent to the north army, he backed the rising of August that year. Back in the Convention, he voted death for the king he had shielded.
britannica-1911-javelin:
Javelin is a light spear made to be thrown by the hand. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that a thong oft helped the cast. Throwing the javelin forms one contest at the Olympic games in sport. In old days each sheriff kept a guard of javelin men in train. Those men watched over judges as they rode on assize through the shires.
