Police now do that guard work in the courts of England. The word came into English from the French word javeline in time. Kin words for spear live in Welsh, Irish, and Norse tongues of old. The root seems Celtic and ties to words for a hook or fork. How the sense moved from fork to spear stays obscure, it says.
britannica-1911-jehoiachin:
Jehoiachin, a king of Judah named in the Bible, is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica article. He was the son of Jehoiakim. He took the throne at age eighteen while Chaldean troops attacked Judah. His reign is said to have lasted three months.

Forced to give up to Nebuchadrezzar, he was taken to Babylon in 597 before Christ. Eight thousand people were also removed, and the Temple lost some of its goods. His uncle was made king in his place. Near forty years later a new king of Babylon freed him. He was then given rank above other captive kings.
britannica-1911-jerkin:
Jerkin is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a man's garment of past centuries. A jerkin is a short, close fitting jacket with no sleeves. It was most often made of leather. For men of the 1500s and 1600s it was the standard upper dress.

The article is frank that the root of the word is not known. A Dutch word for a child's frock is often named as the source. The text rules that claim out on grounds of sound and sense. The word also lives on in talk of building. A jerkin roof names a gable end cut off half way up. From that cut the roof slopes back like a hipped roof to the edge. The link between the two uses is dark, the text allows.
britannica-1911-john-margrave-of-branden:
John, or Hans (1513–1571), margrave of Brandenburg-Cüstrin, was the younger son of Joachim I, elector of Brandenburg, born at Tangermünde on the 3rd of August 1513. Despite a family law that barred division of the electorate, he inherited the new mark of Brandenburg on his father's death in July 1535.

Raised a strict Catholic, he moved by 1538 to the side of the Reformers and joined the league of Schmalkalden. Imperial promises then drew him back to Charles V. He opposed the Augsburg Interim of 1548 and led the princes who formed a league in February 1550 to defend Lutheran teaching. After fresh quarrels he returned to the emperor's side. His last years went to ruling the new mark with care and thrift. He bought Beeskow and Storkow and fortified Cüstrin and Peitz. He died at Cüstrin on the 13th of January 1571, leaving no sons.
britannica-1911-joncieres-victorin:
Victorin Joncieres, a French composer born in Paris in eighteen thirty nine, first gave his mind to painting. He later took up the serious study of music in its place. He entered the Paris Conservatoire but did not stay long there. He had backed the cause of Wagner too warmly against his professor. His operas began to appear in eighteen sixty seven with Sardanapale.

More operas followed across the next three decades of his life and work. They include works on Pompeii, on Queen Berthe, and on Lancelot. He also wrote music for Hamlet, a symphony, and other pieces. His love of Wagner shows in a musical more than a dramatic sense. He kept the set forms of French opera in his own works. From eighteen seventy one he served as music critic for a Paris paper.
britannica-1911-jones-alfred-gilpin:
Alfred Gilpin Jones, a Canadian politician who lived from 1824 to 1906, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Weymouth in Nova Scotia, he was the grandson of a United Empire Loyalist. In 1865 he opposed the federation of the British American provinces. His anger at Britain's refusal to repeal parts of the act for Nova Scotia led to a famed speech.

That speech won him the nickname Haul down the flag Jones, the entry says. He sat for many years in the federal Parliament. For a few months in 1878 he was minister of militia under a Liberal government. Largely through his sway, his party held to free trade that year and lost the election. In 1900 he became lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia, holding the post till his death.
britannica-1911-kain:
Kain is the name of a sub province and of a town in Khorasan, Persia. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kailas entry. The sub province runs about 300 miles north to south, from Khāf to Seīstān, and about 150 miles west to east, from the hills of Tūn to the Afghan frontier. It is very hilly, with wide plains and rich villages at a mean height of 4000 feet.

About 150,000 people lived there. The land rears great numbers of camels and yields much grain, saffron, wool, silk, and opium. Its felts and woollen goods are famed, above all its carpets, the best made at Darakhsh. The town of Kain was the capital until 1740, when Birjend took its place. It stands 65 miles north of Birjend, walled in mud, with barely 5000 people, and a ruined castle on a hill above the plain.
britannica-1911-kammin:
Kammin, or Cammin, is a town in the Prussian province of Pomerania. It stands 21 miles and a half from the Baltic, on the Kamminsche Bodden, a lake joined to the sea by the Dievenow. Its population in 1905 was 5923. Among its four Protestant churches, the cathedral and the church of St Mary stand out. Iron founding and brewing are carried on, with some fishing and shipping, and steamers run to Stettin, about 40 miles south southwest.

Kammin is of Wendish origin and gained town rights in 1274. From about 1200 until 1628 it was the seat of a bishopric. The see then became a secular principality, and in 1648 the town was folded into Brandenburg. The entry is a compact gazetteer note: place, waters, churches, trades, and four centuries of church rule summed in a few lines.
britannica-1911-kaolin:
Kaolin is a pure white clay, known also as china clay, since it is a chief material in the making of china, or porcelain. The word is said to be a corruption of the Chinese Kau ling, High Ridge, the name of a hill east of King te chen. From that hill came the first samples sent to Europe, by the Jesuit Père d'Entrecolles, early in the 18th century.

His samples, tested in Paris by Réaumur, showed that true porcelain held two chief materials. They came to be known as kaolin and petuntse, our china clay and china stone. Kaolin gives the paste its shaping power in the kiln. Petuntse gives the glassy quality of porcelain. Early finds were made at Aue in Saxony and St Yrieix near Limoges. In England it was found in Cornwall about 1750 by William Cookworthy.
britannica-1911-kazvin:
Kazvin is a province and town of Persia, northwest of Teheran and south of Gilan, with Khamseh on its west. The province pays a yearly revenue of about £22,000. It holds many rich villages that yield much grain and fruit, great amounts of the fruit being dried and sent abroad.

Kazvin, the capital, stands at 4165 feet, 92 miles by road from Teheran. The city is said to have been founded in the 4th century by the Sassanian king Shapur II. Earthquakes have damaged it again and again. Many streets and most of the grand buildings seen by Chardin in 1674 now lie in ruins. The chief remains are the palace of the Safawid shahs and the mosque with its large blue dome. In the 16th century Shah Tahmasp I made Kazvin his capital, and it stayed so until Shah Abbas I moved the seat of rule to Isfahan.
britannica-1911-keewatin:
Keewatin is a district of Canada. Hudson and James bays bound it on the east, and the Albany and English rivers, Manitoba, and Lake Winnipeg on the south. The 100th meridian bounds it on the west and Arctic straits on the north. It takes in 445,000 square miles.

Its surface is in general barren and rocky, studded with countless lakes, with forest below 60 degrees north and bare moss and lichen ground beyond, the so called barren lands. Save for a strip of younger rocks and a few patches of older ones, the district is built of Laurentian rock. Its chief river is the Nelson, which with its great feeder the Saskatchewan runs 1450 miles. The Hayes and the Severn also drain it. The survey treats a vast, thinly known north in the gazetteer's order of bounds, rock, river, and climate.
britannica-1911-kennicott-benjamin:
Benjamin Kennicott (1718–1783) was an English divine and Hebrew scholar, born at Totnes in Devonshire on the 4th of April 1718. He followed his father as master of a charity school. By the kindness of friends he was able to go to Wadham College, Oxford, in 1744, where he stood out in Hebrew and divinity.

While still an undergraduate he published two studies, on the Tree of Life in Paradise and on the offerings of Cain and Abel. They won him his bachelor's degree before the set time. In 1747 he was elected fellow of Exeter College, and in 1750 he took his master's degree. In 1764 he joined the Royal Society, and in 1767 he became keeper of the Radcliffe Library. The entry goes on to the great task of his life, the gathering and comparison of Hebrew manuscripts of the Old Testament.
britannica-1911-killin:
Killin is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Killin is a village and parish of Perthshire, Scotland, at the south west end of Loch Tay. It stands near where the rivers and glens of the Dochart and Lochay meet. The parish count of 1901 was a little over fourteen hundred. The village is a liked tourist centre, with steamer trips across the lake to Kenmore. Tweeds are made there.

In a field near the village a stone marks the spot known as Fingal's Grove. Earls of Breadalbane lie in ground by it, where the family's new tomb house stands. Three miles up the Lochay the river forms a fine fall. A ruined castle on an islet in the loch once belonged to the Campbells of Lochawe.
britannica-1911-kin:
Kin is a word for persons linked by blood from a shared forebear. Its word entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Old English form cyn appears in most Teutonic tongues in like forms. Its root means to beget or produce, as in genus and kindred terms.

In law, next of kin names those in the nearest blood degree to a dead person. They share the estate of a person who dies with no will. The phrase kith and kin joins words for known land and for blood kin. A suffix kin in names acts as a small form in Flanders and Holland. Words like pumpkin and firkin look the same but lack that sense.
britannica-1911-king-s-mountain:
King's Mountain, a ridge on the border of North and South Carolina, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It runs as an outlying spur of the Blue Ridge, with a crest marked by sharp and broken notches. Its highest point stands in North Carolina. The entry gives most of its space to the battle fought there in the war for American freedom.

The battle took place on the seventh of October 1780, on a narrow top some sixty feet above the land around. About a thousand Loyalist men under Major Patrick Ferguson faced some nine hundred American backwoodsmen led by five colonels. The Americans won. The British loss is given as 119 killed, 123 wounded, and 664 taken prisoner. The American loss was 28 killed and 62 wounded. The entry says the win did much to shape the course of the war.
britannica-1911-kreutzer-konradin:
Konradin Kreutzer (1780–1849) was a German composer, born on the 22nd of November 1780 at Messkirch in Baden. He died on the 14th of December 1849 at Riga. His fame rests almost wholly on one opera, Das Nachtlager von Granada (1834). Written in the manner of Weber, it held the stage for half a century, through all the changes of musical taste, thanks to its flow of true melody and depth of feeling.

The same gifts mark Kreutzer's part-songs for men's voices, once very popular in Germany. Among them "Der Tag des Herrn" ("The Lord's Day") is named as the finest. Kreutzer wrote many operas for the Vienna stage, but they have vanished and are not likely to return. He was Kapellmeister to the king of Württemberg from 1812 to 1816, and in 1840 he became conductor of the opera at Cologne. His daughter Cecilia was a singer of some note.
britannica-1911-krotoschin:
Krotoschin, in Polish Krotoszyn, is a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Posen, 32 miles S.E. of Posen. In 1900 it held 12,373 people. It has three churches and a synagogue, steam saw-mills and a steam brewery, and trades in grain and seeds.

Its castle is the chief place of a mediatized principality. That small state was formed in 1819 out of lands of the Prussian crown. It was granted to the prince of Thurn and Taxis, to make up for his giving up the monopoly of the Prussian postal system, which his family had held before.
britannica-1911-la-voisin:
Catherine Monvoisin, known as "La Voisin" (d. 1680), French sorceress, was a chief figure in the affaire des poisons of the reign of Louis XIV. Her husband was a failed jeweller, and she built their fortunes back up by palmistry and face-reading, then by witchcraft. With the renegade priest Étienne Guibourg, who celebrated a "black mass," she practised medicine and midwifery, procured abortions, and sold love powders and poisons. Her own article sits inside a chunk file that also carries neighbouring articles.

The great ladies of Paris flocked to her, among them the comtesse de Soissons and Mme de Montespan. After the Brinvilliers executions of 1676 a royal commission opened in April 1679. When Montespan's plan to poison the king came out, Louis closed the court, and La Voisin was executed on the 20th of February 1680. Thirty-five others were executed, five sent to the galleys and twenty-three banished.
britannica-1911-labe-louise-charlin-perr:
Louise Labé (c. 1525–1566), French poet called La Belle Cordière, was born at Lyons about 1525, the daughter of a rich ropemaker. At the siege of Perpignan she is said to have fought on horseback in the dauphin's ranks. Before 1551 she married Ennemond Perrin, also a ropemaker. She built up a library and gathered round her the learned ladies of Lyons — Pernette du Guillet, the Scève sisters, Clémence de Bourges. Poets such as Maurice Scève and Pontus de Tyard came too, with Marot and probably Rabelais among the visitors.

About 1550 the poet Olivier de Magny passed through Lyons and she fell in love with him. Her passion for Magny fired her verse: the elegies voice her grief at his absence, and her Sonnets, printed in 1555, quickly won great popularity. Magny's jealous ode to her husband, the "Sire Aymon," ruined her reputation.
britannica-1911-lane-george-martin:
George Martin Lane, an American scholar who lived from 1823 to 1897, is profiled in a short life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Charlestown in Massachusetts, he graduated at Harvard in 1846. He then studied for four years at four German universities. In 1851 he gained his doctor degree at Gottingen for a work on the city of Smyrna.

On his return Lane became professor of Latin at Harvard. He held the Pope chair of Latin from 1869 until he retired in 1894. His 1871 work on Latin pronunciation helped end the old English method in the United States. His Latin Grammar, finished by a colleague after his death, is held in high regard. He also helped make Harpers Latin word books. The entry notes his light verse, writ with humour and ease.
britannica-1911-lanolin:
Lanolin is the trade name for a skin mix. Wool-fat and water form the mix. The British list of drugs sets the mix at seven ounces of wool-fat. Three fluid ounces of water go with it. The fat comes from raw sheep's wool. Workers wash out a brown grease before spinning. Cleaning makes that grease fit for use.

Clean wool-fat is clear and soft. It takes up large amounts of water. Such mixes split apart only slowly. The fat sinks into skin with ease. Plain wool-fat and lanolin thus form the base of many ointments. Blends with vaseline or fatty oils are common. Two traits help its use. It acts mildly against germs. It does not turn rancid.
britannica-1911-lantara-simon-mathurin:
Simon Mathurin Lantara (1729-1778) was a French painter of landscape scenes, born at Oncy on 24 March 1729. A weaver's son who began as a herd boy, he caught the eye of his master's son and was placed with a painter at Versailles. Quick skill won him early notice.

Steady life chafed him. While money from a sale lasted he lived free of care among plain workmen, and rich patrons who took him in found that ease and fine living stopped his hand. He died in Paris on 22 December 1778. His works are few and now prized; the Louvre holds one signed landscape, Morning, dated 1761. Other painters, Vernet among them, are said to have added figures to his scenes.
britannica-1911-lappenberg-johann-martin:
Johann Martin Lappenberg is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lappenberg was a German historian, born at Hamburg in 1794. He first studied medicine, then turned to history at Edinburgh. He went on studying in London, Berlin, and Gottingen, taking a law degree in 1816.

In 1820 the Hamburg senate sent him as resident minister to the Prussian court. Three years later he became keeper of the Hamburg archives. That office gave him full scope for the slow, critical research on which his fame rests. He held the post for forty years, until failing eyes forced him to resign in 1863. He also sat for Hamburg in the German parliament at Frankfort in 1850. The entry honors an archivist whose care with records shaped the writing of German history.
britannica-1911-lekain:
Lekain was the stage name of Henri Louis Cain (1728-1778), a French actor, and his struggle and fame fill an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, son of a silversmith, he was educated at the College Mazarin and joined an amateur company. Voltaire backed him and let him act in his private theatre.

The entry tells how hostility from the actors kept him out of the Comedie Francaise for seventeen months, until Louis XV ordered his admission, when his success was instant. Though short, stout, and plain of face, he excelled in tragic roles. He also drove stage reforms, clearing the benches of onlookers from the stage and fighting sing-song delivery.
britannica-1911-lemierre-antoine-marin:
Antoine Marin Lemierre was a French writer of stage plays and verse who lived from seventeen thirty-three to seventeen ninety-three. He was born in Paris to poor folk. A tax chief took him as a clerk and backed his work. His first stage hit came in seventeen fifty-eight.

Some of his sad plays failed for their themes, while the rest did well. His tale of William Tell was brought back in seventeen eighty-six to great cheers. He came to rue that play when revolt turned to blood. The entry says the dread of those days sped his death. His verse tales of paint and the year are also named.
britannica-1911-linares-spain:
Linares is a town of southern Spain in Jaen. It sits among the south foothills of the Sierra Morena. Height above the sea is 1,375 feet. The Guadalimar runs three miles south-east. The count of 1900 gave 38,245 people. Four branch rail lines tie it to rich lead mines north-west.

Town growth came late and fast. Town hall, bull-ring, and theatre rose in the late 1800s. A fine fountain of Roman birth is the chief old thing. Lead rules work life here. Powder, dynamite, blasting fuse, and rope serve the pits. Plant comes from abroad, chiefly England. British firms smelt the ore and roll its sheets and pipes. Linares lead holds top rank for grade, though yield tends to fall. Grain, wine, and oil feed a brisk home trade. Old Castulo's scraps lie two miles south.
britannica-1911-lobenstein:
Lobenstein, a town in Germany in the state of Reuss, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Lemnitz stream in a pleasant and fertile tract, 25 miles north west of Hof by rail. Its count in 1905 was 2,990. The town is grouped round a rock that bears the ruins of its old castle, and the text calls it a most pleasing sight.

A large parish church and a palace are the chief buildings named for the town. The palace was the home of the princes of Reuss Lobenstein until 1824. A water cure house draws guests who seek health in the town. Trades listed for Lobenstein are dyeing, brewing, and cigar making, a small but mixed set for so small a place.
britannica-1911-loisy-alfred-firmin:
Alfred Firmin Loisy (born 1857) was a French Catholic scholar of the Bible. Ambrières in Lorraine was his birthplace. Peasant kin had tilled that soil for ages. A frail boy, he went to church school at St Dizier. No priestly path was planned. He chose it all the same and entered the seminary in 1874.

Orders came in 1879 and two village cures followed. Paris study at the Institut Catholique began in 1881. Abbé Martin taught him Bible tongues and text craft. Abbé Duchesne gave him a sharp eye for hard Bible facts. His degree came in March 1890. A first book, on the canon of the Old Testament, came that year. Chair work at the Institut followed. Books on the New Testament canon, on Bible text and versions, and on the first three Gospels poured out by 1894. His own journal carried much of it.
britannica-1911-longomontanus-christian-:
Danish star watcher Christian Severin Longomontanus, born at Longberg in fifteen sixty two, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His Latin name came from the name of his birth village in Jutland. His father, a poor labourer, died when the boy was eight.

An uncle saw to his schooling for a time, then sent him back to field work. His mother let him study in winter with the parish priest. In fifteen seventy seven he ran away to Viborg to learn more. He worked with his hands to pay his way. At Copenhagen in fifteen eighty eight he had a high name for learning. Tycho Brahe took him on at his great observatory the next year.
britannica-1911-lord-chamberlain:
The Lord Chamberlain, in England, is a great officer of the kings household, not to be mixed with the lord great chamberlain. The 1911 Britannica entry ranks him as the second man of the court. He is at all times a peer, a sworn adviser to the crown, and a member of the ruling team of the day.

His signs of office are a white staff and a gold or jeweled key, for the palace key held to be in his charge. He plans all that a state rite needs: crownings, royal weddings, name days, and funerals. Claims to be shown at court pass through his hands, and all bids to court go out in his name by the kings command. At court meets he stands by the throne and names each guest as they draw near.
britannica-1911-m-carthy-justin:
Justin M'Carthy is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Cork on the twenty second of November 1830, he was an Irish public man, historian, and writer of tales. He started work as a news writer at the age of eighteen.

The article follows his move to London in 1860. There he edited a morning paper and later wrote leaders for a great daily. He sat in parliament for Irish seats from 1879 to 1900. After the fall of Parnell he chaired the larger Irish party for six years. The text calls his temper mild and his views in good order. His chief work was a history of his own times in five books. It runs from the rise of Queen Victoria to her diamond jubilee.
britannica-1911-maclaurin-colin:
Colin Maclaurin (1698-1746) was a Scottish mathematician, born at Kilmodan in Argyllshire, the son of a clergyman, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He entered the university of Glasgow in 1709 and showed a clear genius for mathematics, above all for geometry. Before he was sixteen he had found many results later printed in his Geometria organica.

In 1717 Maclaurin won the chair of mathematics at Marischal College, Aberdeen, by open contest. Two years later he became a fellow of the Royal Society and met Sir Isaac Newton. His Geometria organica of 1719 set out several results due to Newton and a way of drawing conic curves that bears his name. It showed that many curves of the third and fourth degree can be traced by two moving angles. An essay on the striking of bodies won him the prize of the French Academy of Sciences for 1724.
britannica-1911-madan-martin:
Martin Madan, an English writer who lived from 1726 to 1790, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was educated at Westminster School and at Christ Church, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1748. For some time he lived a very gay life, till a sermon by John Wesley turned his ways.

Madan took holy orders and became chaplain to the Lock Hospital in London. He was closely tied to the Calvinistic Methodist movement backed by the Countess of Huntingdon, and he preached on the road at times. He was a first cousin of the poet William Cowper. In 1780 his book Thelyphthora raised a storm. In it he argued for polygamy as the cure for the evils he deplored, on scriptural grounds. The book drew many angry replies, and Madan gave up his chaplainship and retired to Epsom.
britannica-1911-marceau-desgraviers-fran:
François Séverin Marceau-Desgraviers, French general born at Chartres on 1 March 1769, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father was a law officer, and the boy was schooled for a legal career. At age sixteen he broke that path and enlisted in a regiment. On leave in Paris he joined the attack on the Bastille in July 1789.

After that day he left the regular army and went home to Chartres. Family money troubles soon drove him back to arms. He rose as drill instructor and then captain in the National Guard. In March 1792 voters made him lieutenant colonel of a battalion from his home department. He helped defend Verdun that year. It fell to him to carry the terms of surrender to the Prussian camp, a grim task that put his life at risk.
britannica-1911-maupeou-rene-nicolas-cha:
Rene Nicolas Charles Augustin Maupeou is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Maupeou was chancellor of France who lived from 1714 to 1792. His father had led the Paris parlement for many years. The son married a rich heiress in 1744. He acted as his father's right hand in fights with the archbishop of Paris.

The article tells how he led the parlement himself in the seventeen sixties. In 1768 he became chancellor of France. He set out to back royal power against the parlement. That body sought to take the role of the states general for itself. He joined with court allies and placed his own man in charge of funds. A hard clash came over a trial that touched a royal duke. The king backed Maupeou and called the judges to give up their case papers.
britannica-1911-maury-jean-siffrein:
Jean Siffrein Maury, a French cardinal, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was born at Valreas in 1746, the son of a poor cobbler. Priests at the Avignon seminary spotted his sharp mind. He was schooled there and took orders. He first made his name by writing formal eulogies. His piece on Fenelon took second place in 1771.

A eulogy of Saint Louis in 1772 won him real advancement. In 1777 he gathered his speeches into a book. That book on pulpit eloquence became a French classic. He became a favourite preacher in Paris. In 1781 he preached the Lent sermons at court. The king joked that he covered every topic but religion. He won a rich priory and then a seat in the Academy. In 1789 the clergy sent him to the states-general. There he became the ablest defender of the old order.
britannica-1911-mcdowell-irvin:
Irvin McDowell, an American soldier who lived from 1818 to 1885, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Columbus in Ohio in October 1818 and educated in France. He took his degree at the military academy of the United States in 1838. From 1841 to 1845 he taught at West Point and served as its adjutant.

He won a brevet as captain in the Mexican War, at Buena Vista. In May 1861 he was made a brigadier-general and put in command for the early campaign in Virginia. It ended in defeat at Bull Run. Under McClellan he rose to corps command. His corps was held back from the Peninsular campaign and sent to chase Jackson in the Shenandoah Valley. It then served under Pope in the ruin of Second Bull Run. He was shelved in 1862 and died at San Francisco in 1885.
britannica-1911-melingue-etienne-marin:
Etienne Marin Melingue, a French actor and sculptor who lived from 1808 to 1875, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Caen, the son of a volunteer of 1792. He went to Paris young and found work as a sculptor on the church of the Madeleine. His love of the stage soon drew him to a travelling company.

Chance gave him his break, and at the Porte Saint Martin he became the star of romantic drama of the Dumas type. One great hit was his Benvenuto Cellini. In that part he could act and sculpt at once, shaping a statue of Hebe on stage before the crowd. He also sent small statues to shows. His wife was an actress picked by Victor Hugo for a lead part.
britannica-1911-menier-emile-justin:
Emile Justin Menier is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French maker and law maker born in Paris in eighteen twenty six. On the death of his father he took charge of a large drug works. His father had also made a small amount of chocolate.

The entry shows how the son chose chocolate as his one trade. He bought cocoa lands abroad and beet fields at home to feed his mills. He sold his share of the drug trade and built a vast chocolate business. In his last years he sat in the French chamber as a firm republican. He also wrote books on tax and farm wealth.
britannica-1911-menin: Menin, in Flemish Meenen, is a town of Belgium in the province of West Flanders. It stands on the Lys, seven miles south of Courtrai. Its people numbered 19,377 in 1904. The town makes linen and flannel, and large fields of tobacco grow in the lands round it. Menin was first walled in 1578. In 1685 Vauban made it one of the strongest places on the French border, but its walls were razed in 1748 by the treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.
britannica-1911-mercie-marius-jean-anton:
Mercie, Marius Jean Antonin is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French sculptor and painter. He was born in Toulouse on the thirtieth of October 1845. He entered the School of Fine Arts in Paris and studied under Falguiere and Jouffroy. In 1868 he won the Grand Prix de Rome.

His first great popular successes were his David and his Gloria Victis. The second won the medal of honour at the Salon, and the bronze later stood in the Square Montholon. His Genius of the Arts, a relief of 1877, is in the Tuileries. A like work of 1879 marks the tomb of Michelet in Pere Lachaise. In 1882 he repeated his patriotic success with a group called Quand Meme. Copies of it stand at Belfort and in the Tuileries garden.
britannica-1911-meunier-constantin:
Constantin Meunier (1831-1905) was a Belgian painter and sculptor, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his turn from monks to miners. He was born at Etterbeek in Brussels, and his first exhibit was a plaster sketch shown at the Brussels Salon in 1851. On the advice of the painter Charles de Groux he soon gave up the chisel for the brush. His first big painting, The Salle St Roch, came in 1857.

More works on Trappist life followed, along with scenes of the Peasants' War. About 1880 he was hired to picture the miners and factory hands in a noted description of Belgium. From that work came paintings of the factory, the smithy, the steel works at Seraing, and men returning from the pit.
britannica-1911-moleskin: Moleskin names both the skin of a mole and a stout cotton cloth that feels like leather, as the short 1911 Britannica entry explains. The cloth is woven as a satin twill on a strong warp. It is shorn before it is dyed or bleached. Its weave is hard-wearing and cheap, so it has been much worn by working men, most of all by men who labour out of doors. It also serves for gun cases, carriage covers, and other uses where a cloth must stand rough handling.
britannica-1911-momein:
Momein is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Chinese city near Burma. Momein is the Burmese name of the city Teng-yueh-chow. It lies in the south west of the province of Yunnan. It was opened to foreign trade by the Burmese Convention of 1897. So far no advantage has been taken of that permission. It lies close to the Burmese frontier. 

Its importance as an outpost of the British Empire is political. That importance is political rather than commercial, the text says. The distance from Teng-yueh to Bhamo is 160 miles by road. That road is generally travelled by pack animals. The trip takes seven or eight days by that route. In a straight line the two towns are only eighty miles apart. Near Momein lies the frontier town of Manwyne. The traveller Margary was assassinated there in 1875.
britannica-1911-montserrat-spain:
Montserrat is the subject of a mountain article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Montserrat is a famed mountain and monastery in northeast Spain. It stands northwest of Barcelona. The mountain is made of grey conglomerate rock, and its girth is about eighteen miles. Its highest point rises over four thousand feet. From that peak the eye can reach the Pyrenees and the sea.

The article describes jagged pinnacles that rise sharply from the base of the mass. Deep ravines cut the rock, and steep cliffs abound. Its name links it to the teeth of a saw, from its jagged look. Spanish legend says the rocks split at the time of the Crucifixion. A monastery stands high on a narrow shelf at the edge of a great fissure. Its fame rests on an image of the Virgin said to have been hidden there from invaders.
britannica-1911-moreto-y-cavana-agustin:
Agustin Moreto y Cavana (1618-1661) was a Spanish playwright. He was baptized at Madrid on 9 April 1618 and took his degree at Alcala in 1639. He lived in Madrid till 1654. He then moved to Toledo, took orders, and became chaplain to the primate of Spain. He died at Toledo on 28 October 1661, at work on a play that a friend finished for him.

The first book of Moreto's dramas came out in 1654, and two more books came after his death. His most famed piece is El Desden con el Desden. Moliere drew on it for a play of his own, and Gozzi and Schreyvogel drew on it in turn. Moreto borrowed freely from other men. Four scenes of that famed play come from four plays of Lope de Vega. He took from Castro and Tirso de Molina as well.
britannica-1911-mortain:
Mortain, a small town in the department of La Manche in France, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of a district. It sits fair on a rock hill above the gorge of the Cance. That stream feeds the Selune.

The parish church is a grand work in the shift style of the early thirteen hundreds. It has a vast tower of the next age and a Norman door from the first church on the site. Near the town stands a white abbey founded in eleven hundred and five. Its church is a pure case of the plain great style of its order. Parts of its old walks still stand. The town count is set at between two and three thousand. In the middle ages Mortain was the head of a great county.
britannica-1911-mortmain:
Mortmain, from old French words for dead hand, is defined in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a state of land law. It is the state of lands held by a body that never dies. Such a body holds the land for good. It can never pass the land on in the free way a man can.

That hold hurt the lord who stood above the land. He lost the dues that came at the death of a tenant, or at his crime, or when his line failed. So law after law in England struck at such grants. The first is named as a clause of the great charter. More laws came under three kings in turn. The rule in force rests on an act of eighteen eighty eight, with a fix in eighteen ninety one.
britannica-1911-mulheim-am-rhein:
Mulheim am Rhein is a town in Germany, on the right bank of the Rhine past Cologne. In truth it is a part of that great town, tied to it by two rail lines. Its count of folk in nineteen five was past fifty thousand. Silk, bands, plush, and sail cloth lead its long list of trades.

Roll shops, pot works, wire works, and a ship yard add to that list, and trade by rail and stream runs brisk. Town rights came in thirteen twenty-two. Much of its wealth came from faith exiles cast out of Cologne. A great flood in the past age hurt it sore.
britannica-1911-muset-colin:
Colin Muset, a French trouvere who worked near the year 1200, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was both poet and musician. He made his living by travel from castle to castle, singing his own songs for his hosts. One of his patrons was Agnes de Bar, duchess of Lorraine.

His songs stand out from the usual love verse of his kind, the piece notes. They hold many small facts about a singer's life on the road. Colin thanks his patrons with plain joy for gifts in kind. He also tells a poet spurned by a cold mistress to seek comfort in good food by a large fire. The article points readers to French literary history for more.
britannica-1911-nyezhin:
Nyezhin, a town in Russia in the government of Chernigov, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Oster river, on the rail line between Kursk and Kiev. About thirty three thousand people lived there. Most were Little Russians and Jews, with some Greeks as well.

The old town sits on the left bank, with two suburbs on the right. Sites include an old cathedral and a famed former high school. The novelist Gogol studied at that school as a youth. The town is named in records as early as 1147. It passed between the princes of Chernigov, Poland, and Russia over the years. In 1649 it became chief town of a key Cossack regiment. It was joined to Russia for good in 1664.
britannica-1911-oelwein:
Oelwein, a city in Fayette county, Iowa, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The city sits in the north-east part of the state, about 132 miles from Des Moines. Its people numbered 6,028 in the 1910 census, up sharply from 830 in 1890. Of the 1900 count, 789 people were foreign-born. Two railways serve the city.

One line, the Chicago Great Western, has large repair shops at Oelwein, where four of its lines meet. The city was named for its founder, August Oelwein, who settled there in 1873. It was incorporated in 1888. In 1897 it was chartered as a city. Readers get a brief, factual sketch of a small rail town whose growth followed the railways.
britannica-1911-pajou-augustin:
Augustin Pajou, who lived from 1730 to 1809, was a French sculptor. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his prize and his busts. He was born in Paris in September 1730. At eighteen he won the Prix de Rome for young artists.

At thirty Pajou showed a Pluto holding the hound of hell chained. That work now sits in the Louvre at Paris. Portrait busts rank among his best and most famed pieces. Buffon and Madame Du Barry sat to him in stone. A statuette of Bossuet shares that high praise as well. He carved new figures for the Fountain of the Innocents in Paris. A bust of an actor stands at the national theatre still. A monument to a Polish queen showed at the Salon of 1769. He died in Paris in 1809.
britannica-1911-paraffin:
Paraffin, a mineral wax and oil, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is also used for a whole series of hydrocarbons, the text notes. In its refined trade form it is a white or bluish white solid with a waxy feel. It has no taste and no smell, and it resists most chemical attack. It is made of about 85 per cent carbon and 15 per cent hydrogen.

Credit for the first close study of solid paraffin, in 1830, goes to Karl Reichenbach, who got it from wood tar. He gave it its name from Latin words for too little love of joining with other stuff. That stress on its inert, stand off nature is the core of the piece. Finds in rock oil and coal tar by other hands are traced from 1809 on to the 1850s.
britannica-1911-paris-alexis-paulin:
Alexis Paulin Paris, a French savant who lived from 1800 to 1881, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Avenay in the Marne in March 1800. In 1824 he brought out a defence of the romantic school and took a live part in the press of Paris. In 1828 he gained a post in the manuscripts room of the royal library.

That post left him free to give his days to the French letters of the middle ages. His chief worth, the article says, is that his many editions of old French poems kept up the work of Meon. They woke a wide love for the epics of chivalry, then all but unknown. In 1837 he joined the Academy of Inscriptions. In 1853 a chair of medieval letters was founded at the College de France, and he was its first holder.
britannica-1911-peary-robert-edwin:
Robert Edwin Peary, an American Arctic explorer who lived from 1856 onward, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Cresson, Pennsylvania, in May 1856, he graduated at Bowdoin College in 1877. In 1881 he became a civil engineer in the United States navy with the rank of lieutenant. In 1884 he joined the Nicaragua Ship Canal surveys, leading them in 1887 and 1888.

In 1886 Peary got leave for a summer trip to Disco Bay on Greenland's west coast. There he travelled nearly a hundred miles inland, and the trip convinced him the ice-cap could serve as a highway for exploration. In 1891 he organized an expedition backed by a Philadelphia academy. The party of seven included his wife. After wintering in Inglefield Gulf, Peary crossed the ice-cap with a young Norwegian. The journey established that Greenland is an island.
britannica-1911-peirce-benjamin:
Benjamin Peirce is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Salem, in the state of Massachusetts, on the fourth of April 1809, he was a worker in maths and star science in the United States. He took his degree at Harvard in 1829 and became a professor there in 1833.

The article rates him first among his country's maths men after 1838. His work on the paths of Uranus and Neptune won him wide fame. In 1849 he became a guiding hand for the national star almanac. New tables of the moon came from his hand in 1852. His study of Saturn's rings led him to hold that they must be fluid. From 1867 to 1874 he ran the Coast Survey. His best known book set out a system of mechanics in 1857.
britannica-1911-pekin:
Pekin is a city and county seat of Tazewell county in Illinois. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the Illinois river in mid state. It lies some eleven miles south of Peoria on the map. Its count in 1910 was 9,897 souls in the town. Eight rail lines serve it for freight and for passengers alike.

Rich farm land and the Illinois coal fields ring the city round. That place makes it a shipping point and a grain market of weight. Goods of many kinds are made in its mills and shops. Factory goods came to a large sum in the year 1905. First settled about 1830, the town was chartered in 1839.
britannica-1911-penguin:
Penguin is the name of a sea bird that cannot fly, as an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The word was first used, so far as is known, for a bird of the seas of Newfoundland. That bird is now called the great auk. In English use the word is kept for birds of the Southern Ocean, placed by scholars in their own family.

For a long time their place in the bird world was ill grasped. Some men set them with the auks, to which they bear a likeness of shape only. Keen eyes saw in them a class apart, and later work set them near the petrel group. Their wings have no quills and cannot bend, though they swing free at the shoulder. Some kinds use them to help move on land.
britannica-1911-pepsin:
Pepsin is a substance article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an enzyme used to aid the digestion of protein foods. Pepsin is got by drying the mucous lining of the fresh, sound stomach of a pig, sheep, or calf. In medicine it comes as a light yellow brown or white powder, or as pale yellow grains or scales, and it dissolves only a little in water or alcohol.

Pepsin digests the albumens but does nothing for fats or carbohydrates, and it can be used to predigest protein foods outside the body. The article gives a kitchen method for peptonizing beef: minced lean beef in water with a touch of hydrochloric acid, warmed with pepsin for three hours, then boiled. A pancreatic solution, it adds, turns starch into sugar and works only in an alkaline medium.
britannica-1911-phelps-austin:
Austin Phelps, an American minister and teacher who lived from 1820 to 1890, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at West Brookfield, Massachusetts, son of a clergyman. He studied at Hobart and Amherst, then took his degree in Pennsylvania. He trained for the ministry at three seminaries and was licensed to preach in 1840.

Phelps served as pastor of a Boston church from 1842 to 1848. He then taught sacred rhetoric and preaching at Andover for thirty years. He was president of that seminary from 1869 until ill health forced him out in 1879. His Theory of Preaching, issued in 1881, became a standard textbook. A book on English style in public speech followed two years later. He also helped edit two hymn books.
britannica-1911-philip-i-king-of-spain:
Philip the First of Spain, the Handsome, is set out in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bruges in 1478, he was the emperor Maximilian's son. His mother Mary left him the Burgundian lands in 1482. In 1496 he wed Joanna, child of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain. That match was one strand in a web of house alliances.

When Spain's lone prince John died, the crown path opened to Joanna. In 1502 the cortes of Castile and Aragon hailed the pair as heirs. Philip went back to Flanders before that year was out in full. His straying and her fierce envy wrecked their home life in time. Her mind broke down under that strain in fits of rage. When Isabella died, Philip was called to rule in Spain.
britannica-1911-philip-ii-king-of-spain:
Philip the Second, king of Spain, was born at Valladolid on 21 May 1527 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of the emperor Charles the Fifth and Isabella of Portugal. The two parents were first cousins. Philip gained his schooling in Spain.

His tutor was a doctor who took a Latin form of his name and also heard his confession. That teaching is judged lax in the entry, though Philip gained a good command of Latin. A master of arms found him a poor pupil. From his earliest years he loved the desk more than the saddle and the pen more than the sword. His father, far off in camps and courts, pressed him by letter to grasp the high fate ahead of him.
britannica-1911-philip-iii-king-of-spain:
Philip the Third, king of Spain, who lived from 1578 to 1621, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Philip the Second and of Anne, a daughter of the emperor Maximilian. He was born at Madrid in April 1578. He took his father's faith but no share of his zeal for work.

The old king had said with grief that God had not given him a son fit to rule his wide lands. The new king laid the whole rule in the hands of his favourite, the duke of Lerma. When Lerma's son rose in his place, the king trusted him in the same way. His own life passed in court shows, on which vast sums were waste, and in acts of piety. He died at Madrid in March 1621.
britannica-1911-philip-iv-king-of-spain:
Philip the Fourth ruled Spain from his birth line as eldest son of Philip the Third, born at Valladolid in 1605. The 1911 Britannica entry calls his reign a long tale of decay and disaster. A few early wins gave way to steady loss of power and land. The entry warns that inner rot, more than the king, drove the fall of Spain.

Philip had more force of mind and body than his father, it concedes. He turned Guicciardini into Spanish by his own hand to learn statecraft from history. Riding and hunting showed his bodily skill and love of sport. His taste in art fed the career of Velazquez at his court.
britannica-1911-philip-v-king-of-spain:
Philip the Fifth was king of Spain and founder of its Bourbon line, born at Versailles as son of the heir to the French throne. When the male line of the Spanish Habsburgs died out, he was named heir in the will of the last king of that house. He had shared the strict schooling given to his elder brother.

The 1911 Britannica entry paints a slow, grave man by nature. Taught morals by a famed church tutor, he held all his life a strong dislike of the loose ways of his grandfather and of most princes of his time. That same strict home life left him swayed in full by his two wives in turn. He wed a princess of Savoy as a youth, and on her death wed a princess of Parma that same year. He showed nerve on the field of war.
britannica-1911-picrotoxin: Picrotoxin is a neutral substance got from Cocculus indicus, the fruit of the plant Anamirta paniculata. Doctors used it on the skin to kill parasites. Taken by mouth, it was used to check the night sweats of consumption. The entry gives its chemical makeup in a short formula. It also warns plainly about what large doses can do to the body and the mind.
britannica-1911-poplin:
Poplin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a mixed textile fabric. It is also called tabinet in the trade. The fabric is made of a silk warp. Its weft is a yarn of worsted wool. That weft is in the form of a stout cord. So the fabric has a ridged structure, like rep. The ridges give depth and softness to its lustre. The silky surface gains much from that build.

Poplins are used for dress purposes in the main. They also serve for rich upholstery work in homes. The making of poplin is of French origin. Huguenot weavers brought the craft into England. It has long been specially associated with Ireland. French makers split poplins into plain and patterned kinds. The patterned kind is likened to Scotch tartans. A large trade in both runs to the United States. That trade flows chiefly from the city of Lyons.
britannica-1911-quatorzain:
Quatorzain is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a form of poem. The word comes from the French for fourteen. In English literature it names a poem of fourteen rhymed lines. Those lines are iambic in their metre. The poem closes with a couplet at its end. A sonnet, strictly kept, never closes in that way. The distinction was long neglected by English readers.

Poets of the sixteenth century had missed the sonnet's true form. They called Italian sonnets by the name quatorzains. They called their own incorrect quatorzains sonnets in return. Almost all Elizabethan sonnet cycles are really quatorzains. Those of Shakespeare, Sidney, Spenser, and Daniel are named. They consist of three quatrains of alternate rhyme. That rhyme is not repeated in successive quatrains. The whole then closes with a couplet as required. A poem by Michael Drayton is quoted as near perfect.
britannica-1911-regnier-mathurin:
Mathurin Regnier (1573-1613), a French satirist, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Chartres, he was the son of a well-to-do townsman. His mother was the sister of the poet Desportes, who was rich in church posts and high in favour at court. The boy was marked for the church at eight, in hope he would follow his uncle.

Little is known of his youth, the article says. He most likely went to Italy in 1587 in the train of a cardinal sent to the papal court. He found the duties dull. After years of travel in that service he came back to France about 1605 and lived on his uncle's kindness. He had begun early to write satire. The feud between his uncle and the poet Malherbe gave him a target, and he attacked Malherbe in verse.
britannica-1911-replevin:
Replevin is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a way for a person to get back goods that were taken from him without right, by a special form of legal process. The word comes from an Anglo French term linked to pledging. The entry splits the matter in two.

First comes the replevy, the steps by which the owner gains the goods themselves. He must give security to carry the case on and to return the goods if he loses. Second comes the action of replevin itself. County courts hold the first kind of business, while a higher court may hear the second. The entry contrasts this swift path with the older, slower action for goods wrongfully held.
britannica-1911-robins-benjamin:
Benjamin Robins, born at Bath in seventeen o seven, was an English man of science and an engineer. His parents were poor Quakers who gave him little schooling. On the advice of Doctor Henry Pemberton, who saw his gifts, he came to London. For a time he taught mathematics to live. Soon he turned to engineering and to the study of forts and guns.

Robins ran a long set of tests in gunnery and set out the results in seventeen forty two. That famed work describes his ballistic pendulum, used to time shot. He also tested how air slows shot in flight and how strong gunpowder is. He matched his theory with the ranges of mortars and cannon. His book gave sound rules for the handling of guns.
britannica-1911-robinson-sir-joseph-benj:
Sir Joseph Benjamin Robinson (born 1845) was a South African mine owner from Cape Colony. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his start as trader and wool buyer at sixteen. News of diamonds in 1867 drew him to the Vaal river at once. Buying stones and then diamond land at Kimberley built his fortune fast.

He served as mayor of Kimberley and sat in the Cape parliament. Gold finds in 1886 led him to buy Rand estates in the west. His view on the reef trend proved right against most opinion then. That call made him one of the richest men in South Africa. He stood apart from other Rand groups in politics.
britannica-1911-romorantin:
Romorantin is a town of central France described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of a district in the department of Loir-et-Cher, thirty-one miles south-east of Blois by rail. The town held 6,836 people in 1906, and the commune held 8,374. It stands on the Sauldre where the Morantin joins it, and that stream gives the town its name.

Points of interest are a church of the twelfth century in the main, a gate of the sixteenth, and some old houses. The scraps of a castle rebuilt by Francis the First serve as the office of the sub-prefect. The town has law courts and a college. Its trades are the making of flannel and cloth, much of it for army dress, and trade in wine, stock, farm goods, and asparagus. In 1560 the town gave its name to an edict that kept the Inquisition out of France.
britannica-1911-rosin:
Rosin is a trade article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the solid part of pine resin, also called colophony. Pines give off an oleo-resin known in trade as crude turpentine. Workers split it by heating it in large copper stills. The spirit of turpentine goes off as vapour, and fluid rosin is left behind.

The rosin is run off through a tap and strained clean. Its colour shifts with the age of the tree and the heat used. It runs from an opaque, near-black mass through browns and yellows to a clear, glassy solid. Trade grades are many, marked by letters from A, the darkest, upward. The palest sorts are called window glass and water white. The entry shows how a raw tree sap becomes a graded good of world trade.
britannica-1911-rosswein:
Rosswein is a town of Germany in the kingdom of Saxony state. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Freiberger Mulde river, south east of Leipzig by rail. Counts from nineteen o five put its people at just over nine thousand.

The town is famed for trade schools for builders and furniture makers. A third school trains ironmongers for their craft in the town shops. Work covers wool and cloth making, dye work, and spin work. Farm machines, cigars, chemicals, bricks, and iron goods are also made. Cloth making thrived in Rosswein as far back as the fourteenth century.
britannica-1911-saccharin:
Saccharin is the name of several chemical substances, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the commercial kind a technical entry. That kind, named for its excessively sweet taste, is a coal tar product. The entry names it in chemical terms as an imide tied to a sulphur bearing acid, and it lists more than one way to prepare it.

Most of the methods start from related coal tar compounds and use oxidation, in one case by electric means. The substance itself is a crystalline powder. It melts at a high heat with partial breakdown, dissolves with difficulty in cold water, more readily in hot water, and freely in alcohol. Strong acid at high heat breaks it back down into ammonia and its parent acid. The entry is written for chemists, with patents and journal references given for each route.
britannica-1911-sakhalin:
Sakhalin, a large island in the North Pacific, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies off the coast of the Russian Maritime Province in East Siberia. At the time it was split between the Russian and Japanese empires. Its own Ainu name, Karafuto, had been restored by the Japanese since 1905. A narrow, shallow strait parts it from the mainland, and another strait parts it from Japan.

The article gives the island as 600 miles long and from 16 to 105 miles broad. Two or three ranges of hills run its length from north to south, rising to near 5,000 feet. Wide low tracts sit between them. The entry admits that its rocks and land forms were still poorly known. It notes old limestones with the shells of huge ammonites and younger beds of gravel, sand, and clay.
britannica-1911-saladin:
Saladin, the first Ayyubite sultan of Egypt who lived from 1138 to 1193, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Tekrit, he rose in a world the entry paints as split and weak. The caliph at Baghdad and the Fatimid rulers at Cairo held power only through their viziers. The Seljuk empire had broken into small Turkish lordships.

Against that split stood the Latin kingdom of Jerusalem, united since 1089. The article tells how Muslim zeal rose to match Christian zeal. Zengi of Mosul began a sacred war in Syria, and his son carried it on with fresh gains. That conscious call for unity, the entry argues, gave Saladin his chance. His life spans the years when the demand for a single leader was ripe.
britannica-1911-schleswig-holstein:
Schleswig-Holstein is a province article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a province in the north-west of Prussia. The province was formed from the once Danish duchies of Schleswig, Holstein, and Lauenburg. It forms the southern half of the Cimbric peninsula, the link between Germany and Denmark.

The entry sets out the province's bounds and parts. The North Sea washes its west and the Baltic its east. The lower Elbe parts it from Hanover to the south. Islands belong to it as well, among them Alsen and Fehmarn in the Baltic. Sylt and Fohr lie in the North Frisian chain. The river Eider splits the land, Holstein to the south and Schleswig to the north. Readers get the frame of a border province whose ownership had long been disputed.
britannica-1911-sea-urchin:
Sea-urchins are the subject of a natural history article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They form a class of the great group of echinoderms. Both their English and their Latin names point to the hedgehog, for their skin is thick with prickles. Under the prickles the skin is stiff with plates of lime that form a hard shell, or test.

The test has two holes, one for the mouth and one for waste. In the regular urchins the shell is round, with the mouth below and the waste hole on top. In the irregular urchins the shell is drawn out to an oval or heart shape. The mouth shifts toward the front and the waste hole toward the back. The article then maps the ten zones of plates and the rows of tube feet with suckers.
britannica-1911-semlin:
Semlin, a town of Croatia-Slavonia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Hungarian it is Zimony, and in Serbian, Zemun. It stands on a tongue of land between the Danube and the Save. The census of 1900 counted about 15,079 people there.

Most of the people were Serbs, with Croats, Jews, Germans, and others beside. The town is the seat of an Orthodox archbishop, yet most folk are Roman Catholic. Standing where two navigable rivers meet, Semlin held a key post for travel. The main rail line from Budapest toward Constantinople ran through it. It served as the chief customs and quarantine station between Austria-Hungary and the Balkan states. Its transit trade in grain, fruit, livestock, and timber outweighed its few factories. On a hill above the Danube stand the ruins of Hunyadi's castle, where he died in 1456.
britannica-1911-shamokin:
Shamokin is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a borough in Northumberland County, Pennsylvania. It stands on Shamokin Creek, about forty-five miles north of Harrisburg. The census of 1910 counted 19,588 people there, up from 18,202 in 1900. Three rail lines and two interurban lines serve the borough.

Its main trades are the mining and shipping of anthracite coal and the making of silk goods and knit wear. It also has foundries, machine shops, and works for powder, shirts, brick, flour, and lumber. The value of its factory output in 1905 was close to one and a half million dollars. The name comes from the creek and is likely a worn form of a Delaware word meaning full of eels. The borough was formed in 1852 from two villages and set up in 1864.
britannica-1911-shanklin:
Shanklin is a watering-place on the Isle of Wight in England, 82 miles south of Ryde by rail. Its urban district held 4,533 people in 1901. The town sits in a fine spot on the cliffs of the south-east coast. High downs shelter it to the west. Its church of St John the Baptist is in the Perpendicular style, and there are newer churches and chapels as well.

Shanklin has many villas, a pier, and a lift that links the town with the esplanade below the cliff. South of the town, a winding chasm cuts through the cliffs. That gap is Shanklin Chine, noted here for its scenic charm. The short article gives the town's place, size, church, pier, and chine as its chief facts.
britannica-1911-silliman-benjamin:
Benjamin Silliman (1779–1864), an American chemist and geologist, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Trumbull, Connecticut, on the eighth of August 1779. He entered Yale College in 1792 and took his degree in 1796. In 1802 Yale made him professor of chemistry and mineralogy.

Silliman held that chair for half a century, retiring in 1853 as professor emeritus. The entry credits him with much work to grow the college. He built up its mineral collections and backed the Trumbull Gallery, the Medical Institution, and the Sheffield Scientific School. Beyond Yale, he drew large crowds to his science lectures. His clear style and bold experiments made him sought after across the north, east, and south.
britannica-1911-simon-of-st-quentin:
Simon of Saint Quentin, a Dominican friar of the 1200s, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He joined an embassy that Pope Innocent the Fourth sent in 1247. Friar Ascelin led the mission to the Mongols. Simon went along and wrote its history. His book is lost in its first form. Large parts survive inside the history of Vincent of Beauvais.

The envoys reached the camp of the Mongol general Baiju in Armenia. The papal letters were rendered into Persian, then into Mongol. The hosts took offence at the friars' proud manner. The friars gave no gifts and would not bow as custom required. For nine weeks no answer to the letters came. Three times Baiju ordered the envoys killed. At last they were sent home with a harsh reply. It ordered the pope to come and submit in person.
britannica-1911-smith-goldwin:
Goldwin Smith, a British writer on the past who lived from 1823 to 1910, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Reading, he shone at Eton and at Magdalen College, Oxford. He then held a fellowship at University College. With Arthur Penrhyn Stanley he threw his sharp mind and keen pen into the cause of reform at Oxford.

Smith served on the royal boards that looked into Oxford reform in the 1850s. His 1868 tract on the remaking of Oxford backed many changes that were later made law. He held the chair of modern history at Oxford from 1858 to 1866. The text notes that his wide range of work kept him from one great book, though he wrote on both Britain and the United States.
britannica-1911-sorolla-y-bastida-joaqui:
Joaquin Sorolla y Bastida was a Spanish painter who was born in Valencia in eighteen sixty-three. He learned art in his home town, then in Italy and Paris. An early work won a gold prize in Madrid and was bought for a hall in Saint Louis. Fame came fast from that point on.

He was soon held as head of the new Spanish school of paint. A scene of men who fish come home won praise at Paris and a state home. Top honours came at the great Paris show of nineteen hundred. His work hangs in halls at Berlin, Venice, and Madrid, and he painted the king and queen.
britannica-1911-soulary-josephin:
Josephin Soulary is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French poet born at Lyons in eighteen fifteen. The son of a merchant, he served five years in a line regiment as a youth. He then held office posts in his home town for most of his life.

The entry lists his verse books across more than forty years of work. His gay sonnets won wide note for their mix of mirth and grief. His skill with hard verse forms won him a craft nickname of high praise. Two stage comedies stand beside his poems in the list. His full poems were gathered in three books before his death in eighteen ninety one.
britannica-1911-st-martin:
Saint Martin is an island in the West Indies, south of Anguilla. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a near triangular shape of hills. Paradise Peak, its high point, rises to just under two thousand feet. Salt had replaced sugar as its main product by that time.

One fact sets the island apart from all others in the Antilles. Two European powers own it jointly in separate parts. France holds the north as a dependency of Guadeloupe. Holland holds the south as a dependency of Curaçao. French freebooters first settled it in 1638. A calm split of the island followed ten years later.
britannica-1911-st-quentin:
St Quentin, a manufacturing town of northern France in the department of Aisne, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 32 miles north-west of Laon by rail, on the right bank of the Somme. Two canals meet the river there. Its people numbered 49,305 in 1906. The port carries a busy traffic in building materials, coal, timber, iron, sugar, and farm produce.

Built on a slope with a southern aspect, the town is dominated by its collegiate church. That church is one of the finest Gothic buildings in the north of France, raised over four centuries. It has no west front, ending instead in a Romanesque tower and portal. Its length is 436 feet and its nave rises 124 feet. The choir recalls that of Reims and carries painted decoration. Under the choir lies an eleventh-century crypt holding the tombs of St Quentin and fellow martyrs.
britannica-1911-stettin:
Stettin, the Oder port of Pomerania, is surveyed in a city entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Oder, thirty miles from the Baltic Sea. Berlin lies eighty-four miles south-west by the rail lines. In 1905 its folk came to over two hundred and twenty thousand. Four bridges tie its hill town to its port suburbs east.

Strong walls girdled the town close till the year 1874. Their bulk choked the growth of trade and of new works. Trade suburbs sprang up past that wall line in great number. When the walls came down, building spread on their old ground. St Peter's church, founded in 1124, is its oldest shrine. It is held the oldest church in all Pomerania land.
britannica-1911-stewart-sir-donald-marti:
Donald Martin Stewart, who lived from 1824 to 1900, was a British field marshal born near Forres in Scotland. The 1911 Britannica article says he entered the Bengal army in 1840. He served in frontier wars in 1854 and 1855. In the Indian Mutiny of 1857 he made a famed ride from Agra to Delhi with dispatches. He served on the staff at the siege and capture of Delhi and of Lucknow. For nine years he held Bengal staff posts.

Stewart led the Bengal brigade in the Abyssinian war of 1867 and rose to major general in 1868. He ran the Andaman Islands penal camp when Lord Mayo was killed there. In the Afghan War of 1878 he led the Kandahar force. In 1880 he marched from Kandahar to Kabul and held command in the north. He was commander in chief in India for five years.
britannica-1911-strickland-hugh-edwin:
Hugh Edwin Strickland, English student of nature and of rocks, was born at Righton in Yorkshire on 2 March 1811 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a grandson of Sir George Strickland. As a lad he gained a taste for natural history that ruled his life. Private tutors gave him his early schooling.

In 1829 he entered Oriel College at Oxford. Talks on anatomy by Dr Kidd and on rocks by Dr Buckland fed his twin loves there. He took his first degree in 1831 and a second the next year. Back home near Tewkesbury, he studied the rocks of the Vale of Evesham. Papers on that work went to the Geological Society of London. Birds drew much of his care as well. In 1835 he travelled through Asia Minor with Hamilton.
britannica-1911-svendsen-johann-severin:
Johann Severin Svendsen was a Norwegian composer born in Christiania in eighteen forty. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father taught him music and violin work in his early years. He served in the army, then toured as a violin player with a band.

Help from the king of Sweden sent Svendsen to study at Leipzig. He led the Euterpe concerts there and wed an American in eighteen seventy one. From eighteen seventy two he led the Christiania Musical Society for five years. In eighteen eighty three he became court music chief at Copenhagen. His first string quartet and his octet won wide fame early on.
britannica-1911-tain:
Tain is a royal and police burgh of the county of Ross and Cromarty, Scotland, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It stands on rising ground within a mile of the south shore of Dornoch Firth, north-east of Dingwall by rail, and had 2,076 people in 1901. Its name, in older forms Tene, Tayne, and Thane, comes from an Icelandic word for an assembly or court.

Chief buildings include the town hall, court house, and an academy opened in 1812, and its trades include distilling and woollen making. It serves as a market and supply centre, and its rainfall is among the lowest in the kingdom. The article dwells on St Duthus, a saint said to be a native of the town. His collegiate church, founded by James III in 1471, drew pilgrimages from James IV and was restored in the 1870s after years of decay.
britannica-1911-tannin:
Tannin, or tannic acid, is the broad name for a wide group of plant products. The group takes its name from the power of these products to turn raw hide into leather. They dissolve in water, and their solutions taste sharp and test acid. Iron salts turn the solutions dark blue or green, a trait used in the making of ink. Much about their inner make-up is still not known, the article says.

Some tannins seem to be glucosides of gallic acid, since they yield that acid and a sugar when split by water. Others yield proto-catechuic acid and phloroglucin. Common tannin is a digallic acid that makes up 50 per cent of gall-nuts. It is also found in tea, sumach, and other plants. It can be drawn from crushed gall-nuts with a mix of ether and alcohol. When pure, it forms a colourless, loose mass.
britannica-1911-tin:
Tin is a soft white metal known since the dawn of the past, as part of bronze. When the pure metal first came in use can not be fixed with care. The tin of old books may in fact be a mix of brass like stuff. Greek words for it shift in sense with time.

Romans in Plinys day did not part tin from lead with care, and gave it a name that means white lead. The chief ore is a stone that holds most of the trade worth. It is found in veins by hard rock and as loose grains in stream beds. Rock mates of the ore are listed in full.
britannica-1911-torell-otto-martin:
Otto Martin Torell was a Swedish geologist who lived from eighteen twenty eight to nineteen hundred. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Varberg, he was educated at Lund for the medical trade. Zeal for animal and earth studies soon drew him to science instead.

Torell held means of his own and gave his life to research work. He studied ice age shifts and the beasts with no backbones first. Glacier study took him to Switzerland, Spitzbergen, and Greenland on two trips. In eighteen sixty six he became a teacher of zoology at Lund. In eighteen seventy one he took charge of the Swedish Geological Survey.
britannica-1911-train:
Train is a word study article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from a Latin root meaning to drag or draw. In general it names anything drawn or trailed behind something else, or the rear part of a thing. So it is used for the lengthened back part of a skirt, robe, or cloak.

In state processions, pages or official bearers hold up the train of a ruler's robes, the entry notes. Rules from the lord chamberlain fix how long a train ladies wear at court. The word has sharper uses too. It can name the trail of a gun carriage that rests on the ground. It can also name a line of gunpowder laid to fire a charge, or, in a figure, an ordered series of things.
britannica-1911-tuticorin:
Tuticorin is a seaport of British India in the Madras lands. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its pearls, port rank, and mills. It is the south end of the South Indian railway. A daily steamer links it with Colombo in Ceylon.

Its count in 1901 was about twenty-eight thousand people. The Dutch held the old town for a long period. A large Roman Catholic share marks its people still. Pearl banks once made it famed across the south seas. Those banks ran from Cape Comorin to the Pamban Channel. Deepening of that channel in 1895 thinned the oyster yield. Conch shells still ship out to Bengal in trade. Rail growth since 1875 raised it to second port of Madras. Rice, cotton, tea, and spices lead its exports today.
britannica-1911-urotropin:
Urotropin is a drug article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a medicine made from ammonia and formaldehyde. In the United States it was sold as Uritone. It is a mass of colourless crystals that dissolve freely in water. The article ranks it among the strongest cleaners of the urinary tract.

Men once thought it worked by freeing formaldehyde in the urine. Research by Cammidge showed that this is not so. The drug is used when the urine is alkaline, loaded with phosphates, or foul. It thus helps in cases of bladder inflammation, and it is mildly helpful in passing water. Its great use, the article says, is in clearing the urine of typhoid patients. That stops the spread of the fever by so-called typhoid carriers. Like drugs, such as cystamine and helmitol, close the account.
britannica-1911-wettin:
The 1911 Britannica article on Wettin traces a great German family. Several royal houses of Europe sprang from it. The family took its name from a castle by a small town on the Saale river. Attempts to trace the line to the Saxon chief Widukind have failed. The earliest known ancestor is Dietrich. He was killed fighting the Hungarians in 982.

The article follows the family's lands and feuds. Its members became margraves of Meissen. The county of Wettin itself was sold in 1288. The buyer was the archbishop of Magdeburg. At their height the Wettin lands stretched from the Oder to the Werra. In 1889 Dresden celebrated 800 years of Wettin rule. The festival marked the family's long hold on Meissen and Saxony.
britannica-1911-whichcote-benjamin:
Benjamin Whichcote is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1609 at Whichcote Hall in Shropshire, he was an English churchman and thinker. He was schooled at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and became a fellow there in 1633.

The article follows his posts in church and college. He lectured at Trinity Church in Cambridge and took livings in Somerset and near Cambridge. In 1644 he became head of King's College, and in 1650 he served as vice chancellor. Cromwell sought his advice on fair treatment for the Jews. At the Restoration he lost his college post for his Puritan views. He is held to be the founder of the Cambridge Platonists, a famed school of thought. His works came out after his death.
britannica-1911-wieland-christoph-martin:
Wieland, Christoph Martin is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German poet and man of letters. He was born at Oberholzheim, near Biberach, on the fifth of September 1733 and died in 1813. His father was the village pastor and took great pains with the boy's schooling. Before fourteen he moved to a noted school near Magdeburg.

He was an early, quick child. When he left school in 1749 he was well read in the Latin classics and in modern French writers. Among German poets he loved Brockes and Klopstock best. At home in the summer of 1750 he fell in love with a kinswoman, Sophie Gutermann. That love spurred him to verse, and he planned his first large work, a teaching poem in six books.
bruno-de-magia-latin:
Giordano Bruno wrote De Magia, on magic, in Latin near the end of his wandering life, around 1590. Bruno treats magic as the art of bonds. All things, he argues, are linked by attractions and sympathies, and the magus works by knowing and pulling those links.

 His system sorts magic into kinds and traces how images, words, and desires bind souls. The treatise is the philosophical peak of Renaissance magic theory. Bruno the thinker of infinite worlds stands behind every page. Burned at Rome in 1600, he left this calm, daring account of his art. Readers meet the mind for which the cosmos itself was the great web of bonds.
c-f-meyer-die-richterin:
A woman holds the power of justice in Charlemagne's age and must judge her own family's crimes. C. F. Meyer's Die Richterin, given here in German, builds its tragedy around Stemma, the judge of its title. Few heroines in German fiction carry her sternness and sorrow in equal measure.

Guilt and atonement govern the plot, as hidden sins surface under her own tribunal. Meyer writes the early medieval world with his usual lapidary force, every scene cut clean. Stemma's strength is real, and so is the price it exacts from her heart. Critics call the novella the master's late masterpiece. Magnificently written, it closes his career on a note of stern, tragic grandeur.
canon-episcopi-latin:
The Canon Episcopi is a church law text from around 900, passed down through Regino of Prüm's collection. It treats the belief that certain women ride at night with Diana or Herodias. The canon declares the night flight an illusion worked by demons, not a bodily fact.
